item.description: Highlighting the egg library's use for program optimization, synthesis, and verification in academic and industrial projects.
item.content:encoded:
Abstract

E-graphs, originally developed for use in automated theorem provers, are data structures that compactly represent a large number of expressions and the equalities between them. Recently, a technique called equality saturation adapted e-graphs for program optimization. Equality saturation can ameliorate issues with traditional, destructive term rewriting since e-graph rewriting only adds information to the e-graph. After rewriting, the e-graph represents a large space of equivalent terms (including the original term), and a final extraction procedure selects the best term according to a user-provided cost function.

The egg library is a fast and flexible open source implementation of e-graphs and equality saturation. Unlike solvers, egg is a white-box library for programmatic use. Users can easily define their own languages, rewrites, and analyses, and they can inspect and manipulate the e-graph directly. It incorporates novel techniques such as e-class analysis, a mechanism for integrating program analyses modulo equality; and rebuilding, a deferred invariant restoration algorithm. egg has been used in hundreds of academic and industrial projects for program optimization, synthesis, and verification in many domains; some are briefly highlighted in this article.

1. Introduction

Equality graphs (e-graphs)15 are data structures that can compactly represent a large number of expressions and the equalities between them. They were originally developed for use in automated theorem provers. One prominent use case is in satisfiability modulo theory (SMT) solvers,1 where e-graphs are used to communicate equality information between different decision procedures via the Nelson-Oppen framework.16

More recently, Tate et al.21 proposed equality saturation, a technique that repurposes e-graphs for rewrite-driven program optimizations. Given an input program p, equality saturation constructs an e-graph E that represents a large set of programs equivalent to p, and then extracts the “best” program from E. The e-graph is grown by repeatedly applying pattern-based rewrites. Critically, these rewrites only add information to the e-graph, eliminating the need for careful ordering that can plague traditional, destructive term rewriting. Upon reaching a fixed point (saturation), E will represent all equivalent ways to express p with respect to the given rewrites. After saturation or a timeout, a final extraction procedure analyzes E and selects the optimal program according to a user-provided cost function.

In principle, equality saturation is an appealingly simple and general approach to program optimization. However, there are many practical challenges, ranging from performance to extensibility. For example, certain common usage patterns can cause e-graphs to grow very large or require domain-specific reasoning that cannot be expressed as syntactic rewrites. It is not feasible to provide a one-size-fits-all implementation of equality saturation, where users can simply plug in their rewrites and get out the best program.

This article describes the egg library, a fast and flexible implementation of e-graphs and equality saturation. egg does not aim to present a solver-like interface as a black-box decision procedure. Instead, egg provides the e-graph à la carte: as a generic data structure, along with a suite of algorithms for manipulating it. Users can easily define a language consisting of their own operators and types, rewrite rules, cost functions for extraction, and analyses to be integrated into the e-graph. egg emphasizes extensibility and programmability; users may inspect and manipulate e-graphs directly, and unused features do not incur overhead. egg is developed openly on GitHub,a is implemented in Rust, and is packaged on Rust’s package registry, crates.io.

To provide this flexibility, egg incorporates two novel techniques that make e-graphs fast and extensible: rebuilding and e-class analysis. Rebuilding is a new amortized algorithm for maintaining e-graph invariants that allows the client to choose when to restore invariants. This is particularly useful for equality saturation, which egg factors into distinct phases of reading and writing the e-graph for increased performance. e-class analysis is a general mechanism for integrating domain-specific analyses into the e-graph. This allows bringing program analyses like interval analysis, constant folding, and others to the e-graph, reducing the need for ad hoc extensions. These analyses operate modulo equality, which can increase their precision.

egg provides all the pieces to build an equality saturation engine, and many users have done so in diverse domains including tensor programs,24 floating point accuracy,17 circuit-level optimizers,6 and databases10 across both academia and industry. Due to its à la carte design, users have rearranged these pieces to build program synthesizers3 and verification tools11 as well that do not neatly fit the equality saturation mold. This article will highlight some of these use cases.

2. Background

E-graphs have been defined in many ways in the literature. Our presentation reflects egg’s design and implementation.

2.1 E-graphs as data structures. 

Intuitively, an e-graph is a set of equivalence classes (e-classes). Each e-class is a set of e-nodes representing equivalent terms from a given language, and an e-node is a function symbol paired with a list of children e-classes. More precisely:

Definition 1 (E-graph).

Given the definitions and syntax in Figure 1, an e-graph is a tuple ( U , H ) where:

  • A union-find data structure20 U stores an equivalence relation (denoted with ≡id) over e-class ids.

  • The hashcons H is a map from e-nodes to e-class ids.

Definition 2 (find).

A union-find U provides a find operation that canonicalizes e-class ids. We omit the first argument of find where clear from context.

  • find(U,a)=find(U,b) iff a≡idb.

  • An e-class id a is canonical iff find(a)=a.

  • An e-node n is canonical iff n=canonicalize(n), where canonicalize maps find over n’s children.

Definition 3 (E-class).

For an e-graph (U,H), define M to map an e-class id to an e-class, i.e., the set of equivalent e-nodes. This is the inverse of the hashcons H:

M [ a ] = { n | H [ n ] ≡ id a }

Note that an e-class has an identity (its canonical e-class id), but an e-node does not. We use e-class id a and the e-class M[a] synonymously when clear from the context.

Definition 4 (Representation).

An e-graph, e-class, or e-node is said to represent a term t if t can be “found” within it. Representation is defined recursively:

  • An e-graph represents t if any of its e-classes do.

  • An e-class c represents t if any e-node n∈cdoes.

  • An e-node f(a1,a2,...) represents a term f(t1,t2,...) with the same function symbol if each e-class M[ai] represents term ti.

When each e-class is a singleton (containing only one e-node), an e-graph is essentially a term graph with sharing. Figure 2a shows an e-graph representing the term (a×2)/2.

Definition 5 (The Congruence Invariant).

The hashcons H must map all canonical e-nodes to their e-class ids. In other words: e – n o d e   n ∈ M [ a ] ⇔ H [ c a n o n i c a l i z e ( n ) ] = f i n d ( a )

If the invariant holds, then a procedure lookup can quickly find which e-class (if any) has an e-node equivalent to a given e-node n: lookup(n)=H[canonicalize(n)]. Note that while the invariant is stated in terms of the hashcons, it implies the e-graph is not only an equivalence relation but also a congruence relation.

E-graphs provide two main low-level mutating operations:

  • add takes an e-node n and returns the id a of the e-class representing n if it exists, else creates a new e-class for n and returns its id.

  • merge (sometimes called assert or union) takes two e-class ids a and b, unions them in the union-find U, and combines the e-classes by setting both M[a] and M[b] to M[a]∪M[b].

Both of these operations must take additional steps to maintain the congruence invariant. Invariant maintenance is discussed in Section 4.

2.2 E-matching and rewriting.

E-graphs can be queried via e-matching7,8 (pattern matching modulo equivalence). The e-matching operation ematch takes a pattern p with variable placeholders (see Figure 1) and returns a list of tuples (σ,c) where σ is a substitution of variables to e-class ids such that p[σ] is represented in e-class c. E-matching only needs to return tuples where the e-class ids are canonical.

E-matching can be implemented in many ways: via simple recursion over the pattern8 all the way to optimized relational joins.25 egg uses a backtracking virtual machine similar to that in Z3.7

These operations can be composed to perform rewriting over the e-graph. To apply a rewrite pℓ→pr to an e-graph, ematch finds tuples (σ,c) where e-class c represents pℓ[σ]. Then, for each tuple, merge(c, add(pr[σ])) adds pr[σ] to the e-graph and unifies it with the matching e-class c.

Figure 2 shows an e-graph undergoing a series of rewrites. Note how the process is only additive; the initial term (a×2)/2 is still represented in the e-graph. Rewriting in an e-graph can also saturate, meaning the e-graph has learned every possible equivalence derivable from the given rewrites. If the user tried to apply x×y→y×x to an e-graph twice, the second time would add no additional e-nodes and perform no new merges; the e-graph can detect this and stop applying that rule.

2.3 Equality saturation.

Term rewriting is a time-tested approach for equational reasoning; it is employed in most tools that manipulate programs (e.g., compilers, theorem provers, and so on). In the conventional setting, term rewriting is typically destructive and “forgets” the matched left-hand side. Consider applying a simple rewrite:

( a × 2 ) / 2 → ( a ≪ 1 ) / 2

The new term carries no information about the initial term. Applying this rewrite at this point prevents us from canceling out 2/2. In the compilers community, this classically tricky question of when to apply which rewrite is called the phase-ordering problem.

One solution lies in manipulating the rewrites themselves into a convergent rewriting system where no matter the order of rewrites, the same final term is reached. When that is not possible, another approach to the phase-ordering problem would be to simply apply all rewrites simultaneously, keeping track of every expression seen. This eliminates the problem of choosing the right rule, but a naive implementation would require space exponential in the number of given rewrites. Equality saturation21 is a technique to do this non-destructive rewriting efficiently using an e-graph.

Figure 3 shows the equality-saturation workflow. First, an initial e-graph is created from the input term. The core of the algorithm runs a set of rewrite rules until the e-graph is saturated (or a timeout is reached). Finally, a procedure called extraction selects the optimal represented term according to some cost function. For simple cost functions, extraction resembles finding a shortest path in a (hyper)graph and be solved greedily.13 For more complex cost functions, approaches based on integer linear programming or stochastic methods have recently been proposed.22,23 egg provides some of these extraction methods and also allows users to implement their own.

3. E-graph Extensions

egg provides several mechanisms that allow e-graphs and equality saturation to apply to a wider variety of problems.

3.1 E-class analysis.

As discussed so far, e-graphs provide an efficient way to implement a non-destructive term-rewriting system. However, program analysis, optimization, or verification may require more than just syntactic rewriting. Instead, transformations can depend on not only the input terms but also semantic facts about that input term, for example, constant value, free variables, nullability, numerical sign, size in memory, and so on. This “purely syntactic” restriction forced previous equality-saturation applications17,21 to resort to ad hoc passes over the e-graph to implement common analyses, such as constant folding.

egg provides a novel mechanism called an e-class analysis to lift a program analysis over the e-graph. An e-class analysis resembles abstract interpretation lifted to the e-graph level, attaching analysis data from a semilattice to each e-class. The e-graph maintains and propagates this data as e-classes get merged and new e-nodes are added (details about maintenance in Section 4). Analysis data can be used directly to modify the e-graph, to inform how or if rewrites apply their right-hand sides, or to determine the cost of terms during the extraction process.

An e-class analysis defines a domain D and associates a value dc∈D to each e-class c. The interface of an e-class analysis is as follows, where G refers to the e-graph, and n and c refer to e-nodes and e-classes within G:

  • make ( n ) → d c

    When a new e-node n is added to G, construct a new value dc∈D to be associated with n’s e-class c, typically by accessing the associated data of n’s children.

  • join ( d c 1 , d c 2 ) → d c

    When e-classes c1,c2 are being merged into c, join dc1,dc2 into a new value dc to be associated with the new e-class c.

  • modify(c)→c′ (optional)

    Modify the e-class c based on dc. A typical use would be to add an e-node to c based on dc.

The domain D together with the join operation should form a join-semilattice. The semilattice perspective is useful for defining the analysis invariant (where ∨ is the join operation):

∀ c ∈ G . d c = ⋁ n ∈ c make ( n ) and modify ( c ) = c

The first part of the analysis invariant states that the data associated with each e-class must be the join of the make for every e-node in that e-class. Since D is a join-semilattice, this means that ∀c,∀n∈c,dc≥make(n). The motivation for the second part is more subtle. Since the analysis can modify an e-class through the modify method, the analysis invariant asserts that these modifications are driven to a fixed point. When the analysis invariant holds, a client looking at the analysis data can be assured that the analysis is “stable” in the sense that recomputing make, join, and modify will not modify the e-graph or any analysis data.

Consider the following example of an interval e-class analysis from Coward et. al.,5 which demonstrates how e-class analyses can combine with equality reasoning to derive more precise information. Let our language be arithmetic expressions, and the analysis domain D be the set of intervals. Consider the following expressions over variables x and y, where x∈[0,1] and y∈[1,2].

x – y x + y ∈ [ – 2 , 0 ] 2 x x + y – 1 ∈ [ – 1 , 1 ]

When these expressions are added to the e-graph, the analysis data for their respective e-classes will be computed by the make function, which computes the interval for an e-node based on the intervals of its children using basic interval arithmetic. Initially, since the variables x and y have known intervals, the analysis data for the above terms will be [–2,0] and [–1,1] as shown above.

E-class analyses react to e-class merges by join-ing the analysis data of the merged e-classes. So, if rewriting discovers that the two above expressions are equivalent (they are), the e-classes will be merged, and the analysis data for the new e-class will be the join of intervals for the merged e-classes. In our interval domain, the join operation is the interval intersection, since if we know that two equivalent terms have intervals, they both must lie in both intervals. So the new analysis data for the merged e-class will be [–1,0], which is more precise than either of the original intervals. The modify function is not needed in this example, but if an expression’s interval were found to be a singleton [c,c], it could add the constant c to the e-class.

3.2 Conditional and dynamic rewrites.

In equality saturation applications, many rewrites are purely syntactic. egg supports these as well as more general notions of rewriting with its notion searchers and appliers. A searcher is a piece of code that inspects a part of the e-graph and produces a set of matches (substitutions). An applier takes a match and modifies the e-graph in some way. For a typical syntactic rewrite, both the searcher and applier would be a pattern; the searcher would e-match the left-hand pattern, and the applier would instantiate the right-hand pattern.

In some cases, additional data may be needed to determine if or how to perform the rewrite. For example, the rewrite x/x→1 is only valid if x≠0. This is an example of a conditional rewrite, where the validity of the rewrite depends on some analysis data. To safely implement this rewrite, an e-class analysis can track whether an e-class is known to be non-zero, and the rewrite can check this fact before applying the right-hand side.

A more complex dynamic rewrite may need to compute the right-hand side based on the substitution or analysis facts from the left-hand side. In these instances, the applier could be a piece of code that takes in the match and manipulates the e-graph to add a new term. Searchers can also be implemented as arbitrary code, allowing for more complex matching behavior. For example, industrial user Cube Dev employs custom searchers and appliers in their use of egg for SQL rewriting.10

3.3 Extraction.

As shown in Figure 3, equality saturation typically ends with extraction. Extraction selects a represented term from a given e-class (typically the same e-class as the input term) that is optimal according to some cost function.

In many applications, AST size (optionally weighted by operators) suffices as a simple cost function. For simple cost functions like this, a greedy algorithm suffices to find the optimal term.13 egg provides built-in support for this extraction algorithm that is modular with respect to the cost function.

Extraction can be formulated as an e-class analysis when the cost function is simple. The analysis data is a tuple (n,k(n)), where n is the cheapest e-node in that e-class and k(n) its cost. The make(n) operation calculates the cost k(n) based on the analysis data (which contains the minimum costs) of n’s children. The merge operation simply takes the tuple with lower cost. The semilattice portion of the analysis invariant then guarantees that the analysis data will contain the lowest-cost e-node in each class. Extraction can then proceed recursively; if the analysis data for e-class c gives f(c1,c2,...) as the optimal e-node, the optimal term represented in c is extract(c)=f(extract(c1),extract(c2),...). This not only further demonstrates the generality of e-class analyses but also provides the ability to do extraction “on the fly”; conditional and dynamic rewrites can determine their behavior based on the cheapest term in an e-class.

Extraction (whether done as a separate pass or an e-class analysis) can also benefit from the analysis data. Typically, a local cost function can only look at the function symbol of the e-node n and the costs of n’s children. When an e-class analysis is attached to the e-graph, however, a cost function may observe the data associated with n’s e-class, as well as the data associated with n’s children. This allows a cost function to depend on computed facts rather than just purely syntactic information. In other words, the cost of an operator may differ based on its inputs. Applications in linear algebra and tensor programming22 have exploited this feature; the cost of an operation depends on the shapes of its inputs, which are tracked by an e-class analysis.

For more complex cost functions, extraction cannot be done greedily. Some applications have therefore explored alternative extraction algorithms, including integer linear programming, GPU-based differentiable optimization,2 and stochastic methods.

4. Rebuilding Invariants

Like many data structures, an e-graph has invariants that a client can expect to be maintained. For egg, these are the congruence invariant (definition 5)—ensuring the e-graphs equivalence relation is a congruence relation—and the e-class analysis invariant (Section 3).

Traditionally,8,15 e-graphs maintain invariants after each operation. This is done with a worklist algorithm that “upward merges” e-classes whose parents may now be congruent whenever two e-classes are merged.12

Part of egg’s take on e-graphs as a data structure loosens the requirement that these invariants always hold. egg allows these to be temporarily violated and provides a mechanism called rebuilding to restore them. The client is responsible for calling the rebuild method at appropriate times to restore the invariants. This deferred approach can significantly improve performance by amortizing the cost of maintaining the invariants. In the empirical evaluation in the full paper, congruence is 88× faster, and equality saturation is 21× faster (in aggregate over all tests using geometric mean), when deferring invariant maintenance with rebuilding.

4.1 Rebuilding and equality saturation.

egg provides a modified equality saturation algorithm to take advantage of rebuilding. Figure 32 shows pseudocode for both traditional equality saturation21 and egg’s variant, which exhibits two key differences:

  1. Each iteration is split into a read phase, which searches for all the rewrite matches, and a write phase that applies those matches.

  2. Rebuilding occurs only once per iteration, at the end.

egg’s separation of the read and write phases means rewrites are truly unordered. In traditional equality saturation, later rewrites in the given rewrite list are favored in the sense that they can “see” the results of earlier rewrites in the same iteration. Therefore, the results depend on the order of the rewrite list if saturation is not reached (which is common on large rewrite lists or input expressions). egg’s equality saturation algorithm is invariant to the order of the rewrite list.

Separating the read and write phases allows egg to safely defer rebuilding. If rebuilding were deferred in the traditional equality-saturation algorithm, rules later in the rewrite list would be searched against an e-graph with broken invariants. Since congruence may not hold, there may be missing equivalences, resulting in missing matches. The separation also allows the read phase to be parallelized, since it is read-only.

4.2 Rebuilding example.

Deferred rebuilding speeds up congruence maintenance by amortizing the work of maintaining the congruence invariant. Consider the following terms in an e-graph:

f 1 ( x ) , . . . , f n ( x ) , y 1 , . . . , y n

Let the workload be merge(x,y1),...,merge(x,yn). Each merge may change the canonical representation of the fi(x)s, so the traditional invariant maintenance strategy could require O(n2) hashcons updates. With deferred rebuilding, the merges happen before the congruence invariant is restored, requiring no more than O(n) hashcons updates. The full version of this paper includes more details and experimental validation that rebuilding provides speedups.

4.3 Maintaining the analysis invariant.

egg’s rebuilding procedure is based on the standard congruence closure algorithm.12 We have extended the algorithm to also maintain the e-class analysis invariant described in Section 3. The essence is the same: When an equality is added via merge, the analysis data of e-classes whose e-nodes mention the merged e-classes may need to be updated. The rebuilding algorithm restores the analysis invariant at the same time as it restores the congruence invariant using a shared worklist.

egg’s implementation of e-class analyses assumes the analysis domain D is indeed a semilattice and that modify is idempotent. Without these properties, egg may fail to restore the analysis invariant on rebuild, or it may not terminate.

5. Case Studies

This section relates three projects from diverse domains that were early adopters of egg. In all three cases, the developers had first rolled their own e-graph implementations. egg allowed them to delete code, gain performance, and in some cases dramatically broaden the project’s scope thanks to egg’s speed and flexibility. In addition to gaining performance, all three projects use egg’s novel extensibility features, such as e-class analyses and dynamic/conditional rewrites. Section 24 briefly presents more recent applications of egg.

5.1 Improving floating point accuracy.

Herbie automatically improves accuracy for floating-point expressions, using random sampling to measure error, a set of rewrite rules for generating program variants, and algorithms that prune and combine program variants to achieve minimal error. Herbie received PLDI 2015’s Distinguished Paper award17 and has been continuously developed since then, sporting hundreds of Github stars, hundreds of downloads, and thousands of users on its online version. Herbie uses e-graphs for algebraic simplification of mathematical expressions, which is especially important for avoiding floating-point errors introduced by cancellation, function inverses, and redundant computation.

Until our case study, Herbie used a custom e-graph implementation written in Racket (Herbie’s implementation language) that closely followed traditional e-graph implementations. With timeouts disabled, e-graph-based simplification consumed the vast majority of Herbie’s run time. As a fix, Herbie sharply limits the simplification process, placing a size limit on the e-graph itself and a time limit on the whole procedure. When the timeout is exceeded, simplification fails altogether. Furthermore, the Herbie authors knew of several features they believed would improve Herbie’s output but could not be implemented because they required more calls to simplification and would thus introduce unacceptable slowdowns. Taken together, slow simplification reduced Herbie’s performance, completeness, and efficacy.

Implementation.  We implemented a egg simplification backend for Herbie. The egg back end is more than 3000× faster than Herbie’s initial simplifier and has been used by default as of Herbie 1.4. Herbie has also backported some of egg’s features, such as batch simplification and rebuilding to its Racket-based e-graph implementation (which is still usable, just not the default), demonstrating the portability of egg’s conceptual improvements.

Herbie is implemented in Racket while egg is in Rust; the egg simplification backend is thus implemented as a Rust library that imports egg and provides a C-level API for Herbie to access via foreign-function interface. The Rust library defines the Herbie expression grammar (with named constants, numeric constants, variables, and operations) as well as the e-class analysis necessary to do constant folding. The library is implemented in roughly 500 lines of Rust.

Herbie’s set of rewrite rules is not fixed; users can leverage command-line flags to select which rewrites to use. Herbie serializes the rewrites to strings, and the egg back end parses and instantiates them on the Rust side.

Herbie separates exact and inexact program constants—exact operations on exact constants (such as the addition of two rational numbers) are evaluated and added to the e-graph, while operations on inexact constants or that yield inexact outputs are not. We thus split numeric constants in the Rust-side grammar between exact rational numbers and inexact constants, which are described by an opaque identifier, and transformed Racket-side expressions into this form before serializing them and passing them to the Rust driver. To evaluate operations on exact constants, we used the constant folding e-class analysis to track the “exact value” of each e-class. Every time an operation e-node is added to the egg e-graph, we check whether all arguments to that operation have exact value (using the analysis data), and if so, perform rational-number arithmetic to evaluate it. The e-class analysis is cleaner than the corresponding code in Herbie’s implementation, which is a built-in pass over the entire e-graph.

Results.  Our egg simplification back end is a drop-in replacement to the existing Herbie simplifier, making it easy to compare speed and results. We compare using Herbie’s standard test suite of roughly 500 benchmarks, with timeouts disabled. Figure 5 shows the results. The egg simplification back end is more than 3000× faster than Herbie’s initial simplifier. This speed-up eliminated Herbie’s largest bottleneck: The initial implementation dominated Herbie’s total run-time at 98.1%, backporting egg improvements into Herbie cuts that to about half the total run-time, and egg simplification takes less than 5% of the total run time. Practically, the run-time of Herbie’s initial implementation was smaller, since timeouts cause tests failures when simplification takes too long. Therefore, the speedup also improved Herbie’s completeness, as simplification now never times out.

Since incorporating egg into Herbie, the Herbie developers have backported some of egg’s key performance improvements into the Racket e-graph implementation. First, batch simplification provides a large speed-up because Herbie simplifies many similar expressions. When done simultaneously in one equality saturation, the e-graph’s structural sharing can massively deduplicate work. Second, deferring rebuilding (as discussed in Section 4) provides a further 2.2× speedup.

5.2 Optimizing linear algebra.

Spores22 is an optimizer for machine learning (ML) programs. It translates linear algebra (LA) expressions to relational algebra (RA), performs rewrites, and finally translates the result back to linear algebra. Spores performs holistic optimization, taking into account the complex interactions among factors like sparsity, common subexpressions, and fusible operators and their impact on execution time.

Implementation.  Spores is implemented entirely in Rust using egg. Spores works in three steps: First, it translates the input LA expression to RA; second, it optimizes the RA expression by equality saturation; and finally, it translates the optimized RA expression back to LA. The translation between LA and RA is straightforward; we will focus discussion on the equality saturation step in RA.

Spores represents a relation as a function from tuples to real numbers: A:(a1,a2,...,an)→R. This is similar to the index notation in linear algebra, where a matrix A can be viewed as a function λi,j.Aij. A tuple is identified with a named record, for example, (1,2)={a1:1,a2:2}={a2:2,a1:1}, so that order in a tuple does not matter. There are just three operations on relations: join, union, and aggregate. Join (⊗) takes two relations and returns their natural join, multiplying the associated real number for joined tuples:

A ⊗ B = λ a ¯ ∪ b ¯ . A ( a ¯ ) × B ( b ¯ )

Here, a¯ is the set of field names for the records in A. In RA terminology, a¯ is the schema of A. Union (⊕) is a join in disguise: It also performs natural join on its two arguments but adds the associated real instead of multiplying it:

A ⊕ B = λ a ¯ ∪ b ¯ . A ( a ¯ ) + B ( b ¯ )

Finally, aggregate (Σ) sums its argument along a given dimension. It coincides precisely with the “sigma notation” in mathematics:

∑ a i A = λ a ¯ – a i . ∑ a i A ( a ¯ )

Spores uses rewrites based on the fundamental identities of RA (see the full paper for details). In addition to these, Spores also supports replacing expressions with fused operators. For example, (X–UV)2 can be replaced by sqloss(X,U,V), which streams values from X,U,V and computes the result without creating intermediate matrices. Each of these fused operators is encoded with a rewrite in egg.

Some rewrites require a way to access the schema (similar to dimensions of a matrix) of an expression during optimization. Spores uses an e-class analysis to annotate e-classes with the appropriate schema. It also leverages the e-class analysis for cost estimation, using a conservative cost model that over-approximates. As a result, equivalent expressions may have different cost estimates. The merge operation on the analysis data takes the lower cost, incrementally improving the cost estimate. Finally, Spores’ e-class analysis also performs constant folding. As a whole, the e-class analysis is a composition of three smaller analyses in a similar style to the product of lattices in abstract interpretation.

Results.  Compared to a conventional baseline, Spores is able to derive all of 84 handwritten rules and heuristics for sum-product optimization. It also discovered novel rewrites that contribute to 1.2× to 5× speed-up in end-to-end experiments. With greedy extraction, all compilations completed within a second.

5.3 Decompiling 3D CAD.

Several tools have emerged that reverse-engineer high-level computer-aided design (CAD) models from polygon meshes and voxels. The output of these tools are constructive solid geometry (CSG) programs. A CSG program comprises 3D solids, such as cubes, spheres, cylinders; affine transformations, such as scale, translate, rotate (which take a 3D vector and a CSG expression as arguments); and binary operator, such as union, intersection, and difference that combine CSG expressions. For repetitive models such as a gear, CSG programs can be too long and therefore difficult to comprehend. A recent tool, Szalinski,14 extracts the inherent structure in the CSG outputs of mesh decompilation tools by automatically inferring maps and folds. Szalinski accomplished this using egg’s extensible equality-saturation system, allowing it to:

  • Discover structure using loop rerolling rules. This allows Szalinski to infer functional patterns like Fold, Map2, Repeat, and Tabulate from flat CSG inputs.

  • Identify equivalence among CAD terms expressed as different expressions by mesh decompilers. Szalinski accomplishes this by using CAD identities. An example of one such CAD identity in Szalinski is e rotate [0 0 0] e. This implies that any CAD expression e is equivalent to a CAD expression that applies a rotation by zero degrees about x, y, and z axes to e.

  • Use external solvers to speculatively add potentially profitable expressions to the e-graph. Mesh decompilers often generate CSG expressions that order and/or group list elements in non-intuitive ways. To recover structure from such expressions, a tool like Szalinski must be able to reorder and regroup lists that expose any latent structure.

Implementation.  egg supports Szalinski’s CAD language in a straightforward manner. Szalinski uses purely syntactic rewrites to express CAD identities and some loop rerolling rules (like inferring a Fold from a list of CAD expressions). Critically, Szalinski relies on egg’s dynamic rewrites and e-class analysis to infer functions for lists.

Consider the flat CSG program in Figure 6b. A structure-finding rewrite first rewrites the flat list of Unions to:

(Fold Union (Map2 Translate
            [(0 0 0) (2 0 0) ...]
            (Repeat Cube 5)))

The list of vectors is stored as Cons elements (sugared above for brevity). Szalinski uses an e-class analysis to track the accumulated lists in a similar style to constant folding. Then, a dynamic rewrite uses an arithmetic solver to rewrite the concrete list of 3D vectors in the analysis data to:

(Tabulate (i 5) ((* 2 i) 0 0)).

A final set of syntactic rewrites can hoist the Tabulate, yielding the result on the right of Figure 6. Thanks to the set of syntactic CAD rewrites, this structure finding even works in the face of CAD identities. For example, the original program may omit the no-op Translate (0 0 0), even though it is necessary to see repetitive structure.

In many cases, the repetitive structure of input CSG expression is further obfuscated because subexpressions may appear in arbitrary order. For these inputs, the arithmetic solvers must first reorder the expressions to find a closed form, such as a Tabulate as shown in Figure 6. However, reordering a list does not preserve equivalence, so adding it to the e-class of the concrete list would be unsound. Szalinski therefore introduces inverse transformations, a novel technique that allows solvers to speculatively reorder and regroup list elements to find a closed form. The solvers annotate the potentially profitable expression with the permutation or grouping that led to the successful discovery of the closed form. Later in the rewriting process, syntactic rewrites eliminate the inverse transformations when possible (e.g., reordering lists under a Fold Union can be eliminated). egg supports this novel technique without modification.

Results.  Szalinski’s initial prototype used a custom e-graph written in OCaml. Switching to egg removed most of the code, eliminated bugs, facilitated the key contributions of solver-backed rewrites and inverse transformations, and made the tool about 1000× faster. egg’s performance allowed a shift from running on small, hand-picked examples to a comprehensive evaluation on more than 2,000 real-world models from a 3D model-sharing forum.

6. Discussion

egg is a flexible and efficient e-graph library that has been adopted in a variety of domains. Its primary technical novelties, rebuilding and e-class analyses, have enabled new applications of e-graphs and equality saturation. Its more prosaic contributions, such as generic, packaged, and documented implementation, have also been important to its adoption. We conclude here with a brief, non-exhaustive survey of some applications and research directions that have emerged since egg’s publication. More details on these topics can be found on the E-Graphs Community website.b

Impact in production systems.  egg has been used and influenced production systems as well as research prototypes. As a notable example, Cube Devc uses egg to rewrite SQL queries as part of its semantic layer product. This is the largest egg application known to us, involving thousands of rewrites, custom analyses, and other bespoke e-graph manipulations. egg has also influenced the design of the intermediate representation of the Cranelift compiler toolchain,9 which uses a variant of e-graphs in its mid-end optimizations.

Hardware.  Hardware design has emerged as a promising equality-saturation application domain since circuit-design tools are are generally willing to trade off more compile time for better results compared to software compilers. In particular, researchers at Intel developed a suite of System Verilog optimization and verification tools using egg.6 Applying these tools to production-level circuit designs, they demonstrated improvements to circuit power, performance, and area. At lower abstraction levels, hardware researchers have pushed the limits of equality-saturation scalability, generating e-graphs that contain hundreds of thousands of e-nodes.4

Verification and synthesis.  egg’s use cases are not limited to program optimization. Applications in program verification and synthesis have sometimes eschewed egg’s built-in equality saturation or extraction algorithm to better suit their needs. Examples include a tool for relational program verification via alignment,11 custom tactics in the Lean and Rocq theorem provers, and program-synthesis tools based on anti-unification.3

Extensions.  Since egg’s publication, researchers have explored various extensions and alternative implementations of e-graphs and equality saturation. These include egglog,25 a language-based approach to equality saturation based on Datalog; Colored e-graphs,19 an extension for reasoning about multiple nested equivalence relations; and Slotted e-graphs,18 which better support binding operators like lambdas and quantifiers.

Future directions.  egg owes a great deal to the work on e-graphs coming from the formal methods community. While their use cases for e-graphs differ from egg’s focus on optimization, we believe that there are many more opportunities to apply the innovations from either community to the other. Continuing this cross-pollination is likely to yield new insights and lead to better approaches to program optimization, synthesis, and verification.

Previously Published  This paper was originally published in Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 5, (Jan. 4, 2021).
