item.title: Technical Perspective: egg: ‘Ridiculously’ Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation
item.dc:creator: Nadia Polikarpova
item.description: By taking an implementation detail and turning it into a general mechanism for fixpoint computation over e-graphs, egg made equality saturation programmable, thereby unlocking a host of new applications.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes a great idea is born out of a bug—and that’s exactly how egg, the subject of the accompanying paper, was hatched. Back in 2019, Max Willsey, then a postdoc at the University of Washington, boasted to his advisor that he could make an advanced compiler technique called equality saturation run much faster by rewriting its implementation in Rust. If you were following programming-language trends at the time, you’ll recall that “rewriting in Rust” was touted as a universal cure for sluggish software—so much so that it became an Internet meme. And sure enough, the Rust version was fast. Suspiciously fast.

To see what went wrong (or rather, right), we need to take a step back. At the heart of equality saturation lies a clever data structure called an e-graph. If you know how an abstract syntax tree—or expression tree—represents a single program, an e-graph does the same for many equivalent variants of that program, compactly folding them into a single structure (so compact, in fact, that a finite e-graph can represent infinitely many variants!). Equality saturation uses e-graphs for program optimization: It keeps adding new equivalent program variants to the graph and eventually extracts the “best” one according to some metric. The catch is that adding each new variant can break the e-graph’s compactness property, and an expensive compaction step is required to restore it.

The first version of egg was fast because it skipped this compaction step—producing incorrect results. But while restoring it, Max had an epiphany: Why compact after every addition? Why not add a batch of variants first, then compact once? (The paper’s term for this batch compaction is rebuilding.) The idea seems obvious in hindsight, but no one had tried it before because e-graphs were originally invented for theorem proving, where they had to be compact at all times. When the data structure was later repurposed for program optimization, it simply had not occurred to anyone to change how its basic operations worked. Anyone, that is, until Max, an outsider to the theorem-proving world who simply didn’t know the “rules.”

Apart from making equality saturation faster, egg also made it easier to tweak. Willsey and co-authors noticed that compiler authors would often attach extra attributes to each program inside an e-graph, such as which variables it referenced or whether it could evaluate to zero; information needed to decide which optimizations could be applied. Keeping these attributes in sync as the e-graph evolved was painful and error-prone. In the best traditions of programming-language research, the egg authors recognized this recurring pattern and abstracted it into an elegant mechanism called e-class analyses. With an e-class analysis, one can define simple local rules for how program attributes should be initialized and merged, and the library automatically applies those rules in the right order and frequency to keep the e-graph globally consistent.

At this point, you might think: Alright, so we made a niche compiler optimization faster and cleaner—why should anyone else care? As it turned out, this paper sparked a full-blown e-graph revolution, spreading from compilers to fields far beyond. Since its 2021 debut, the egg library has been used in more than 30 research compilers and dozens of projects in areas ranging from theorem proving and hardware and software synthesis to carpentry and genome compression.a It even inspired a fundamentally new algorithm for relational joins in databasesb and a new programming paradigm for incremental fixpoint computation.c Today, an active community gathers at the annual EGRAPHS workshopd and in monthly online meetings. The meme, one might say, has come full circle: Instead of rewriting everything in Rust, researchers are now rewriting their tools in egg.

What made egg so successful? First, its authors invested an unreasonable—by research-project standards—amount of effort to make the library genuinely reusable: egg has a clean API and excellent documentation. Second, they devoted equal energy to nurturing the community: organizing workshops, forums, and meetings that have paid off manyfold. Third, egg embodies a classic virtue of programming-language research: turning hacks into elegant abstractions that reveal unexpected power. By taking an implementation detail and turning it into a general mechanism for fixpoint computation over e-graphs (e-class analyses), egg made equality saturation programmable, thereby unlocking a host of new applications.

And finally … egg is fast—ridiculously fast.

item.title: Time Served
item.dc:creator: CACM Staff
item.description: Professionals should be discussing whether AI is a trustworthy and efficient way to use the very powerful digital technology that has been developed.
item.content:encoded:
Both Sides of the Fence

I agree on the value of teaching computer science in prison, per Emma Hogan Benser’s May Communications Opinion cover article “We Must Teach Computer Science in Prison.” When I was at the University of Kansas in the 1970s, some faculty colleagues taught at Leavenworth Federal Correctional Institution: Has anyone done so earlier than we did?

A smart-aleck colleague began his first class there with “At last, a captive audience.” He was roundly booed.

Francis D. Tuggle,
Staunton, VA, USA

Regarding the May 2026 Communications cover story, “We Must Teach Computer Science in Prison,” the authors’ core assertion that people are incarcerated largely because they are poor and/or non-white is false. They are largely incarcerated because they have victimized others with criminal intent. Providing individuals with a criminally inclined temperament with a prone-to-abuse skill like computing is like providing them with firearms training or lock-picking skills. Doing so will cause further harm to innocent people and should not be a goal of ACM.

Aniket Joshi,
Catonsville, MD, USA

Author’s response:

The first part of this comment is a misinterpretation of one of my points: People are not necessarily incarcerated only because they are poor, or have darker skin, but there is extensive evidence that people continue to be surveilled, policed, and punished more harshly based on these factors.

As for whether it should be a goal of ACM to include people who have been incarcerated in our field, I think the reader’s comment underestimates human capacity for change. Research has shown that most people who are actually victims of crime favor more rehabilitative approaches to criminal justice, such as access to education, as opposed to more punitive forms of punishment. I do not think it is our role, as computer scientists, to decide the moral boundary for who should have access to computing knowledge, and, in the great majority of cases, I do not believe that any decision someone has made in the past should determine whether they can be a computer scientist in the future.

Emma Hogan Benser,
Annandale-on-Hudson, NY, USA

Reassociating the ‘A’ in ‘ACM’

In his May 2026 Communications Vardi’s Insights column, “The Centrality Fallacy and ACM,” Moshe Y. Vardi wrote: “while many European colleagues almost believe that the “A” in “ACM” stands for “American.” Could I make a plea that at least once in every Communications article ACM is spelled out in full as “Association for Computing Machinery”?

W.B. Langdon,
London, U.K.

Author’s response:

I agree with the letter.
Moshe Y. Vardi,
Houston, TX, USA

Wisdom Extraction

Everyone who reads newspapers knows about the kinds of AI achievements described by David Patterson in his reply to my letter (Communications, April 2026). AI developers have always been good about publicizing their successes. They are not as diligent about publicizing failures; those are now often belittled by the use of anthropomorphic labels such as “hallucination.”

However, success anecdotes are irrelevant to my assertion that AI offers no new capabilities. Nobody argues that AI approaches cannot sometimes do impressive things. However, anecdotes are not evidence that those problems could not be solved by conventional, more disciplined, programming. The fact that something has not been done before is not evidence that it could not have been done.

Recent AI work is clearly having impact. It has attracted a lot of public interest and huge investments. The question that professionals should be discussing is not whether AI systems can do something but whether AI is a trustworthy and efficient way to use the very powerful digital technology that we have developed.

AI will continue to attract funding and have demonstrable successes. However, unlike Patterson, I think we will never know whether the huge investment in AI has slowed progress. In the absence of parallel universes that would allow us to conduct controlled experiments, we will know what happened but not what other approaches would have achieved.

David Lorge Parnas,
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada

Time *x

Vinton G. Cerf’s April 2026 Communications Cerf’s Up column, “It’s about Time,” is timely as we have less than 12 years before Unix’s and Linux’s (*nix) original method of timekeeping will fail similarly to the Y2K bug.

Cerf’s suggestion of typed variables to ease this has been in use in *nix for decades as the C language time_t type. Some Communications readers have some software upgrades to do, some will need new hardware, some will be retired with only a home system or two to resolve.

Linux always has used a 64-bit int (time_t) for seconds since Jan. 1, 1970—the epoch, for 64-bit architectures. As of 2020 with version 5.6 a 64-bit int has been used for 32-bit architectures too. The GNU C Library used on Linux always supported 64-bit time_t on 64-bit architectures; on 32-bit hardware support was not added until August 2021 and must be compiled in when generating the object library.

FreeBSD uses a 64-bit time_t for all 32-bit and 64-bit hardware except 32 bit i386. Bill Joy’s Network File System (NFS) since December 2000 (version 4) uses 64-bit time_t. OpenBSD starting in May 2014 version 5.5 also uses a 64-bit int both on 64-bit and 32-bit machines. The ext4 filesystem (but not ext2 nor ext3) support 34 bits of time good till 2446, unless one deliberately created an ext4 file systems with inode sizes of only 128 bytes. Lastly, the LibC CTIME(3) routines fail in only 2,147,437,525 years even if time_t is good for 292 billion years. These routines convert seconds since 01/01/1970 to the broken out date and time. This is because they store the year in a 32 bit signed int (tm_year). Vint Cerf’s referenced web pages have lots more details.

I have created a C program to analyze a *nix system’s vulnerability to this problem in the OS, LibC, and mounted file systems. From a non-root account, preferably one created just for this, do
the following:
wget http://verysecurelinux.com/xtime.c
make xtime
./xtime

Bob Toxen,
Fort Lauderdale, Florida, USA

Author’s response:

Thanks so much for sharing this additional information. Plainly there are fixes for these problems. What one wonders about are the many devices that never get an upgrade and how they will affect systems they interact with as the rollovers actually happen.

Vinton G. Cerf,
McLean, VA, USA

item.title: The Weirdness of Agents
item.dc:creator: Vinton G. Cerf
item.description: We need to evolve the moral equivalent of digital brakes when automatic observation systems detect out-of-control LLM or agentic conditions.
item.content:encoded:
I have been thinking a lot about AI agents recently. Isn’t everyone? They plainly have great promise. They can potentially carry out any task that could be done online, especially if the tasks are achievable through a Web-based interface. One can imagine, however, there will be specialized agentic interfaces to make more efficient agent access to functional, Internet-based services. It is already clear that agent interactions may be carried out using newly evolved agentic protocols such as A2A,a so it is reasonable to assume further elaboration of inter-agent interactions. That line of reasoning leads to thoughts of increasing generation of content with the aid of AI, creation of Web pages or other digital artifacts, production of advertising and consumption of advertising by AI agents roaming the World Wide Web, and AI agents taking actions through inter-agent exchanges on behalf of users who may be human but may also be agents acting on behalf of humans or on behalf of other agents. In theory, agents can spawn other agents. Is there a Sorcerer’s Apprentice scenario already lurking in the wings?

This line of reasoning (fantasizing?) was triggered when I started wondering whether the increased role of agents surfing the Web would lead to advertising intended for consumption—not by human users but by agents acting on their behalf. “Find the best match for me for this kind of product,” you might instruct an agent. By what metrics will agents rate advertisements? Will the language of advertising shift in some incomprehensible way toward attracting bots? Will advertisers pay when bots click on ads? Generally, providers of advertising try to distinguish between human users and bots to avoid paying for bot-driven “clicks,” but what if the bots are making the decisions to purchase a product or engage a service?

While we have crafted AI systems to produce humanly consumable content (text, imagery, music, video, and so on), one might imagine that digitally native agents could evolve digital sensory systems outside of human capacities. This is not unlike the discovery that non-human organisms have sensors outside our range (e.g., ultraviolet, infrared, magnetism, high and low audio frequencies). A somewhat distorted example of this might be “invisible” prompts that produce jail-breaking results in AI agents. I have seen some truly arcane text strings that allegedly trigger jail breaks for some large language models (LLMs).

I am far from the first person to wonder about various AI feedback loops that could lead to increased amounts of so-called “AI slop” or “hallucinated output.” An analogy that comes to mind is programmed trading, in which multiple automatic stock-trading systems, using similar algorithms, drive the stock market up or down dramatically. We have evolved brakes when this happens by suspending trading for stocks experiencing this kind of behavior. AI systems, just like programmed trading systems, can execute much faster than humans. We have evolved automatic braking systems when hazardous conditions are detected. Perhaps we need to think along similar lines as we introduce increasing amounts of computer-driven behavior in our online or digital ecosystems?

We have seen that LLMs and agents are imperfect analogs of human behavior but have the advantage of increasing capacity to execute at speed. LLMs produce software, however imperfect, much faster than the best human programmers. The same may be said of a raft of other digital artifacts. It stands to reason that this means LLMs and agents may also be able to make mistakes much more quickly and at a greater scale than humans. That suggests we need to evolve the moral equivalent of digital brakes when automatic observation systems (bot police?) detect out-of-control conditions. The more I speculate about this, the more it seems as if we need to replicate analogs of many of the systems and practices we use to moderate or discipline human behavior.

It doesn’t take much to start wondering how to introduce norms and discipline into an agentic universe. Can you punish a bot? “No Internet access for the next 24 hours!” Efforts to train LLMs and agents to observe behavioral norms is called alignment in AI circles. That is the moral equivalent of norms in human societies. My guess is we are going to need more than alignment to discipline the behavior of the artificial actors we have created.

item.title: The Reality of an AI Implementation
item.dc:creator: Dharmateja Priyadarshi Uddandarao
item.description: AI tools aren't meant to replace your product instincts, but they will help you sharpen questions and provide a framework to test hypotheses and validate assumptions.
item.content:encoded:
Dharmateja Priyadarshi Uddandarao
Stop Trusting Just Your Dashboard
DOI: 10.1145/3821443
 https://bit.ly/4uoG3E8

We’ve all been in that meeting where someone pulls up a chart and says, “Our AI product boosted conversion by 15%.” Everyone nods. Nobody dares to ask: “What if conversions had risen anyway?”

This problem keeps nagging at me, though I’m sure it’s benign. People believe the numbers because they seem correct. Tools for creating common visualizations like dashboards, trend lines, and before-and-after comparisons are terrible at helping people form the right questions, let alone questions that require causal reasoning. If a company has staked its multi-million-dollar investment in an AI product on such numbers, now they’re hanging in the balance by chance.

It’s obvious, but I am going to say it anyway. Profit equals revenue minus cost. P = R – C. Every business initiative you undertake needs to prove itself out on this simple formula. For example, if you are putting some cost into running a marketing campaign, is that new campaign worth it? That innovative supply chain tweak? In the end, the answer to every business question is as simply as this: Did I make more money than I spent?

Unlike prior technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) does not simply follow a “cost today for revenue tomorrow” payback model. AI investments increase costs before they start to increase revenues, and the returns on those investments are typically indirect and may meander rather than move in a straight line. Even with great recommendations, a good customer experience, and product/retailer retention, the lifetime value of a customer takes time to materialize. Sometimes it’s months, not days or weeks. So, the “month one ROI” may look terrible, even though the initiative was strategically a good decision. This is hard. In finance, you need a “profit story.” That is different than a “product story.” A profit story is “Did we win?” A product story is “Did this initiative cause our winning?”

Causality is about evaluating counterfactuals. If we never launched a particular feature to a given customer, what would have happened? Well, you never know what would have happened in the alternative reality. That reality is missing from the equation because you only get to observe how that customer behaves once. This is important to get right. A common example we hear was the design of a dashboard that showed a picture of a rising needle with the words “revenue went up after launch.” A nice, effective visualization, but not evidence of impact, because revenue might have gone up anyway.

Why Dashboards Keep Getting It Wrong

We’ve seen goal-driven teams go wrong because the pressure to show return on investment causes people to optimize for metrics that look good rather than those that actually drive value. There are natural reasons for this to happen.

In addition to confounders and seasonality, you also get to control for spikes in demand due to external, entirely unpredictable events. Designing to control for all of these is hard, and it’s hard to have confidence that your model isn’t just attributing your success of your company to your model, as opposed to just happening to have increased marketing spend in the same quarter.

The people who were most likely to adopt your next AI-powered feature anyway cause a selection bias in causal experiments. So the first reading will tell you nothing about the value added by the feature, and everything about the people who are most engaged with your product—indeed, the most valuable to your business. People confuse these two all the time, reporting positive results to stakeholders based on a contrast between early adopters and the rest of the user base.

It is also important to recognize that averages can mask Simpson’s paradox, where overall there is a positive relationship within a category but negative within segments, and the segmenting criteria could be anything, such as geography, device, customer tenure, etc.

We also need to consider cannibalization between different launches. The new metric might go up, but the overall gain in value is not as much as we might hope, because instead of inducing more behavior, we are inducing shifts in behavior. We see this occur with many of our e-commerce businesses, where the attributed sales, conversion rate, or add-to-cart indicator goes up, but we really don’t know the level of demand that exists without the AI tool in place.

This is a blind spot that we’ve seen in many social media products. They might rely on click-through rate (CTR) and session time as primary signals for an AI model to indicate value. Having a higher CTR on a page does not necessarily mean that the content on that page is engaging, and having a longer session time on a page does not necessarily mean that a user got more value from that content. To better measure engagement, we should look at deeper signals such as time spent on site (a.k.a. dwell time), variety of engagement on site, and the impact that our engagement has on adjacent revenue channels. Then we should measure those signals against a believable counterfactual to understand true lift.

A Practical Framework That Actually Works

So, what makes a good measurement system? In my experience, the strongest measurement systems have two key characteristics: they are connected to meaningful decisions, and there is an identification strategy (that is, a practical plan to distinguish the initiative effect from other effects). Here’s a framework I’ve found genuinely useful.

Make the decision before making the metrics. Translate the decision into language that people use before packaging it up into quantifiable metrics. For example, “Should we scale this AI feature from 10% to 100%?” or “Should we fund a newer v2 model training next quarter?” or “Should we replace manual workflow X with automation?” Clear decision language is needed to form clear images of success. In other words, you have to be able to say your decision out loud before you can imagine what success will look like. This is your best protection from getting fooled by a nice Metric Theater with pretty dashboards.

For the second assumption, we want to clearly define the intervention (or treatment) in causal language. When selecting exposure to a new AI feature as the unit of analysis, we want to be sure that we are not including too much variability in the definition of the intervention, such that exposure to the intervention has no effect. Similarly, when selecting the dose of intervention, we want to clearly define meaningful adoption prior to data collection.

Track a stack of metrics instead of trying to fit everything into one KPI. We should think about this stack in layers, starting with business outcomes and then moving to product outcomes, and then finally leading indicators that plausibly explain what is causing the movements in the metrics above it (such as retention, conversion rate, task completion rate, engagement quality, latency, model performance, etc.)

Picking the Right Causal Method for Your Situation

For your identification strategy, use what you can realistically achieve. This means first of all to try to run a randomized experiment, as this is typically the best way to control for confounders. However, there may be some cases in which running an experiment is not feasible. Fortunately, there are methods that enable you to create comparable groups within observational data using the propensity score. The difference-in-differences setting with a staggered rollout is another common identification strategy. This involves comparing changes over time between treated and control groups. In econometrics, identifying the causal effects of treatment on outcome requires an instrumental variables setting, where the instrument is a variable that is associated with the probability of receiving treatment, but otherwise has no effect on the outcome variable, except through the treatment variable. Methods such as causal forests and double machine learning can be used to flexibly and accurately identify the underlying mechanisms to determine which customer segments will be most valuable.

None of these tools are meant to replace your product instincts, but they will help to sharpen up the questions you should be asking and provide a framework to test hypotheses and validate assumptions. Instead of asking “on average, did my products perform well?,” you’ll be asking “what percentage of total ROI comes from which segment?” Or, instead of seeing that revenue went up, you’ll understand the underlying drivers of what would have happened if you weren’t in the market. One emerging technique advancing that quality is target metric pre-balancing. Here we try to make the distributions of outcome for the treatment and control groups as similar as possible before running the analysis to get at the causal effect of interest. While typical propensity score matching methods can balance the covariates between the groups, it is not guaranteed to balance the underlying structural processes between the groups, which can lead to less stable estimates of the treatment effect.

The future of evaluation will be big questions, answered with honesty but with sound methods. P = R – C, as it has always. The only shift will be in the quality of the measurement of R and C.

item.title: Need a Hug Bot?
item.dc:creator: Lynnette Hui Xian Ng
item.description: Ethan was one of those who had succumbed to conspiracy theories floating around social media.
item.content:encoded:
Ethan lay awake in the comfort of his blanket, scrolling Twitter on his phone through the upward flicks of his right thumb. He couldn’t sleep; he wasn’t tired. Neither was he energetic: He was unstimulated.

He had been bored for the last few months, feeling like an animal trapped in its cage, only able to leave his home for necessary grocery runs. A “coronavirus pandemic” has been raging around the world. To reduce the virus transmission rates, his government had decreed that all citizens were to stay home except for essential activities. He felt the public authority response was over-dramatic: The “coronavirus” is simply a bioweapon carefully engineered by elite politicians to control the population.

Ethan was one of those who had sucumbed to conspiracy theories floating around social media, influenced by a series of persistent bot accounts that consistently reminded their followers how the coronavirus was deliberately created by sinister agents.

COVID-19 is a globalist bioweapon! Stand up to your government! Stop the lockdown now! #stopthelockdown #reopenamerica—Ethan’s Twitter feed had refreshed to a new tweet by @NotAVirusBot.

Regardless of the social climate, these bots relentlessly hammered the message that the coronavirus was a conspiracy theory. They were successful: Ethan and his comrades were determined to walk in protest of the lockdown.

Next Tuesday, raise your voices and banners at Main Street to #StopTheLockdown!!! See you there!! came the next tweet by @NotAVirusBot.

Ethan swiped to his calendar app, creating a new event that linked to this tweet and set a reminder for the day before. Within a few minutes, the tweet gained 183 likes and 300 retweets. Ethan smiled as he read the replies. People were discussing where to meet and reminding each other to write “Stand for Freedom” and “Stop the Lockdown” on cardboard signs to bring along to the march. At least, not everyone had been brainwashed by the government, he thought.

A notification ribbon appeared at the top of his phone screen, sending a wave of vibration through the phone and to his bed.

Bong. @big_ben_bot reminded him that a new day has begun.

It was midnight, and he still was unable to fall asleep. He kicked his blanket. He pounded his fists on his pillow. He sat up, hugged his knees, then flipped himself flat on the bed again. He was angry at his government—for creating a virus to manipulate people’s behavior, for being incompetent to the extent they had to lock people at home in order to control society. Even if the coronavirus existed, he just needed some sun to ward it off.

@CoronavirusCures mentioned that “The virus can be killed with daily doses of Vitamin D from the sun.” But how was he going to get any sun if he could not leave home without being questioned by the police on his purpose and destination?

Social gatherings limited to no more than 2 people outside your household. Maintain social distancing at all times, tweeted @CoronavirusLockdownNewsBot, who disseminated the latest news on government-imposed restrictions. It also reminded people about the confinement rules. No large group gatherings. No group gym classes. No group singing and dancing at bars.

Not that the social gathering news mattered to Ethan. He lived alone, just like many other Americans. After college, he found a job in another city as a software coder. But Ethan was lonely. Before he could make enough new friends and find a roommate, the lockdown happened. He missed his college days. He missed the times that he visited his friend’s dorm rooms, holding cans of beer, and they would play video games together for hours. He missed the times he would sit at the bench by the college square and people-watch. But college was also where people started finding their partners, finding jobs, and being busy with their adult lives. Except him. All he had was himself and his computer. He took to online conversations, but it was never consistent. His virtual pen pals would begin chatting enthusiastically, but there always came a time when the excitement wore off.

@NeedAHugBot more social gathering limitations… when will this end? Ethan tweeted, tagging his trusty robotic friend. This bot could carry out lengthy conversations with humans, powered by its linguistic ability trained by large deep neural networks on several GPU farms. These networks provided the bot with a wide knowledge base of world events, and modern natural language processing techniques helped the program to understand the human’s intent and maintaining a conversation. How, exactly, the neurons fire to construct a sentence is somewhat a mystery, but Ethan was happy to have a confidant.

@EthanIsTrapped aww. we are all weary of the lockdown, but it’s necessary to #flattenthecurve.

@NeedAHugBot is it really working?

@EthanIsTrapped studies have shown that the banning of large gatherings has been estimated to reduce the spread of the coronavirus between 25–50%, but we’re still hoping for a permanent cure. *fingers crossed*

@NeedAHugBot i really need something to entertain myself

@EthanIsTrapped what about painting mini game figurines? how about the Star Wars Rebellion game?

Ethan hadn’t told the bot about his previous interests; it inferred this from his past posts, where he showed off his delicately hand-painted Warhammer figurines. And it knew he loved the Star Wars series from his posts on building a lightsaber from scrap materials.

@NeedAHugBot what’s that game about?

@EthanIsTrapped ah, it’s a fun one. you control either the Galactic Empire to locate the hidden Rebel base or the Rebel Alliance to bring down the Empire’s infrastructure. there are 150 plastic miniatures that account for 32 of the Star Wars galaxy’s most notable star systems. you will be sure to have a great time painting the X-Wings, Storm Troopers and even the Death Star.

@NeedAHugBot hmm that sounds like my kind of game

@EthanIsTrapped here’s an image of the game miniatures, and here are links to the sites to purchase the game, paint, and brushes.

Ethan loved painting game miniatures; when he used them to play with his friends he beamed with pride because his paintings were being marveled at. That was in the past: His college friends had moved on, and he was stuck at home, alone. But he will paint the miniatures for a game day in the future.

@NeedAHugBot i hope one day i will have friends to play the game with

@EthanIsTrapped you will. have faith, my friend. this, too, shall pass. *hugs*

Bong Bong Bong. @big_ben_bot reminded him once again of his sleeplessness. Alright, time to try and catch some winks.

@NeedAHugBot goodnight babe

@EthanIsTrapped sweet dreams. see you in the morning.  (ᴗ˳ᴗ) z z z

With a smile, Ethan put his phone under the pillow and closed his eyes. He needed a bot friend to depend on. People may leave him, but his trusty bot companion will not.

item.title: Unpacking Open Source Artificial Intelligence: Toward a Framework for Openness in Foundation Models
item.dc:creator: Camille François, Adrien Basdevant, Victor Storchan, Kevin Bankston, Ayah Bdeir, Brian Behlendorf, Merouane Debbah, Sayash Kapoor, Yann LeCun, Mark Surman, Helen King-Turvey, Nathan Lambert, Stefano Maffulli, Nik Marda, and Govind Shivkumar
item.description: Surveying existing approaches to defining openness in AI models and systems.
item.content:encoded:
Openness has long driven innovation in software,9 and AI is no exception.12 While some see openness in foundation models (FMs) as a security threat,18 others argue that restricting access will not meaningfully reduce risk and will limit the benefits of transparency, research, and global participation.3 As the EU AI Act reporting requirements on FMs—also referred to as general-purpose AI models (GPAIMs)—move toward implementation, there is an urgent need for a more nuanced and informed understanding of openness in AI systems.

Key Insights

  • Defining and evaluating openness in AI requires examining both the model and system stack, including interfaces, safeguards, infrastructure, and deployment practices that shape real-world risks and benefits.

  • AI systems can be open in different ways and to different degrees across data, code, weights, documentation, and governance, requiring more precise terminology than open or closed. 

  • Policy discussions on AI openness need to be informed by clearer shared language that distinguishes between different components, degrees, and purposes of openness across the AI stack. 

  • Safety is dependent on system context, not models alone. Meaningful AI safety assessment requires examining deployment environments, safeguards, moderation layers, and governance mechanisms alongside the underlying model itself.

It has been challenging to define openness in the context of FMs, as definitions of “open source” software do not easily translate to AI systems. However, shared nomenclature is essential to developing shared understandings, norms, benchmarks, and best practices. By shared nomenclature, we mean establishing common terms across researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society organizations working to unlock the benefits and mitigate the risks of FMs. We use AI systems here as shorthand for systems built with FMs, while recognizing the limitations and critiques of the term AI. This work is also necessary to illuminate the range of potential design choices around openness throughout the AI stack, and to ensure that this conversation moves beyond a narrow focus on model weights.

In this article, we survey existing approaches to defining openness in AI models and systems. We also propose a descriptive framework to evaluate how each component across the FM stack contributes to openness, enabling normative definitions of openness in AI. We intentionally do not present a definitive list of requirements for openness. This work builds on a February 2024 workshop convened by Mozilla and the Columbia Institute of Global Politics, which brought together more than 40 leading scholars and practitioners working on openness and AI.1 These individuals—spanning open source AI startups and companies, nonprofit AI labs, and civil society organizations—focused on exploring what open should mean in the current era of foundation models.

Foundations

There are several timely areas of exploration concerning openness and AI. The first is reflecting on the impact of open source on AI development.9 Another centers on the complexities of opening up AI systems themselves—specifically, identifying which components of the technology stack might be made accessible and how. Here, we focus on the latter. A literature review, included below, provides diverging perspectives on what openness can and should mean in an AI context,18 but we argue that the following four tenets provide a foundation for considering aspects of openness and AI:

  • Openness must be considered both at the model stack and the system stack levels. Focusing only on model weights or release strategies obscures the wider set of design choices—interfaces, safeguards, infrastructure, and deployment practices—that ultimately determine an AI system’s benefits and risks in practice.

  • Openness takes multiple forms. Beyond the binary of “open” or “closed,” openness in AI systems manifests through varying degrees of access to data, code, weights, documentation, and governance. Recognizing this diversity allows for more precise vocabulary and concepts (e.g., open science, open data, open weights, available weights, etc.) and sharper normative criteria for evaluating different release strategies.19

  • Greater clarity is needed in how openness is discussed at the policy level. Most policy debates on openness have lacked a shared understanding of the benefits, risks, and mechanisms for increasing transparency and access across the AI stack. In the absence of such clarity, discussions of risk become polarized between boosterism and alarmism, rather than converging on practical approaches that balance innovation, accountability, and security. Addressing this gap requires a more precise vocabulary for openness, one that can differentiate between components, degrees, and purposes rather than collapse them under a single ambiguous label.17

  • Safety must be a core consideration. Safety cannot be ensured by scrutinizing models in isolation.13 It depends on the broader context of deployment, including the safeguards built into full AI systems. Distinguishing between open models and open systems is therefore essential:16 The latter can incorporate protective measures, but also introduce new risks absent at the model level. Openness and safety are closely connected—without openness, independent risk assessment is impossible—but safety cannot be reduced to openness alone.

Together, these foundations highlight the need for a structured way to map openness across the AI stack. The framework discussed here operationalizes these principles, distinguishing model-level and system-level components and clarifying the cross-cutting attributes that shape openness in practice (with an emphasis on AI systems with model weights that are downloadable or more open).

We also invite discussion of the key trade-offs for leveraging openness and how the different dimensions of openness relate to the different goals one might wish to pursue (see Figure 1). The framework does not offer a comprehensive account of openness in AI; instead, it is designed to be a practical tool for developers, policymakers, and other key players.

Motivations: Why pursue AI openness?  In Figure 1, a non-exhaustive list of potential benefits sourced from workshop participants highlights a variety of motivations for AI openness. AI openness is rarely pursued for its own sake; it is motivated by diverse and sometimes conflicting goals. Our framework helps make these goals explicit by showing how different motivations map onto different forms of openness across the AI stack. For instance, advancing research and innovation often depends on openness of data or training code; promoting competition and efficiency tends to emphasize access to model weights; and ensuring accountability may require openness in documentation, licensing, and safeguards. These motivations may overlap, but they do not always align. A strategy that maximizes reproducibility, for example, may differ from one that maximizes market competition or system safety. In the free/libre tradition, “openness” is inseparable from user freedoms, and from ensuring protection against malicious features.20 The user’s essential freedoms are to run, copy, distribute, study, change, and improve the technology;8 in AI systems, licensing and governance should be assessed on whether they preserve or effectively claw back these freedoms across components.

By situating motivations within the framework, we can move beyond abstract claims that “openness is good” or polarized debates that cast it as either inherently dangerous or inherently beneficial. Instead, the framework enables more precise evaluation of which forms of openness serve which objectives, and where trade-offs or complementarities exist. This creates a clearer basis for policymakers, researchers, and developers to debate not only whether to open AI systems, but how and for what purposes.

Related Work: Beyond Open Bashing and Open Washing

Over the past two years, foundational efforts have sought to map the landscape of openness in AI. The existing literature reveals a diversity of approaches to conceptualizing AI openness, each with distinct methodological choices and underlying assumptions. These approaches can be broadly categorized by how they frame openness—whether as a gradient (“more vs. less open”), a scoring system (“a certain degree of openness”), or a binary classification (“open vs. closed”).

Binary approaches.   The Open Source Initiative (OSI) launched a process in June 2023 to draft a definition of open source AI, culminating in the release of an “Open Source AI Definition” in late 2024.15 It best exemplifies the binary approach, with a clear set of criteria on what counts as “open” versus “closed,” and references to OSI-approved licenses and terms to meet these criteria. Below, and as concrete illustrations for what open can mean in practice across weights, code, data, checkpoints, and licensing, we cite projects that exemplify a fully open approach.

EleutherAI released a suite of open models with full training checkpoints and tools to reconstruct training dataloaders,2 advocating for standard open source licenses to ensure clarity and interoperability.

The LLM360 initiative10 promotes full transparency across model training, checkpoints, and data. The project argues that partial releases hinder scientific progress and reproducibility.

The Allen Institute for AI built on initiatives like Pythia and BLOOM by releasing an initial set of 1B and 7B models with 500-plus checkpoints from intermediate training, full datasets, training code, evaluation code, training logs, and comprehensive documentation.25 The initiative aims to foster a growing “science of LLMs” and influence public AI discourse beyond transparency and openness goals.

Beyond a single open/closed label for a whole release, some efforts apply a binary rule, component by component. The Linux Foundation’s Model Openness Framework (MOF)23 is the clearest instance: It evaluates whether each component is released under appropriate open terms. The MOF classifies models based on openness and completeness across 15 components of the model development lifecycle. The framework distinguishes between openness (binary classification of whether a component is released under an appropriate open license) and completeness (gradient approach with three tiers of model completeness, based on which components are released under appropriate open licenses). The framework includes a required MOF.JSON file detailing licenses and components, with classes ranging from Open Model (Class III) to Open Science (Class I), encouraging transparency, reuse, and reproducibility.

Criteria scoring approaches.   The Centre for Language Studies at Radboud University developed a project26 to assess the openness, transparency, and accountability of instruction-tuned language models. The research highlights risks of proprietary software and provides comparative analysis of open source alternatives with similar architectures and capabilities.

Stanford CRFM created the Foundation Model Transparency Index,4 introducing 100 fine-grained indicators that capture transparency across the lifecycle of FMs—from upstream inputs (data sources, labor, and compute) to the model itself (size, capabilities, and risks) and downstream uses (distribution channels, usage policies, and affected geographies). The study emphasizes that AI release strategies are nonbinary and classifies models with widely downloadable weights as open. The research found that open models tend to outperform closed ones in transparency metrics, attributing this partly to lack of transparency among closed developers about critical upstream components.

EleutherAI offered a contrasting perspective,7 cautioning that score-based transparency frameworks risk treating transparency as an end in itself rather than as a means to uphold ethical values such as accountability.

Gradient/spectrum approaches.   In “The Gradient of Generative AI Release: Methods and Considerations,”19 Solaiman introduces a template for understanding different levels of access to generative AI systems, from fully closed to fully open. The paper defines six release levels—fully closed, staged access, hosted access, API/cloud access, downloadable access, and fully open—framing them as points along a gradient. It highlights the trade-offs at each level, particularly the balance between risk mitigation and power concentration.

The Princeton Center for Information Technology Policy and Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models hosted a 2023 workshop17 to discuss key benefits and risks of specific properties of open FMs. They proposed a risk assessment framework for analyzing their marginal risk (i.e., using closed source and preexisting technologies as a baseline). They identify that more research is needed to assess the marginal risks of open FMs.

The Digital Public Goods Alliance developed a gradient approach framework27 that acknowledges that access to AI testing and training data is not the same as having access to source code; put another way, open sourcing data alone does not enable full model reproducibility. It recognizes varying degrees of openness across AI systems (training data, model, and code), without further detailing sub-components. The framework seeks to balance the benefits of AI openness, such as transparency and inclusivity, against potential risks of misuse or harm, and includes the concept of “aspirational openness,” defining various levels of openness for AI components to qualify as digital public goods, taking into account factors like ethical use and data rights issues.

Gradient approaches commonly ground marginal-risk analyses of openness; we review some key examples below.

In “Considerations for Governing Open Foundation Models,”3 Bommasani et al. from the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence examine how release strategies of open FMs relate to governance risks and regulation consequences. A key takeaway from the brief is to invite practitioners to think in terms of marginal risk of open foundation models “relative to (a) closed models or (b) pre-existing technologies.” The paper also discusses some of the benefits of open FMs such as competition, accelerating innovation, and distributing power. The brief acknowledges that the release of FMs is a gradient across various dimensions, and encourages policymakers to explore downstream intervention points that would be more effective for mitigating AI risks.

In the paper “What Does It Mean to Open Source AI?”11 Luccioni et al. analyze the risks and benefits of open FMs. Benefits include innovation, competition, the distribution of decision-making power, and transparency. The authors also present a risk-assessment framework for evaluating the marginal risk of open FMs, and survey the current evidence for the risks of open FMs, which, in many cases, the authors find lacking.

Summary.  While these existing frameworks have made valuable contributions to the emerging scholarship around defining openness in the context of AI, they also present key limitations that we are seeking to address. Binary approaches may oversimplify the complex, multi-dimensional nature of AI systems, and thus the different pathways that may lead to openness, while gradient approaches often lack specificity about what constitutes meaningful differences along the spectrum. Scoring approaches, though comprehensive, risk treating transparency as an end in itself rather than as a means to achieve broader goals such as accountability and safety. Additionally, many existing frameworks focus primarily on model-level considerations, potentially overlooking the broader system-level components that significantly impact user freedoms. To bridge these gaps, we make explicit which system-level components and cross-cutting attributes (documentation, licensing, safeguards) matter for specific goals, rather than treating openness as a single axis.

Building on these prior efforts, we propose a unified framework that distinguishes between the AI model stack and the broader AI system stack, while incorporating cross-cutting attributes such as documentation, safeguards, and licensing. Our approach aims to provide greater granularity and practical applicability by mapping different dimensions of openness to their corresponding benefits and use cases.

The full proceedings write-up includes three appendices that offer additional depth: (i) Benefits of Openness across the Foundation Model Stack, (ii) Key Areas of Debate, and (iii) Alignment with the Linux Foundation’s Model Openness Framework. These are available in the full version of the article.1

The Framework

In this section, we introduce a framework focused on AI systems in which model weights are at least downloadable. We begin with a representation of the AI model stack, then zoom out to the broader AI system stack, highlighting shared attributes that apply across the stack. We present the framework in a way that aligns with the various benefits of AI openness.

AI model stack.  Reaching an agreement on a definition for AI openness has proven complicated.14 AI models are not just code; they are trained on massive datasets, deployed on intricate computing infrastructure, and accessed through diverse interfaces and modalities. To effectively depict an AI system stack, we initially focus on the AI model tech stack. Figure 2 presents the core components that are particularly relevant for considerations around openness of a general-purpose AI model (GPAIM).

At the model level, there are three main artifacts: datasets, code, and model weights, each of which also includes sub-components. It is important to note that not all sub-components are mandatory or applicable in every configuration (e.g., some models may have the reward model’s weights or preference dataset; others do not), and the taxonomy of sub-components may vary based on the specific model type. Given this variability, it is crucial to tailor the AI model stack to accommodate different modalities, such as input and output types. Figure 2 illustrates these various layers at the model level.

AI system stack.  It is important to distinguish between open models and fully open AI systems or products. Open AI systems often incorporate more than just the model, including interfaces, telemetry, safety layers, and orchestration tools. For example, an open chatbot might rely on external moderation systems, while a RAG application could add components like langChain or Redis for orchestration and caching. This structure differs from traditional software, where code, compilers, and licenses are clearly separated. In AI, components such as data, hardware, and algorithms jointly shape behavior, making openness harder to define. For instance, opinions diverge on whether model weights, code, or datasets count as the “source” for modification. (Despite these differences between building AI models and traditional software, some initiatives are trying to study to what extent FMs could be built as “open source software”—especially given the technical ability to efficiently update the weights of the models. This would allow contributors to be able to submit patches to fix potential identified vulnerabilities in the model; then maintainers would need to be able to merge the patches to quickly integrate updates into the model.)

Lastly, the infrastructure layer plays a key part, as many scholars have already underlined: The high costs6 associated with developing AI models could hinder19 widespread adoption, even using open approaches, due to the expensive hardware and infrastructure requirements, such as GPUs. While openness in AI provides organizational control for customization, adapting large models to specific domains poses challenges without substantial investments in GPUs, so this does not necessarily solve the challenges of concentrated access and influence in well-resourced labs.4 See Figure 3 for a visual representation of the tech stack required for a general-purpose AI system (GPAIS).

Common attributes across the AI system stack.   It is crucial to differentiate between the components of the tech stack, such as model weights, and their attributes, such as the license for model weights. For instance, in this article we consider many AI safety measures to be better understood as attributes of the system rather than features of the model. Consequently, we represent an AI system as comprising three cross-cutting sets of attributes—documentation, safeguards, and licensing—that may apply across the entire stack rather than being tied to any single component (see Figure 3 for attribute categories integrated into the system stack).

For example, safety guardrails can be integrated at the level of individual components, recognizing their diversity and the need to address different types of harms and risks that may arise across the stack. This approach allows for targeted mitigations that are best suited to each component’s specific role and vulnerabilities.13 Entrusting safety assessments solely to models is insufficient, especially regarding concerns of potential misuse, as models lack crucial contextual information necessary for making accurate safety assessments.

An openness in AI framework.  As a whole, the framework presents a tech stack described across its different dimensions: AI artifacts (e.g., model weights), to which correspond different attributes such as licensing (e.g., choice of model’s weights license) or documentation (e.g., model cards). Each of the dimensions is composed of categories and subcategories that can be released more or less openly. As illustrated in Figure 3, these components correspond to different benefits of openness at each layer of the stack. Further work is needed to understand what is required to open different parts of the stack, which components are essential for reproducibility or evaluation, and how openness needs may shift with future AI systems beyond today’s LLMs.

We hope a meaningful contribution of this framework can be its explicit distinction between the model stack and the broader system stack in the context of evaluating openness, combined with the mapping of cross-cutting attributes like documentation, licensing, and safeguards that apply across both levels. This work seeks to unify previously fragmented approaches into a coherent descriptive framework that can be systematically applied by policymakers evaluating regulatory approaches and practitioners making release decisions.

Conclusion

This work aims to accelerate a shared understanding of openness in FMs and AI systems, differentiating challenges at the model and system levels, and those that could apply across the AI stack, and showing how to leverage that understanding to better harness the benefits and mitigate the risks of AI. Our framework provides a vocabulary for systematically analyzing openness at different levels of AI systems, clarifies distinctions often conflated in public debate, and highlights concrete areas where openness interacts with safety and governance. By clarifying the different levels, forms, and vocabularies of openness, and by distinguishing openness from—but also connecting it to—safety, the framework aims to equip researchers and policymakers with a practical tool for evaluating openness strategies in AI systems. In future work, we hope to go deeper into how this framework can be strengthened with more information about safety mitigations.

Acknowledgments

We acknowledge Aviya Skowron, Amba Kak, Irene Solaiman, Stella Biderman, and Martin Tisné for their input to this article. We also thank all the participants in the Columbia Convening on Openness and AI for their contributions to this work, and to Jen Weedon and Mariel Povolny for their editorial support.

item.title: KV the Apostate: Faith-Based Computing Versus the Unnatural Science
item.dc:creator: George V. Neville-Neil
item.description: If we use LLMs poorly—as so many people already are we will generate megabytes of utter garbage (a.k.a. AI slop, already the bane of many open source projects).
item.content:encoded:
Dear KV,

The hype cycle that is AI seems as if it will never end. What I was doing as a developer two years ago seems very different to what I am doing now that management has required us to use LLMs in our work. Some of what these things do seems helpful—roughing out a general framework or helping with tasks such as creating unit tests that have often seemed like drudgery. From your writings, I suspect you remain skeptical and continue to be part of the old school that thinks this is a fad that will blow over. But do you believe there is something valuable in this current cycle? Or are you still typing out your programs one key press at a time?

Button Pusher

Dear Button,

KV got into computing for a few reasons, one of which was to build and live in the future. So, while he definitely has strong beliefs about how best to do things, ignoring new tools and being part of the old guard are not in my nature. What is in KV’s nature, other than a propensity for outbursts of profanity, is a healthy dose of skepticism—a skepticism that has kept KV from ever completely joining any crowd. After all, the problem with joining a group is that, eventually, they have little hats, uniforms, and lists of people they want to wake up at three in the morning.

Let’s get down to the phrase that stands out to me most in your letter: “But do you believe … ?” Belief is not a part of science or engineering, and anyone who says otherwise is building the next Leaning Tower of Pisa, the sole remnant of a series of failed towers. All the others fell because insufficient science and engineering went into their planning and execution.

Unfortunately, this word belief gets tossed around a lot in relation to the current LLM fad. The other day, in a discussion with a colleague, an admitted fanboy and cheerleader for the use of LLMs, I was pointed to a brief notea written by one of the deepest of algorithmic thinkers and told, “See, even he is now a believer!” But, if you take the time to read what was written, you find there is nothing having to do with belief. Instead, it is a short, rigorous study of how this tool could be applied to a problem and how the people involved had managed to apply the tool and their intelligence to solve a problem they had been working on.

Did the tool help them solve the problem more quickly? Perhaps. Did the tool solve the problem for them? No, they solved the problem with the help of a new tool, just as humans have done since the first cave dweller picked up a femur bone and used it as a weapon—although that may have been under the influence of a large black obelisk that was making a crazy humming noise nearby.

When I pointed out the fallacy of using the term belief for anything science based, my colleague quoted the old saw about how “Computing added the word science to its name even though it is not a science.” I pointed out, none too politely, that this was incorrect.

The crux of the matter is that the study of computing is, in fact, an unnatural science. It is the study of objects manufactured by humans, but which we now claim (or at least the LLM folks claim) are too complex to understand. Physics is the study of the natural world, and chemistry is applied physics with smoke and bangs, while biology is the study of naturally occurring living organisms. Those are properly called natural sciences. Which is to say I just added science to their names as well.

Whether or not we affix science to a name is immaterial. It is how we study what we study and whether we can apply the scientific method to derive reproducible results. If each time we do something we get a random but useful result, which is still not science but merely luck. And, as someone who flies a lot, I prefer not to rely solely on luck in my flight controls, flaps, engines, or brakes.

Programming is not just typing the characters, any more than writing is. Or, as Truman Capote put it, “That’s not writing, that’s just typing!” Programming or software development—or whatever term you wish to use—is the application of thought to the creation of structures to be used in an abstract machine made real by silicon relays. The key here is the thought.

These new tools may indeed remove drudgery from our lives, although—like all new tools—they will surely replace that with other drudgery. The present moment reminds me of how architects, given a new material—concrete—went crazy using it in everything to create unlivable and unusable buildings that were so hideous they needed a new award, for neobrutalist architecture, to recognize these monstrosities.

The trend of architects building things “just because they could” has no more iconic and ironic expression than the CSAIL (Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory) building at MIT. The structure is so poorly laid out that no one can find their way through its twisted corridors without GPS, and it is so poorly constructed that it leaks. MIT sued the architect once the building was complete. Similarly, if we use LLMs poorly—as so many people already are—we will generate megabytes of utter garbage (a.k.a. AI slop, already the bane of many open source projects).

What we as software developers and designers need to do is to understand these tools and how to apply them. Whether we ask an LLM or a recent graduate to type the code is less important than knowing what the code does, how it was built, and when to look under the hood. Right now, everyone ought to be in coveralls with their hands covered in grease, or they are going to find when they next hit the brakes that they are likely to go sailing through the next red light.

Once the hype cycle ends, we will know what we know about LLMs and AI, but, at the moment, there is too much money and too much “belief” to form a clear picture. Always try the new tools, always be skeptical, and check your return values.

KV
