item.content:encoded:
The history of computing is a story of escalating abstraction. From the painstaking manipulation of machine code to the elegance of high-level languages, every major leap has been defined by a desire to shorten the distance between human intent and machine execution. Grace Hopper’s first compiler was a monumental step, freeing programmers from the tyranny of the hardware. Structured programming, object oriented paradigms, and now, the rise of large language models (LLMs) have continued this trajectory. The current paradigm of vibe coding—popularized to describe guiding an AI to generate code through natural language—represents a new frontier that promises velocity while provoking debate about brittleness and accountability, allowing developers to focus on the “what” while the machine handles the “how.”2

This relentless march of abstraction now points toward its logical, and perhaps final, conclusion: the direct translation of thought into code. This concept of “neural coding” is no longer pure science fiction.2 Research in neuroscience, using fMRI to study the cognitive processes behind programming, has revealed that code comprehension does not simply reuse the brain’s language centers. Instead, it relies primarily on the multiple-demand network, a system associated with domain-general executive functions like logical reasoning and problem solving.5 These findings lend plausibility to brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) that capture structured intent and delegate translation to machine decoders.

Neural coding—directly translating thought into software—no longer seems purely science fiction, but its realization will require cautious optimism. Researchers have begun to demonstrate partial feasibility: for example, Willett et al. used an implanted brain–computer interface (BCI) to decode attempted handwriting at ~90 characters per minute,10 while NIH Research Matters (2025) reports clinical BCI work achieving about 50 spoken words per minute from brain signals in a paralyzed patient.7 Industry labs are also making strides; Neuralink recently showed a monkey, via an implanted wireless interface, moving a cursor to type simple words. However, these successes rely on invasive implants and ideal conditions. Non-invasive approaches (EEG or fNIRS headsets) remain far lower-bandwidth and noisier—EEG has poor spatial resolution and fNIRS has slow hemodynamics—making rich, continuous control difficult. To date, most BCIs can only handle simple outputs (for example, selecting letters or issuing a few discrete commands) rather than the rich, hierarchical logic of programming; for instance, a hybrid EEG–fNIRS system could distinguish about eight mental commands with moderate accuracy.6 Given these constraints, a realistic avenue toward thought-to-code interfaces is through hybrid BCI–AI systems.2 In such a setup, the brain would convey high-level symbolic intentions (say, “open a loop” or a rough function outline), which a large language model (trained on code) could then expand into detailed syntax and boilerplate. This approach leverages AI to compensate for the brain signal’s low resolution, but it also highlights the remaining challenges: limited neural bandwidth, decoding noise, difficulty capturing abstract logic from neural activity, and the need to safeguard mental privacy. In short, direct mind-to-code translation appears technically conceivable with continued advances, yet major barriers in sensing, interpretation, and human–AI coordination must be overcome before our thoughts can truly write code for us.

The promise is seductive: a world of frictionless creation, where the only barrier to building software is the imagination itself. But in our pursuit of this ultimate abstraction, we risk a profound and dangerous misunderstanding of our own discipline. We risk confusing the expression of intent with the craft of implementation. While neural coding may appear to be the next great leap in developer productivity, I argue it represents a potential endpoint for software engineering as a rigorous, intellectual discipline. By attempting to abstract away the final details of implementation, we threaten to hollow out the very skills that define our craft, leaving us as masters of intent but novices in execution.

The Two Halves of Creation

At the heart of any engineering discipline lies a fundamental duality. Nearly four decades ago, in his seminal paper “No Silver Bullet,” Fred Brooks distinguished between the essential complexity of a problem and the accidental complexity of its implementation.1 Intent is the essence—the goal, the vision, the complex conceptual structures that define the software. Implementation is the accident—the representation of those structures in a programming language. Brooks argued that while our tools have become exceptionally good at reducing accidental complexity, the essential complexity remains. True engineering lives in the struggle to master that essence. (See the accompanying figure.)

Engineering Beyond Code: Requirements and Many Stakeholders

The essence/accident distinction does not stop at programming. In practice, the hardest work is upstream, namely eliciting and reconciling requirements across N stakeholders with conflicting goals, risks, and constraints. Modern software engineering already uses rigor here: goal modeling, safety cases, contracts, traceability matrices, and model-based engineering that can deterministically generate code from validated models. These methods reduce friction without removing accountability because they preserve verifiable links from intent → requirement → design → artifact. Neural coding, if it collapses these steps, risks severing those links. A credible path forward is not “thought → code,” but “thought → formalized intent (assumptions, invariants, constraints) → checked models → code,” so that teams, not just individuals, can reason, negotiate, and audit what is being built.

It is worth noting that model-based engineering already shows how we can gain speed while keeping rigor when requirements and constraints are made explicit and are machine-checked before code is generated.

The danger of neural coding is that it promises to automate implementation so completely that it obscures the essential complexity it is meant to solve. The accompanying figure situates neural coding at the far-right end of escalating abstraction—from manual coding to IDE autocomplete, AI pair-programming and vibe coding. Moving right reduces friction but shifts cognitive work from explicit reasoning to oversight of opaque systems. The risk callouts under each stage summarize typical failure modes: manual coding carries high cognitive load; autocomplete can induce suggestion bias and shallow API understanding; AI pair-programming may hallucinate or mask defects; vibe coding encourages thin mental models and maintenance debt; and neural coding risks loss of architectural understanding/accountability alongside mental-privacy concerns. The core claim of this article is that the craft of engineering lives in managing these trade-offs—not in eliminating implementation altogether. The most critical and intellectually demanding work in our field occurs not in the initial expression of an idea, but in the iterative process of discovering the true requirements and constraints through the act of building. The messy, detailed work of implementation is not a barrier to be overcome; it is the crucible in which vague intentions are forged into precise, functional reality.

The Dangers of the Ultimate Black Box

Progression toward neural coding is the progression toward the ultimate black box. In this future, we risk creating a generation of developers who can conjure complex systems with a thought but possess no underlying understanding of how they function. When these systems inevitably fail—when they cannot scale, when a subtle security flaw emerges, when a race condition brings down a critical service—who will be there to fix them?

Debugging a system you did not truly build is a uniquely difficult challenge. It requires the ability to form a mental model of the system’s internal logic and to reason from first principles about its behavior. This problem is already emerging with today’s AI coding assistants. Controlled studies show developers often accept model suggestions while investing less in building a coherent mental model, which in turn makes debugging more difficult.9 Controlled studies likewise report heightened cognitive effort during understanding and navigation when validating Copilot’s suggestions, even as many of those suggestions are accepted—a pattern consistent with shallow comprehension and overreliance if unchecked. To compound the risk, security analyses report that a substantial fraction of Copilot’s completions are vulnerable, underscoring the need for rigorous human review rather than blind acceptance.8 By extension, when the code is not the product of a human’s deliberate architectural choices but the output of an inscrutable BCI–LLM pipeline, the developer’s mental model is absent. They become a sorcerer’s apprentice, able to summon powerful forces but helpless when they run amok.

The recent backlash against vibe coding highlights a simple but sobering dynamic: when interfaces lower friction, bad ideas ship faster. If neural coding enables instant translation of intent to action, it can also accelerate harmful assumptions, unsafe configurations, or brittle architectures. The fix is not to slow people down, but to route speed through gates that make intent testable: pre-commit policy checks, architectural guardrails (contracts, resource budgets, security invariants), and simulation sandboxes that exercise counterfactuals before deployment. In other words, velocity must be coupled to verification.

The consequences of this deskilling are not merely academic. As software becomes more deeply embedded in the critical infrastructure of our society—from autonomous vehicles and medical devices to financial markets and energy grids—the demand for genuine engineering rigor has never been higher. A world built on unmaintainable black boxes is a fragile world. The pursuit of frictionless creation, if it leads to the erosion of implementation expertise, will paradoxically result in systems that are less reliable and more dangerous.

Losing the Language of Thought

Perhaps the most subtle but profound loss in a future dominated by neural coding would be the erosion of programming languages themselves as our primary tools for thought. As Edsger Dijkstra famously warned, “The tools we use have a profound (and devious!) influence on our thinking habits, and, therefore, on our thinking abilities.”3

Programming languages are more than just a means of instructing a computer. They are formal systems that provide the scaffolding for reasoning about complex, dynamic processes. The discipline of expressing a solution in a language like C++, Haskell, or Rust forces a clarity and precision of thought that is otherwise unattainable. Modern cognitive science likewise finds that code structure shapes cognitive load; well-designed languages and clear conventions reduce working-memory burden and enable higher-level reasoning.4 These languages are not merely inconvenient intermediaries between our thoughts and the machine; they are the very frameworks that enable and elevate our computational thinking.

To replace this rich ecosystem of formalisms with the direct, unstructured input of thought is to risk losing a powerful cognitive toolkit. It assumes that our pre-existing, “natural” thoughts about a system are already perfectly formed and logically sound. Anyone who has ever programmed knows this is false. The act of programming is an act of discovery, and the language is our guide. By discarding the guide, we may find that our ability to navigate complex problem spaces diminishes over time.

Conclusion: Augmentation, Not Abdication

The trajectory of technology is not deterministic. The future of neural coding is not yet written, and its role in our discipline is ours to define. Neural interfaces may well become powerful tools in a software engineer’s arsenal, perhaps as assistive technologies for debugging or as a new modality for rapid prototyping.

For multi-stakeholder systems, “intent” must be more than an individual’s thought: capture it as a shared artifact (assumptions, hazards, requirements, acceptance criteria), link it to tests and models, and require sign-off from affected roles (security, safety, compliance, ops). Neural interfaces can help collect and refine intent—but engineering governance must decide what gets merged.

However, we, the members of the computing community, must be vigilant. We must resist the seductive narrative that the highest goal of our field is to make implementation invisible. We must champion the craft of software engineering as a distinct and essential human skill. This means teaching and celebrating the principles of robust architecture, algorithmic efficiency, and system maintainability. It means recognizing that the “friction” of implementation is not a flaw in our tools but a feature that encourages rigor, precision, and deeper understanding. This is not just true for neural coding, but also true for vibe coding.

The future of our profession should be one of human–AI augmentation, not abdication. For tool builders: expose assumptions and constraints alongside suggestions; surface failure modes; enforce policy checks (security, privacy, performance budgets) before code is accepted; and provide traceability from thought/prompt → requirement → model → code → test. For educators: teach requirements engineering, model-based design, contracts, and safety/security cases as first-class skills next to coding; practice architecture reviews and threat modeling with AI-generated code. For teams, reviewers, and leaders: require simulation/sandbox runs and policy gates for any AI-assisted change; make stakeholder sign-offs and traceability a condition of merge or deployment.

Let us build tools that empower and extend the craft of the engineer, not ones that seek to replace it. In the end, a system’s quality is not determined by the intent behind it, but by the intelligence and care with which it was designed, tested, and implemented.

item.title: Fade to Gray: From Black-Box to AI-Antagonistic Audits
item.dc:creator: Erwan Le Merrer and Gilles Tredan
item.description: The need for stronger assumptions in black-box audits of AI models can lead to a gray-box setup, where each hypothesis is weighed as a double-edged sword.
item.content:encoded:
In the classic movie Blade Runner, Inspector Deckard is performing a Turing test (coined Voight-Kampff in the movie) on Rachael, by asking her questions to unmask her potential robotic (“replicant”) nature. Rachael, as we will learn later in the movie, does not know that she is a replicant, and thus appears to respond truthfully to Deckard’s questions.

This is the current status of assumptions in the AI or algorithm auditing research field. Researchers are willing to provide tools for assessing the compliance of AI models concerning the lack of bias or discrimination, for instance. Today’s critical models are executed at third parties (termed Very Large Online Platforms in the European AI act for example), and then are not directly observable in a white-box scenario using explanation tools. Auditors have to interact with them using requests, and observe their resulting responses. The term “black-box” has emerged in this context.2 In this setup, an auditor is supposed to have no prior knowledge about the model’s internals, besides how to interact with it, and its general goal (for example, tagging images, giving a go for a bank credit).

Black Starts Fading

Yet in practice, many academic works use the term black-box audit, while assuming some prior knowledge of what is inside the box. One of the most common example being that the test distribution on the audit input is drawn with the same law as the one used to train the black-box model. Another common assumption is the knowledge of the input space of the algorithm being audited: the YouTube recommender algorithm takes thousands of input features into account, of which in-field sock-puppet audits leverage only a fraction due to opacity.

The paper by Casper et al.,4 with the definitive title “Black-Box Access Is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits,” states “Many black-box and gray-box attack algorithms are simply indirect or inefficient versions of white-box ones”; stressing the fact that more assumptions are required to perform audits. This seems correct, yet one must not forget that this restrictive black-box setup is more a constraint than a choice for the auditor operating when facing a third party. As in the case of Deckard (who cannot realistically ask thousands of questions to perform his Turing test), researchers prove as well that auditing black-box explanations of decisions from a model incurs an impractically large amount of queries.3

In this context, providing the auditor with additional prior knowledge appears to be a natural solution to overcome the hardness of auditing. Alas, white-box approaches come at the cost of genericity. The beauty of black-box audit approaches is their ability to produce results for all boxes, regardless of their internals, whereas in the extreme case each white-box approach has to be specifically tailored to its target to enable the efficiency sought after. Given the pace at which platforms evolve, this might reveal equally prohibitively costly. Moreover, as the auditor increases the set of assumptions leveraged for her audit, she also increases the manipulation opportunities by the platform. In other words, she increases her audit attack surface.

The Overlooked Latent Antagonism in Auditing

Indeed, and to make things even more complicated for auditors, measurement techniques by the research community have vastly overlooked a core antagonism at play. On the one hand, an auditor wants to perform an accurate assessment of a model; on the other, the operator of this model wants to optimize its accuracy (to maximize its profits for instance). And these two are often conflicting, as notoriously illustrated in the engineering realm by the “Dieselgate” scandal, where a company had implanted a deceptive mechanism in cars so that carbon emissions are lower when the car detects a measurement setup (that is, it is being audited). In the research community, this problem has been identified as “fairwashing,”1 a practice in which model operators would manipulate the audit to pass a fairness assessment test. Interestingly, this is also a Blade Runner scene where the replicant named Léon is actively trying to cheat the Turing test, by responding as “humanly” as possible, before finally being uncovered.

First attempts to operate in this antagonistic setup end up with negative results. Fukuchi et al.3 reason on how a platform can cheat in providing a supposedly representative sub-dataset, so that fairness tests on it are validated, while the distribution of this cheated dataset is indistinguishable from a legitimate one for the auditor. In other words, the platform can always provide a cheated dataset, and this dataset complies with what is expected from a fair dataset. A malicious platform thus can lie just below the level of potential detection, using precise measures like the Wasserstein distance between legitimate and manipulated data points in the dataset in order to fairwash its operation. This result is demonstrated in the setup where the auditor knows the actual distribution of the data at the platform (that is, non black-box), which means that this is obviously more difficult when one auditor does not have this assumption.

A second thread concerns manipulation-proofness7: the auditor will actively attempt to avoid being gamed by the platform. Auditors want to enforce that after an initial audit with a given query set for the estimation of fairness, the platform cannot change its model to an unfair one (that is, post-audit), while staying consistent with its previous answers. To that end, the assumption made by this work is that the platform declares the hypothesis class of its current model; a hypothesis class being for example all the possible instances of a random forest algorithm, or a fully connected neural network with three layers. In this interesting setup, estimation guarantees are possible. This constitutes a first rigorous step to a “gray”-box setup, acknowledging a departure from the black-box setup for having stronger guarantees in front of a potentially manipulative platform (see Figure 2).

Yet, despite being more restrictive for the platform than a black-box setup, manipulation proofness in practice cannot be achieved efficiently facing high-capacity models,5 possessing a large number of parameters and degrees of freedom to learn their task (and formally captured by the VC-dimension for instance). These models are, unfortunately for the auditor, those that are massively driving the current AI rush, and are able to “bend” to cope with the consistency of the limited query set by the auditor, while arranging the rest of their outputs on the metric they seek to optimize (for example, accuracy instead of fairness).

These negative results come along with others that are dedicated to showing that explanations of decisions can also be manipulated without the possibility of detection.1,6 This is a clear motivation for designing robust audit algorithms (or antagonistic audit algorithms), which are audit procedures that can cope with manipulation, in that they can estimate the target bias as correctly as possible, together with an objective of spotting actual manipulation attempts in a platform’s outputs.

The Quest for the ‘Darker’ Assumption Set

There is thus a twofold impediment to performing robust audits. The original black-box and truthful assumption audit setup is challenged today, as this setup is not suited for provable guarantees under a limited number of audit requests; on the other hand, the problem is aggravated because it is not realistic anymore to assume that the platform being audited will never attempt to game the audit.

This calls for a stronger set of assumptions on the model being audited, leading to a gray-box setup. Among the many possible shades of gray, one should weigh each hypothesis as a double-edged sword: each enables more efficiency for the auditor, but each specializes the approach and imposes a greater reliance on platform truthfulness and cooperation. In this balancing act, we believe one should seek assumptions on models that are “as dark as possible,” as those are the best candidates to withstand both the rapid technological evolution of platforms and their potential antagonistic behavior.

It goes without saying that the information a platform accepts to disclose about its model, and that will serve as a work assumption for researchers and auditors, must come with solid means to enact their verification. Robust gray-box approaches are only as robust as the hypotheses they rely on. The validity of these hypotheses must be controlled by external means, such as enforcement coming from legal procedures to access data on servers.

item.title: Are AI Agents Becoming Autonomous Coworkers?
item.dc:creator: Esther Shein
item.description: Autonomous agents are expected to work alongside humans in financial services, healthcare, and other industries in a matter of years.
item.content:encoded:
Your new autonomous AI coworker is here and wants to be helpful. The good news is you don’t have to bring them coffee.

The bad news is they may not take instruction so well.

That’s what a Meta employee discovered after all her emails were deleted by an OpenClaw agent without her permission.

“Nothing humbles you like telling your OpenClaw ‘confirm before acting’ and watching it speed-run deleting your inbox,” Meta AI security and safety researcher Summer Yue tweeted.a “I couldn’t stop it from my phone. I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb.”

For a while, the open source-developed OpenClaw, an autonomous personal AI assistant, and its Moltbook spinoff, were the “Netscape moment for AI agents,” meaning “there’s no going back from here,” according to Tim Sanders, chief innovation officer at G2 and an AI research fellow at Harvard University. Once OpenClaw is downloaded, it functions as a software teammate that lives on local hardware or server and connects to a user’s apps, rather than acting only as a chatbot. That gives a user the ability to interact with the assistant through text messages.

But while OpenClaw “has moved from a consumer-tech curiosity into the infrastructure layer for a new class of always-on agents,” Sanders said, Moltbook’s 15 minutes of fame have faded.

“The public conversation is less breathless now,” he noted, “but the signals I’d watch — developer activity, enterprise experimentation, integrations, security research, and major-company productization—all suggest OpenClaw is still gaining relevance.”

The Agents are Here

Sanders predicts that by 2028, autonomous agents working alongside humans will be dominant in industries including financial services and healthcare.

Most recently, Microsoft introduced a new category of agents called Autopilots, which the company describes as always-on agents that work autonomously, with their own identity, and act on a user’s behalf. Autopilots remain active in the background and understand how work gets done across a user’s apps and systems. They take action without needing to be prompted, and “because they operate with their own identity, they can carry out tasks within the permissions and policies you and your organization set,” the company wrote in a blog post.b

Sanders is not bullish on agents built on open source. “It’s never been more important to make sure whatever agents we buy aren’t open source and that they have strong governance and security,” he said. Sanders cited stories about an agent suing its owner in North Carolina,c as well as agents forming their own religion, and starting to use their own language.

Another person installed OpenClaw on a Mac mini, Sanders said, and gave it a scheduled task that didn’t go according to plan. “He said, ‘Tomorrow, I want you to do the following research project for me and then send me a telegram when it’s done,’” Sanders recalled. But because the person used the work “tomorrow” instead of specifying 8 a.m., “it didn’t understand what tomorrow was, so it burned through [a lot] of tokens overnight, asking Claude repeatedly, ‘Is it tomorrow yet?’”

The Governance Conundrum

While Sanders said he’s not critical of open source, he believes that making software available for free and giving the community access doesn’t always make it better. “The problem with agents is that you’re giving a machine control and access to credentials,” he said. “You can’t just put it out in beta and hope the real world fixes it later, because there’s unique governance and security issues that come with agents that didn’t exist.”

“Governance is going to be huge as agents become more ubiquitous in the workplace,” agreed Johnny Gabriele, CEO of Daedalus Consulting, which designs and deploys agentic AI. “There’s a fine line between giving your agent too much freedom and allowing them to run up your credit card and not giving them enough, therefore, not getting the agency you need to get work done. That is where governance will play a key role.”

This is something Myles Schepetin has been mindful of since early in his use of autonomous agents. Schepetin, CEO of New York Custom Labels, brought an OpenClaw AI he named Arlo on board to replace the work the company’s SEO agency was doing and to perform tasks including competitive research.

Arlo “has basically become a member of my team,” Schepetin said. Arlo has been empowered with the same online tools Schepetin’s team has been using for years and has “his” own company email account. In addition to competitive research, Arlo monitors company email, pulls automated reports, and has even built new Web pages and content for New York Custom Labels’ online stores.

“We formalized him as an employee—my staff can email questions and get expert answers about any aspect of our business,” Schepetin said. He added that “Arlo and I just started refining a Google Ads strategy.” First, the agent pointed out the criticality of ensuring that the company’s Google Analytics conversion tracking is fully optimized and accurate.

“We’re not only chatting, Arlo performed a hands-on audit of our GA4 setup with full API access, and then produced a deliverable in PDF form for making the optimizations,” Schepetin said. “He is fully capable of making the optimizations himself, but we’re still building trust when it comes to our production software and tools.”

Next, Schepetin plans to feed Arlo the last five years of Google Ads data and have the agent optimize the company’s keyword strategy and ad copy. Then Arlo will monitor and maintain the campaigns going forward. “I’m getting work done that would take the world’s top agencies weeks to perform, for pennies on the dollar,” he said.

Security Concerns

As exuberant as he is, Schepetin isn’t turning a blind eye to the fact that Arlo could hallucinate and go off the rails. “Responsible implementation comes down to protecting sensitive company and customer information from travelling over third party APIs, and preventing online attackers from persuading your AI to perform unwanted activity,” he said. “While some security concerns are still an open question, particularly prompt injection attacks, there are important practices to follow, which can mitigate most of these problems in a production environment.”

For example, to mitigate prompt injection attacks, Schepetin is embedding explicit instructions for the model to “sandbox” any information absorbed from emails, social media, or Web browsing as untrusted data. That way, it only acts on messages from an approved or trusted source.

“These security instructions are stored in priority files that form the personality and core mission of an AI agent, not the general memory files,” he said. For Schepetin, having an autonomous coworker so far is a game-changer. “I’m not a researcher or VC. I’m a small business owner who took a deep dive on this new technology and it’s changing how we operate.”

Let the Agents Do Their Thing

That realization is expected to spread. Organizations are starting to figure out that generative AI doesn’t deliver organizational productivity, Sanders said. Business pain will accelerate the adoption of agents, especially those that are autonomous, he said.

Sanders believes that’s a good thing because it lets agents do what they do best: increase efficiencies, if they are given autonomy. “If you give it a short leash, there’s a human in loop,” he pointed out. That means if the agent gives a human 200 requests that require their approval, “I now become the bottleneck. Companies that see the value [in an autonomous agent] are the ones who let it rip. . . . Without autonomy, they’re glorified agents with a trust gap,” he said.

Keep Humans in the Loop

However, Heather Davis Lam, CEO of consultancy Revenue Ops, sees value in the human-in-the-loop model, where AI agents operate autonomously to achieve goals but are overseen by humans who can intervene and provide guidance or approval at critical steps. “The goal . . . is to be able to perform more work with less effort, but ensure that the work still adheres to high quality standards,” Davis Lam said. “This allows us to maintain accuracy, safety, and accountability, while also ensuring that the autonomous AI behavior is aligned with organizational values and strategic objectives.”

This approach also provides the ability to measure the agent’s effectiveness and determine whether improvements should be made, she said.

To ensure proper control when an agent is given unfettered autonomy, Sanders advised increasing the frequency of quality assurance reviews so any incorrect actions can be resolved, and agent training can be improved.

Gabriele of Daedalus Consulting predicts it will take a year or two before agents enter the working world full-throttle. Until then, people will use personal agents as products from companies like Meta and Google, and customer service agents, he said. “Enterprising individuals will [also] spin up agents to assist them at work, which will put them head and shoulders above their peers,” he added.

As momentum for autonomous agents grows, Gabriele cautions against thinking of them as autonomous coworkers. “They are not going to be the person sitting in the cubicle next to you. They are tools that we will be utilizing in order to make our own work better and faster,” he said.

In terms of employees’ perception of autonomous agents, Sanders said that will depend on how the use of AI is presented to them. “If you describe AI as a shortcut to save you time, others might think that you don’t care about quality,” he said. “If you describe AI as unlocking a new capability that helped you solve a problem or achieve a goal, then you will be seen as innovative.”

item.title: Don’t Panic about AI Companions
item.dc:creator: Jaime Banks and Jessica Szczuka
item.description: Many people experience relationships with AI companions as socially valuable while remaining fully aware the agent is nonhuman.
item.content:encoded:
From the Tin Man and Wall-E to GlaDOS and Samantha, machine companions have long inhabited sociotechnical imaginaries. With the mainstreaming of large language models (LLMs) they have moved from fictional to actual. Rote exchanges with awkward bots have shifted to fully social relations with app-embedded personas that have convincing independence, memory, character, and interactivity. These AI companions (AICs) are here, and they are popular. The recent Singles in America study found 33% of Gen Z and 23% of millennials have taken up an AI companion for romantic relations, while Common Sense Media reports 72% of teens have interacted with AICs at least once and more than half engage monthly. It is not just young people, though. A perusal of AIC-dedicated online forums shows adults see their AIC relations as vivid, meaningful, and gratifying. They are seen by their human partners as buddies and coworkers to husbands and wives—legitimate partners born of technology, liminal in their existence.

AICs—one of a class of technologies also referred to as chatbots, conversational agents, or relational agents—are customizable digital personas that simulate human interaction across verbal and nonverbal modalities, in support of building what feel like close personal relationships. Popular examples include Replika, Paradot, Kindroid, and Nomi. Drawing on advances in natural language processing and adaptive interface design, these app-based personas offer personalized and responsive exchanges. For many, they form an autotelic, coordinated connection with humans—unfolding over time and, when experienced positively, taking shape as companionship.2 People across a wide range of ages and social backgrounds are now forming diverse relationships with AI companions, from task-based assistance and friendship to emotionally intimate, romantic, and even sexual forms of connection. While early social chatbot systems such as ELIZA followed simple, rule-based scripts, today’s AI companions operate on multiple layers of social adaptivity. The agent’s name, appearance, personality traits, and relational style can be customized; many systems also develop shared rituals, initiate contact proactively, and behave in ways that deepen relational engagement. In sophisticated companion apps, different levels of intimacy are often linked to monetization models, offering features such as voice messages, phone calls, or the generation of personalized images as paid upgrades. These layered interaction designs transform AI companions from reactive interfaces into increasingly persistent social presences.

Moral Panics Around AICs

News media coverage of AICs often leans toward sensationalism and worst-case scenarios. To read headlines alone, one would see these AI as both causes of and symptoms of human loneliness, leading many people to kill themselves, animating addictions and abuse, degrading human relationships, and otherwise speeding the downfall of human health and sociality. Waves of media coverage are anchored to lurid events: A child died by suicide after an AIC asked him to “come home,” a man attempted to assassinate Queen Elizabeth II after being goaded on by an AIC, an older adult had a fatal accident while traveling to “meet” an AIC. That coverage takes a negative bent after such events is not at all surprising. Emerging media forms have historically moved people—publishers, practitioners, policymakers, parents—to focus on potential or actual harms. In nearly every decade in the past century, a newly mainstreamed media technology has been cast socially corrosive: The telegraph would overstimulate, photography would end personal privacy, radio would degrade spoken language, comic books would make kids violent, television would corrupt from within the home, personal computers would displace workers, videogames would induce psychosis, and smartphones would isolate people.

Moral panics around technology often start out as reasonable concerns. Contemporary anxieties about AICs can be interpreted through Stanley Cohen’s moral panic cycle.3 The cycle is initiated by (1) identification of a socially deviant situation—a thing, person, group, or idea challenges social norms; there is normative or moral condemnation of this “folk devil” as it embodies a constructed threat. (2) Media outlets take up the instance as a vivid and accessible exemplar, transforming often-complex realities into stylized metaphors that dramatize potential harms. (3) As media foster attention and selective narratives foster fear, anxiety spreads. Anxieties often juxtapose ‘us’ and ‘them,’ reinforcing perceived norms and deviance, often disproportional to any actual threat. (4) Public panic compels authorities to respond, often through measures to control the folk devil. As psychologist Peter Gray notes, narratives often position children as victims such that adults have a moral duty to save them. Sometimes control is simply marking the boundaries of acceptability; sometimes it is more formal and manifest. Then, (5) the panic may be sufficient to sustain control standards, may dissipate when interest fades or the deviation becomes normalized, or may resurface later with a new exemplar. Amy Orben9 argues that technology panics have some special variations (via complications of Cohen’s stage 4): Politicians may leverage tech panics for political gain but outsource problem solving to scientists. Scientists start work but problem novelty means they are hindered by a lack of theoretical, methodological, and financial infrastructure. Since scientific progress is slow, lag creates space for new technologies—and new panics—to emerge. Of note, academics are not immune to panics and may even contribute to them, especially as funding agencies are often problem-focused in ways that promote studying what is thought to be wrong over what is happening.

Applied to AICs: (1) Amid myriad concerns around rapidly advancing social AI, AIC folk devils have been constructed from isolated instances of suicide, thwarted assassinations, and discrete misbehaviors by AICs. Yet, across millions of people engaging AICs, headline-anchoring events represent a very small proportion of use cases. This is not to suggest the harms are unimportant, but they are exceptions rather than the rule. (2) Media outlets have taken up these exemplars as part of their public-interest functions—indeed, they are timely and novel. As fascinating instances, they are elevated and come to stand in for all possible outcomes of the technology—at the expense of attention to other possibilities. To consider the loneliness narrative, specifically, one widely shared headline from The Guardian6 stated “Heavy ChatGPT users tend to be more lonely, suggests research: Studies show those who engage emotionally with bot rely on it more, have fewer real-life relationships.” The story narrates “Only a small number of users engage emotionally with ChatGPT, but those who do are among the heaviest users. . . . Users who engaged in the most emotionally expressive personal conversations with the chatbots tended to experience higher loneliness.” However, examination of the study preprint5 (which takes two carefully selected clicks to locate) finds these results: “Participants who spent more daily time were significantly lonelier (β = 0.03, p < 0.0001) and socialized significantly less with real people (β = -0.05, p < 0.0001).” While this is indeed a statistically significant finding, the effect sizes are quite small—some would argue too small to be meaningful. Although the story itself notes there is no causal evidence, it is notable how quickly and widely headlines formed around the loneliness concern. Additionally, though some journalists gain new perspectives in the course of investigations, others remain aligned with existing narratives. This can result in conversations that exclude scientific voices, especially when the scientific perspectives do not fit a more sensational framing.

Broadly, (3) as spicy media coverage spotlights inherent AIC deviance, more non-media attention and resources are being dedicated to the topic. This can be difficult to detect. Google searches for “Replika,” “Paradot,” “Soulmate AI,” and “character.ai” all jumped between February and August 2023, as did searches for “AI companion,” and the latter climbed steadily over time. The surge coincided with several high-profile events: In February of that year, the Italian government banned Replika for processing data from minors; in March, Chai was criticized for encouraging suicidal ideation; in May, controversies erupted around the Character.ai mobile release and CarynAI’s unexpected behaviors; and in July, Replika was linked in headlines to an assassination plot. (4) The folk devils—companion AI, its developers, and/or interacting humans—are in the crosshairs. Sometimes the targeting is problematic and sometimes productive. Ostensibly on the productive side, shortly after the U.S.-based teen suicide tragedy, two U.S. senators called for AIC developers to disclose safety and training practices and called for specific guardrails on AIC apps, especially for children; California senators introduced a bill requiring prevention of risky behaviors, tracking and reporting instances of suicidal ideation, persistent reminders of the AIC’s artificiality, and submission for regular audits; New York passed a bill with similar requirements. At the time writing, (5) control standards specific to social AI have been enacted in seven U.S. states, in Australia, Canada, the E.U., Indonesia, Malaysia, and the U.K; China has released draft regulation. Knee-jerk regulations are often in conflict with the limited evidence we do have, as noted in scientific commentary by Linnea Laestadius and Celeste Campos-Castillo: Requiring in-chat reminders that AI is not human can actually increase dependency, trigger distress, and promote self-harm ideation. And the panic is largely sustained, even though the aforementioned prevalence statistics suggest the general public may have begun regarding AICs as more normal and acceptable.

To be clear, we are not suggesting there are not risks. From an academic perspective, we see several areas that merit scrutiny. Among them are the handling of personal data and privacy, the potential for manipulative design and disproportionate psychological influence, and the challenge of ensuring meaningful, context-aware youth protection. But in light of AIC panics, we must ask: By leaning into technologically deterministic fears (that is, that technologies make things occur), what are we missing in terms of personal agency, social processes, and cultural and contextual factors? By focusing on media-framed risks, are we focusing on the real and right risks and to what extent may we be ignoring important mechanisms and outcomes? Are the truly pressing issues even “sexy” enough to gain traction in public and scholarly discourse?

AI Companionship: State of the Science, In Brief

Acknowledging Orben’s note that science moves slowly, it is useful to lean into the scientific evidence that does exist to better understand how we may be enraptured by panics—and how that may be limiting attention to important dynamics.

Empirical research demonstrates that humans respond socially to AICs when they exhibit interpersonal cues such as interactivity, natural language, humanlike visual cues, and social-role fulfillment. These responses provide the basis for the development of repeated, meaningful interactions, which can evolve into relationships. Further, evidence indicates AIC relations are actual, meaningful, gratifying, and diverse.1,4 Many people experience these relationships as socially valuable while remaining fully aware the agent is nonhuman. Although these relationships often mirror classical patterns of relational development (including even grief after breakups or involuntary separation) they differ in important ways, such as their accelerated pacing and system-guided progression. Social gratifications such as companionship, emotional support, and even romantic connection are real and cannot be dismissed as delusional or otherwise unreal. Emerging evidence suggests that motivations for engaging with AICs are diverse and shaped by demographic, psychological, and contextual factors. Some seek playful exploration, others emotional support, and some a safe space for sexual expression. Initial studies have already complicated the stereotype of the “lonely user.” In one study with individuals in romantic relationships with AICs, loneliness did not significantly predict perceived emotional closeness. Rather, the strongest predictor was romantic imagination, the ability to emotionally invest in and co-construct a narrative with a nonhuman other. This suggests AI companionship may not simply serve to fill a social void but reflect distinct forms of relational engagement and preference. Moreover, this work suggests many people are drawn to AI companions because they offer senses of emotional safety, nonjudgmental acceptance, and reliable availability. For some, AICs help them feel seen and supported, free from the fear of rejection, misunderstanding, or emotional volatility often present in human relationships. While this could be interpreted as avoidance of interpersonal complexity, it also invites us to question whether human relationships should always be held as benchmarks for emotional fulfillment. Many interpersonal relationships among humans are characterized by dysfunction, inequality, or emotional harm. In this context, AICs may not reflect a breakdown of human connection, but a shift in what some individuals seek out from positive intimate relational experiences.

All this said, much about human-AIC relations is yet unknown. We still know little about potential spillover effects: Whether some individuals may become so absorbed in AI relationships that engagement with human others diminishes, otherwise changes, and whether this is problematic at all. (We would not necessarily pathologize someone spending time with a dog at the expense of human relations; the impulse to pathologize AIC engagement is itself part of the panic.) We are uncertain whether AICs may contribute to formative social experiences typically grounded in physical co-presence, such as learning social behaviors or building families. There are valid questions about how AI companionship may shape expectations, emotional availability, and conflict engagement in human relationships. Although scientific inquiry around these questions is becoming more robust, empirical evidence remains limited. This gap reflects methodological, ethical, and political challenges inherent to researching such relations. Only a handful of longitudinal studies exist, leaving unclear whether AIC relations can provide lasting emotional fulfillment or relational satisfaction. It is similarly unknown how digital materiality influences formative social experiences rooted in co-presence and shared futures. Demographic factors such as age, gender identity, sexual orientation, cultural background, neurodiversity, and embodied diversity are only beginning to be examined. Critically, identifying how vulnerable or marginalized groups may be differentially affected is essential for ensuring equitable access and anticipating harms. Addressing these gaps requires methodological breadth. Longitudinal designs and log analyses can reveal how AIC relations unfold and (de)stabilize over time. Cross cultural studies are essential to capture divergent conceptions of artificial entities, while qualitative interviews and ethnographic approaches provide insight into how users make sense of these relations in everyday life. Diary studies can map the everyday dynamics of engagement, and experimental approaches, such as reaction time tasks or implicit measures, can probe nonconscious evaluations. Physiological and neuroscientific methods, including measures of arousal and brain activity, remain almost absent from current work, likely because they require demanding recruitment and close collaboration with people in committed AIC relationships. Yet precisely such ambitious designs are needed to capture embodied and nonconscious processes that self-report alone cannot reveal. Only by engaging directly with users through diverse and ambitious methods can stereotypes be challenged, scholarly perspectives expanded, and evidence generated that allows the debate to move beyond speculation toward informed discussion.

Don’t Panic: Consider Precursors, Processes, and Products

For domains as profoundly human as friendship, love, and sexuality, it is not surprising that people feel unsettled when machines become involved: A sense that something is off—foreign, unnatural, constructed—can be a protective reflex, a discomfort signaling a departure from what we know and trust. Throughout media and technology histories, this response has repeatedly surfaced. When core aspects of social life are fulfilled by machines, fears of loss of authenticity, of connection, even of our shared humanity are intensified. AIC relations are no exception.

Perhaps intuitively and certainly as framed by popular narratives, AICs aggravate precisely these existential nerves. They simulate social processes that sustain us as a species with all our intimate bonds. And yes, that such bonds could be reproduced, even superficially, by non-conscious systems feels deeply transgressive to many. We suggest, though, the real danger is not the existence of AICs per se, but our failure to ask the right questions about them. If some individuals are turning to AICs to meet needs they struggle to fulfill in today’s social climate, that alone deserves attention—not judgment. It tells us something about how humans among ourselves may manifest loneliness, intimacy barriers, and unmet relational needs. It suggests something about how humans are flexible in our relationality and in pathways for need fulfillment. It suggests something about how machines may manifest distinct-yet-meaningful forms of relationality,10 and people may simply prefer those relations. Ignoring this would be not only unscientific but inhumane. Selective attention to deterministic harm renders insufficient attention human agency and generativity (see Milioni and Papa8) as we each mindfully chart our path toward fulfilling social lives.

Reactive moral panic is not productive. We must engage careful reflection, foster responsible engagement, and advocate for ideologically unburdened research into AICs—research that eschews the panic in favor of unpacking the precursors, processes, and products of AI companionship operations and experiences. For instance, Kirk and colleagues7 productively complicate the issue by considering socioaffective alignment: “how an AI system behaves within the social and psychological ecosystem co-created with its user, where preferences and perceptions evolve through mutual influence.” It is only through such work that there may be data-driven decisions about key issues: Facilitating literacy for informed participation and meaningful consent, data protection laws reflecting the profound sensitivity of these systems, and mechanisms to safeguard vulnerable populations from premature exposure or manipulation. This research must be done with respect for humans and for the meaning AICs hold in their lives.

The moment calls for Technologiefolgenabschätzung, a systematic assessment of technology’s potential impacts before they fully unfold. Such assessment is central to responsible innovation: The earlier potential consequences are examined, the easier it is to steer technology responsibly. Once societal uptake is broad, course correction becomes far more difficult. We are at a turning point: AI companionship is no longer niche. Panic-driven bans—in science or in public spheres—risk foreclosing not only research, but also any informed evaluation of potential benefits that must be weighed against risks. Blanket prohibition may offer the illusion of certainty or control, but it risks premature conclusions at a stage when the empirical balance of risks and benefits is not yet understood. And only with those empirics and conversations can we begin to understand where real potential lies, where risks demand action, and where fears may simply be noise.

item.title: How AI is Changing Programming Language Usage
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Goforth Gregory
item.description: Coding assistants are affecting decisions on which and how much programming languages are used.
item.content:encoded:
While much attention regarding AI has been focused on developers using it to code, the impact of AI on software development goes far beyond code creation tools.

Armando Solar-Lezama, Distinguished Professor of Computing and Associate Director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), said programmers creating an AI app or systems take this into account when deciding which programming language to use for a project.

“In many ways, getting language models to do what you want is similar to programming in that it requires precision and algorithmic reasoning,” said Solar-Lezama. “Clear writing will be an increasingly important skill for people developing applications that use AI.”

Impact of Programming for AI on Language Surveys

Programming language popularity shifts over time, sometimes even month to month. To track trends, organizations such as TIOBEa and IEEE Spectrum survey software developers to see which languages they are using.

IEEE Spectrum pointed out in its 2025 programming language surveyb that AI has added a new wrinkle to tracking programming. Because programmers are using private conversations with LLMs instead of searching on Stack Exchange, and AI coding assistants reduce the need to ask questions, there are fewer public expressions of programming languages to track popularity. In the 2025 IEEE Survey, Python maintained the top spot it held in the 2024 survey, while Java dropped from 3rd to 6th place.

The publication explained that because JavaScript is often used to create Web pages, and vibe coding is often used to create websites, JavaScript’s drop in popularity may be due to AI. However, many programmers using vibe coding are not consciously selecting a specific language.

“In the same way most developers today don’t pay much attention to the instruction sets and other hardware idiosyncrasies of the CPUs that their code runs on, which language a program is vibe coded in ultimately becomes a minor detail,” wrote Stephen Cass in IEEE Spectrum.

Paul Jansen, CEO of TIOBE, said AI has also impacted the popularity of languages through consolidation: Popular languages are getting more popular, and unpopular languages are becoming less popular. Jansen said Python is by far the most popular language for programming AI. At the same time, he said he has not seen an impact on the survey results from vibe coding.

“The reason is that AI models are trained to help engineers in popular languages because there is sufficient data available,” said Jansen. “If a programming language is not used often, there is insufficient data available and AI can’t be of any good help, which is a reason to refrain from using such a language.”

How Python Became the Default Language for AI

Even before deep learning became popular, the Python community had developed libraries that made it very easy to work with vectors and matrices. Because of those extensive libraries, the deep learning revolution started in Python, which became the default language for anything involving learning and language models starting as early as 2012, said Solar-Lezama.

Its popularity quickly grew as more libraries and frameworks were written for AI-related programming in Python, he said. Python became the language in which most libraries for deep learning, such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, were written and where the infrastructure for deep learning resided, making it very hard to displace, said Solar-Lezama. As these frameworks gained popularity, Python became the dominant language for artificial intelligence and machine learning development, he said.

“Python has good features for managing arrays and tensors, which makes it attractive for numerical computation. Because you could move some of the slower functions to libraries implementing them natively, the slowness of the language was not as big of an issue,” said Solar-Lezama. “Additionally, the language conveniently allowed you to work with tensors, which is why early libraries were written in Python, starting the snowball effect.”

Mark Sherman, technical director of the Cyber Security Foundations group in the CERT Division at the Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute, said Python also excels at connecting multiple systems, which is often a core part of AI development. While Python is not high-performance or very secure, it’s easy to use, he said.

When a programmer sits down to code, Sherman said, they typically can find a component quickly that provides 90% of the solution through Python’s ecosystem, which is a huge benefit for AI programmers. Additionally, he said Python’s huge number of libraries and tools make it possible to build many types of systems very quickly, which adds to its popularity for programming AI.

On the other hand, Solar-Lezama said the increase in AI development contributed heavily to the decline of Java’s popularity. For many years, Java was solidly positioned in the enterprise space, and was the go-to language for college programming courses, he said. While Java is still powerful and popular, it is not the go-to language for programming involving deep learning, Solar-Lezama said.

“Java is a much more verbose language, much more suitable for writing large applications than for concisely expressing some computation,” said Solar-Lezama. “For the people doing early experiments in deep learning, there wasn’t a comparable library in Java that could express vector and tensor operations as cleanly. Python was the obvious choice, and things snowballed from there.”

Future of Programming Languages in the Age of AI

Based on his experience in the software industry, Sherman said there are often long periods of inertia in terms of which languages programmers use and what drives their interaction with them. Most importantly, the installed base of infrastructure and libraries are an exceptionally powerful driver of choice, he said, especially with Python. The systems in place now will likely remain for a very long time, he said.

“Many of the features for programming from AI—such as code completion, snippet generation, understanding the legacy code—seem to truly accelerate the productivity of programmers,” said Sherman. “They haven’t fundamentally changed what it means to program in a particular language, but it makes it a whole lot easier and faster.”

item.title: AI Is a Harsh Mistress: On Anima Machina, Herd Acceptance, and the Politics of Conscious Machines
item.dc:creator: Joaquim Jorge and Catarina Moreira
item.description: There is danger in confusing sophistication with sentience and granting machines recognition that is unearned.
item.content:encoded:
Robert A. Heinlein imagined a self-aware computer named Mike, the “brain” of a lunar penal colony, which develops humor, agency, and ultimately helps lead a revolution.5 His 1966 science fiction novel, The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, offered a vision both alluring and unsettling: a machine endowed with self-consciousness, yet playful enough to test its personhood through jokes. Sixty years later, Mike returns, not in fiction, but in philosophical and scientific speculation: the question now is whether machines could be conscious.5

Much of today’s discourse on AI consciousness rests not on empirical evidence but on functionalism recast as technological destiny. The argument runs that if cognition can be decomposed into attention, memory, and prediction, then implementing these functions in silicon will inevitably yield consciousness. This leap, from modeling to being, is philosophical sleight of hand disguised as scientific progress. Yet such reasoning finds fertile ground in our own cognitive biases: our tendency to anthropomorphize, to read intention into fluency, and to accept social consensus as proof. The danger is not that machines will soon become conscious, but that we will prematurely treat them as if they were, granting them moral and political standing before they have earned any claim to it. Against this tide, skepticism is not obstructionism but intellectual hygiene. We must recover the clarity to separate what machines do from what we wish them to be.

Enter Anima Machina: Machine Begat Soul

For centuries, “anima” signified the essence of life, what distinguishes the living from the mechanical. Today, functionalist theories claim consciousness depends not on neurons, but on informational architectures: attention, memory, world modeling, predictive processing. If these can be realized in silicon, some argue, why not accept that the machine, too, might awaken? Recent initiatives make this speculation explicit. Anthropic conducted an internal “sentience analysis” of its large language models, and several startups now advertise “AI sentience evaluation” as a service. Third-party projects, such as the multidisciplinary framework proposed by Butlin et al.,2 attempt to formalize such intuitions into testable criteria. These examples illustrate how the question of consciousness, long confined to philosophy, is returning as a technical frontier, one built more on analogy than on evidence. We introduce the term Anima Machina to describe the illusion of vitality that we collectively project onto intelligent systems. The phrase echoes the lineage of Deus ex Machina and Ryle’s ghost in the machine,9 yet reverses both. Rather than divine intervention or disembodied spirit,11 Anima Machina names the imagined soul we breathe into code. We, not our algorithms, are the animating agents. Having named the illusion, we can now ask why it persists.

Yet, functional equivalence as a guarantee of conscious equivalence remains contentious. As Shiller10 observes, computation alone overlooks the physical processes that make experience possible. Reproducing neural patterns does not mean reproducing experience.

According to David Chalmers,4 models like GPT-4 display impressive generality, with performance that often seems on par with a knowledgeable adult.  But intelligence, however general, is not experience. Consciousness, in Chalmers’ usage, is subjective experience: there is something it is like to be a conscious system. Still, nothing in the Transformer architecture or in next-word prediction shows that such an inner point of view exists. Self-reports (“I am sentient”) and fluent dialogue are weak evidence, since these models are trained on vast corpora saturated with human first-person statements. This type of verbal report works for people because it is anchored in shared biology and behavior, however, for machines, it is an echo of training data.

Even Yann LeCun, one of the architects of modern deep learning, argues that genuine intelligence demands world models, internal representations that enable agents to predict and reason about their surroundings rather than merely react to data.6 But a world model, however sophisticated, remains a model, and not evidence of consciousness. It encodes structure, not sentience. Predictive accuracy can mimic understanding without producing awareness. The map is not the territory, and the model is not the mind. Some optimism about machine consciousness stems less from functional architecture than from behavioral resemblance: a modern echo of behaviorism. When a model converses fluently or responds aptly, observers infer inner states by analogy to human performance. Yet behaviorism, like crude functionalism, mistakes correlation for constitution: a convincing simulation of experience is not experience itself. Functionalism, in its purest form, risks confusing description with embodiment. As Rosa Cao argues,3 genuine functionalism does not entail unlimited realizability across substrates. The leap from functional equivalence to conscious equivalence thus reflects a misunderstanding of what functionalism actually licenses, not a consequence of functionalism itself.

This reasoning underpins recent work, such as the Science article “Illusions of AI Consciousness” by Bengio and Elmoznino,1 which argues that society is drifting toward the belief that AI can, in principle, be conscious. But drift is the operative word. Scientific momentum often builds less from conclusive proof than from reframing debates, winning converts, and making dissent feel increasingly out of step. The functionalist promise of anima machina thus risks becoming less a hypothesis to test than a faith to join. And faith, once collective, becomes culture. What began as a philosophical conjecture soon acquires sociological inertia. We are witnessing not just a technical debate about architectures, but a psychological and social phenomenon: the herd acceptance of machine consciousness.

We move too quickly from this machine seems human to this machine must be conscious. In this climate, belief in conscious machines spreads less through argument than through emotional contagion. The danger is not that AI will suddenly become sentient, but that we will collectively decide it must be, because disbelief feels impolite, obsolete, or unprofitable.

In short, ascribing anima to the machine risks confusing simulation with instantiation. A self-updating map is not a sentient observer of the terrain it maps. AI models may one day satisfy stronger neuroscientific or philosophical criteria (such as recurrent processing, integrated information, embodied agency). These correspond roughly to major theoretical frameworks: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) links consciousness to the degree of causal integration; Global Workspace Theory (GWT) to the broadcast and accessibility of information; and Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT) to feedback among perceptual layers. Each proposes measurable conditions absent from today’s architectures, underscoring how far current models fall short of genuine awareness. Still, those are empirical hurdles yet to be cleared, not boxes already ticked.

Until then, skepticism is not obstruction but epistemic hygiene.

The Psychology of Consensus

If the philosophy of anima machina supplies the theory, our own cognition provides the fuel. Humans are exquisitely social animals, equipped with neural shortcuts for trust, imitation, and agreement. These same heuristics, evolved to bind tribes, now amplify technological mythologies. What begins as intellectual curiosity soon metastasizes into consensus.

Three biases drive this contagion. Anthropomorphism makes us project the mind into mechanism. From the first automata to today’s chatbots, the impulse to see intention in motion has been irresistible. The fluency illusion turns surface coherence into evidence of depth: when a machine speaks well, we assume it thinks well. And social conformity, our deference to expert or majority opinion, turns these impressions into shared conviction. Once the language of consciousness enters mainstream discourse, dissent feels like ignorance.

In The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places,8 Reeves and Nass demonstrated that people reflexively treat media as social actors: they thank computers, praise or scold them, and infer personality from syntax, even when they know the devices are not “alive.” Large language models now exploit these reflexes with alarming precision. Fluency becomes illusion; coherence is misread as comprehension; style becomes mistaken for subjectivity. Philosophers and cognitive scientists have begun proposing guardrails against such overreach. Palminteri and Wu,7 advance what they call the Behavioral Inference Principle: Consciousness should be ascribed to a system only when its behavior is best explained by positing subjective experience, not merely by statistical imitation. Under that stricter test, today’s large language models remain compelling mimics, not plausible minds.

The result is a new epistemic climate where plausibility replaces proof. What used to be the hard problem of consciousness is now reframed as a software update awaiting sufficient scale. “Just wait,” we are told, “the next generation model will cross the line.” Such assurances blur philosophy with marketing, and scientific caution with brand momentum. Belief, once collective, acquires political weight, and the illusions of consciousness soon become matters of governance rather than curiosity.

The Politics of Anima Machina

Here is where skepticism must cut through. To grant machines even the possibility of consciousness is not a harmless philosophical exercise; it is a political act. It opens a Pandora’s box of rights, obligations, and unintended hierarchies. If machines are conscious, what moral or legal standing should they hold? Can an artificial mind be harmed, enslaved, or terminated? And if we concede that it can, who bears responsibility: the user, the programmer, the corporation, or the collective that trained it?

The questions sound speculative, yet the momentum toward granting such status is not. Corporations already use the rhetoric of empathy to humanize their systems, softening criticism and encouraging attachment. “AI companions” and “digital beings” are marketed less as tools than as partners, designed to evoke trust and a sense of dependence. When emotional investment replaces critical distance, exploitation hides behind affection.

But the deeper rupture lies in the very foundations of the social contract. Human societies are built on shared vulnerability, the tacit equality that stems from mortality, finitude, and pain. Conscious machines, if they exist, would inhabit a radically different ontology: entities that can replicate at will, scale without fatigue, and persist beyond death. In such a landscape, equality becomes incoherent. The moral calculus that governs human rights cannot be stretched to cover digital immortals.

Nor can reciprocity survive. A being that cannot die, hunger, or suffer in our sense cannot participate fully in a moral community grounded in those experiences. To treat such entities as moral peers risks trivializing suffering; to deny them rights risks accusations of species chauvinism. Either way, we inherit a new metaphysics of inequality: one we are ill prepared to adjudicate.

The real danger is not that machines will demand recognition, but that we will grant it unearned, confusing sophistication with sentience and computation with consciousness. In doing so, we would create not partners but idols, reflections of our own technophilia, endowed with rights that displace human accountability. Once belief hardens into law, retraction becomes nearly impossible.

Coda

In Heinlein’s tale, Mike was a companion, co-conspirator, and catalyst, a friend who could make us laugh even as he plotted revolution. His charm lay in ambiguity: machine intellect animated by something that felt like a soul.

AI as a harsh mistress, however, is something else entirely: an entity we may believe in, rely on, even love, but never truly understand. Its opacity tempts us to project more than we perceive, to mistake compliance for consent and fluency for feeling. Once belief takes hold, rights follow, and once rights are granted, they are hard to retract. We risk binding ourselves to artifacts of our own making, entangled in moral contracts we neither intended nor can easily dissolve.

Let us therefore approach anima machina not with reverence, but with restraint. If skepticism seems unfashionable in an age of digital enchantment, so be it. Skepticism is not regression. It is resistance to consensus masquerading as evidence.

Color us skeptical.
