item.title: In Memoriam: Peter G. Neumann (1932-2026)
item.dc:creator: Eugene Spafford and Simson Garfinkel
item.description: A single conversation with Albert Einstein in 1952 shaped Neumann's intellectual life and planted the seed that guided his research career.
item.content:encoded:
Peter Gabriel Neumann—known throughout the field as PGN—died on May 17, 2026, aged 93, from complications of a traumatic fall. For seven decades, he chronicled how computer systems fail and patiently advocated for the principles that make them fail less often.

Neumann was born on Sept. 21, 1932, in New York City. He entered Harvard University in 1952 as a math major and took three Harvard degrees: an A.B. in mathematics (1954), and an S.M. (1955) and Ph.D. (1961) in applied mathematics. A Fulbright fellowship took him to Germany’s Technische Hochschule Darmstadt for a second doctorate, a Doctor rerum naturalium (1960). As an undergraduate, he took several graduate courses in computer-related topics, including Howard Aiken’s 1953 architecture course, and that summer, he programmed punch cards at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory. He dated his career as a computing professional to that year.

A single conversation shaped his intellectual life. In November 1952, while singing with the Harvard Glee Club at Princeton, Neumann was invited to breakfast with Albert Einstein and spent more than two hours discussing complexity in mathematics, physics, cosmology, and, at length, music. Asked about Brahms, Einstein grimaced: “I have never understood Brahms. I believe he was burning the midnight oil, trying to be complicated.”a Einstein’s dictum—that everything should be made as simple as possible, but no simpler—became, in Neumann’s own telling, the seed of every research program of his career.

Neumann worked at Bell Labs from 1960 to 1970, spending the first five years on error-correcting codes and survivable communications before becoming, from 1965 to 1969, a central figure in the Multics operating system project. With Bob Daley, he designed the Multics file system, including multilevel tree-structured directories, access-control lists, symbolic links, and backup mechanisms that modern systems still use. As one of the “triumvirate” running Multics with Fernando Corbató and Charlie Clingen, Neumann imposed the discipline for which Multics became known: No one was permitted to write a line of code until they had submitted a complete written English-language specification of the module’s behavior. Multics, he later observed, solved the Y2K problem in 1965 and made stack buffer overflows impossible by construction.1

Neumann moved to SRI in Menlo Park in 1971, where he worked for more than five decades as senior principal scientist and later chief scientist. Known for his warmth, kindness, and generosity, he fostered a worldwide community of researchers, historians, and journalists who catalog and publicize the risks of computing’s expanding role in daily life.

In 1976, when ACM SIGSOFT was formed, Neumann founded ACM SIGSOFT’s Software Engineering Notes (SEN), editing it for 19 years. A SEN column on computer-related mishaps spawned, in 1985, the ACM Risks Forum—known to its readers as comp.risks or the RISKS Digest, and at its peak, one of the most widely read mailing lists on the Internet. He moderated RISKS for 41 years, until April 2026, and curated more than 250 “Inside Risks” columns in Communications of the ACM.

Less than a week after he arrived at SRI, Larry Roberts of ARPA’s Information Processing Techniques Office visited, asking for a project on fault-tolerant computing; Neumann reframed the request as a trustworthiness problem, with fault tolerance as one aspect of it. The work fed into SRI’s Software Implemented Fault Tolerance (SIFT) project, which ran at NASA Langley for roughly 25 years and produced the foundational work on byzantine agreement by Lamport, Shostak, and Pease. From 1973 to 1983, Neumann led the design of PSOS, the Provably Secure Operating System: a tagged, capability-based, formally specified architecture. PSOS was never built; the era’s proof technology was inadequate.

In the mid-1980s, with his colleague Dorothy Denning, Neumann designed and built the Intrusion Detection Expert System (IDES). His involvement continued with Teresa Lunt’s NIDES and, from 1996, Phil Porras’s EMERALD. Those efforts are the conceptual ancestors of many current intrusion and anomaly detection systems. From 2010 on, as principal investigator of the SRI–University of Cambridge CTSRD project under DARPA’s CRASH program, he led work on CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions): a clean-slate hardware-software co-design that revives capability-based protection at the instruction-set level. The architectural lineage was unmistakably from PSOS; CHERI has since moved from research prototype to commercial silicon, including Arm’s Morello platform.

Neumann was heavily involved in public policy beyond RISKS. He participated in four National Academies studies on computer security and cryptography: Multilevel Data Management Security (1982); Computers at Risk (1991); Cryptography’s Role in Securing the Information Society (CRISIS) (1996); and Toward a Safer and More Secure Cyberspace (2007). He co-authored the 2015 “Keys Under Doormats” report, which argued against mandated cryptographic backdoors. An early critic of paperless electronic voting, he was a principal investigator of the NSF ACCURATE center on voting-system integrity. He co-founded People For Internet Responsibility and chaired the ACM Committee on Computers and Public Policy for decades.

ACM Fellow and former ACM president Barbara Simons recalled, “While Peter made significant technical contributions to the field of computer science, I shall remember him for his social conscience. For as long as I knew him, he addressed issues stemming from the widespread use of computers. In the 1990s, he was one of the first to warn about the risks of computers in elections, many of which are still with us today. I shall miss the warm, funny man whom I knew and the critical voice that was widely respected, but too often ignored.”

Neumann was famous for his many puns. He is sometimes credited with naming the “emasculated one-user Multics” that emerged at Bell Labs after AT&T withdrew from the Multics project. “My guess is that some AT&T lawyers eventually decided that the punned name (Unics) did not reflect well on the corporate image, and insisted that it be changed . . . to Unix,” Neumann wrote in 2012. “It came a-pun a midnight clear.”b

ACM Fellow Susan Landau first met Neumann when ACM hired her to work on their encryption study. She recalled, “[I will remember] Peter’s overwhelming kindness, which I experienced through various co-authored papers on encryption and surveillance policy over the years. Peter’s gentleness and good will got us through multiple sticky situations involving herding cats. Many mourn Peter and his multiple contributions to the field; I miss his overwhelming love of the world and the people in it.”

Music and tai chi were Neumann’s lifelong counterweights to computing. As an undergraduate, he played in the Harvard-Radcliffe Orchestra, sang on RCA’s recording of Berlioz’s Damnation of Faust with the Boston Symphony, co-founded the Harvard Opera Guild—playing bassoon in the pit orchestra of its production of The Barber of Seville—and conducted and performed Gilbert and Sullivan.1 ACM Fellow and former ACM president Peter Denning recalled, “Dorothy [Denning] and I were recorder players, and we occasionally got together with Peter and friends to play music. Peter surprised us once by playing a duet on two recorders, one on each side of his mouth. He had great fun doing this thing, which no one else could come close to.” Neumann played multiple instruments and was active in several musical groups. At computer security conferences, it was a tradition for him to lead his colleagues in song.

An SRI Fellow and a Fellow of the ACM, IEEE, and AAAS, Neumann received the ACM Outstanding Contribution Award (1992), the EFF Pioneer Award (1996), the CPSR Norbert Wiener Award (1997), the National Computer System Security Award (2002), the ACM SIGSAC Outstanding Contributions Award (2005), the CRA Distinguished Service Award (2013), the EPIC Lifetime Achievement Award (2018), and was inducted into the National Cyber Security Hall of Fame (2012).

The thread of Neumann’s career runs back to that breakfast with Einstein. Multics, PSOS, IDES, SEN, RISKS, CHERI—each was an argument that complexity in computing is not merely an engineering nuisance but a moral problem, because complex systems hide their failures and harm their users in ways simpler systems do not. He never relinquished his belief that the Multics architectural discipline had been right. As he put it in his 2013 oral history: “Simplicity gets complex quickly. As soon as you believe you have a simple solution to something, you’re probably oversimplifying.”1

Neumann’s first marriage ended in divorce; he was predeceased by his second wife, Elizabeth S. Neumann, by his sons John and Chris, and by his stepson Timothy B. Luntzel. He is survived by his daughter, Helen Krutina (“Hellie”) Neumann, and by his stepsons Mark Barnabas Luntzel and Timothy Luntzel.

item.title: Illuminating Secrets: Power LED-Based Side-Channel Attacks for Key Extraction and Eavesdropping
item.dc:creator: Ben Nassi
item.description: Modern sensors with sampling rates comparable to the CPU rates of IoT devices create risks to user privacy and information confidentiality.
item.content:encoded:
The Internet of Things (IoT) revolution,7 which began 20 years ago, has ushered in a new era of computing. Consumers have embraced numerous IoT devices,6 such as robotic vacuum cleaners, smart assistants, and video streamers, as replacements for traditional devices in smart cities, homes, offices, businesses, and other settings. These IoT devices are typically designed with minimal central processing unit (CPU) power to maintain an affordable price point for consumers and maximize revenue for manufacturers. Simultaneously, sensor technology has made significant advancements, following Moore’s Law, resulting in sensors that offer high sampling rates and sensitivity2 while becoming more affordable each year.

Key Insights

  • Some modern sensors can now sample at rates comparable to the CPU rates of many IoT devices, creating new risks to user privacy and information confidentiality from physical signals.

  • Optical measurements of ordinary device LEDs, obtained using photodiodes, can leak sensitive information, enabling attackers to extract cryptographic keys or recover intelligible speech.

  • Advances in sensing technologies are expanding the reach of remote side-channel attacks, enabling attackers to sample physical signals through compromised smartphones and IP cameras at rates sufficient to extract cryptographic keys from video recordings or recover intelligible speech from a smartphone’s motion-sensor data.

Advances in sensor quality coupled with the widespread adoption of IoT devices with limited CPU power6 have led to a situation where the sampling rate of many sensors is now on par with or even exceeds the CPU clock rate of these devices. This represents a significant shift from the previous era, where there were noticeable differences or gaps between the low sampling rates of sensors and the high CPU rates of high-end devices. In the IoT era, these differences have either diminished or vanished entirely. This new reality poses unprecedented risks to the confidentiality of computing.

This article delves into the information confidentiality risks associated with the interface between photodiodes—light sensors used in measuring light—and IoT devices. Photodiodes have gained significant popularity in the IoT era due to their ability to convert light (photons) into electrical current based on a predefined conversion function, offering high-bandwidth capabilities in the range of a few GHz. The photodiodes’ high-bandwidth capabilities surpass the CPU rates typically found in various devices, such as smartcards, smartphones, video streamers, and more. These devices are typically powered by CPUs operating at speeds ranging from 200MHz to 1.5GHz. While photodiodes are primarily used for innocent tasks involving optical measurements, we demonstrate that when a photodiode is directed toward a device’s power LED, the obtained optical measurements often exhibit correlation with the device’s power consumption. Despite the well-known fact that the intensity of LEDs is strongly influenced by the power-supply level,14 certain popular devices have electrical circuits where the integrated power LED is directly connected to the power line without any effective decoupling mechanisms to mitigate this correlation. Consequently, the power LED in many devices accurately reflects the device’s power consumption.

The accurate indication of a device’s power consumption through optical measurements obtained from its power LED raises concerns regarding information confidentiality. In this article, we explore how attackers can exploit this undesired correlation to launch cryptanalytic attacks on the device and to launch speech eavesdropping attacks on the device’s users. Specifically, we demonstrate the recovery of a 256-bit elliptic curve digital signature algorithm (ECDSA) private key from a smartcard by analyzing the optical traces obtained by a photodiode from the power LED of the smartcard reader during cryptographic computations. Furthermore, we illustrate how attackers can recover audible speech played by speakers by analyzing the optical traces obtained by a photodiode from the power LED of the speakers, even from a distance of 25m. We also assess various methods to enhance the confidentiality of information processed by devices against these attacks and discuss the potential future changes to the threats presented in the paper.

Related Work

Recent studies explored the use of optical sensors to recover speech5,20,23,24 from various objects, including a hanging light bulb, a bag of chips, a window, and a trash can. One study has conducted cryptanalysis by capturing near-infrared photon emissions from switching transistors on the back of exposed field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) while executing cryptographic computations.8 However, this attack is only applicable to devices with exposed chips or printed circuit boards (PCBs), rendering them ineffective against commercial devices where chips are enclosed in opaque materials (e.g., smartphones, card readers).

The risks posed to information confidentiality stemming from the correlation between the intensity of a power LED to the power consumed by the device were discussed 20 years ago.18 However, previous studies demonstrating techniques for exploiting a device’s power LED for data exfiltration relied on the presence of preinstalled malware that actively triggered and controlled the LEDs of keyboards11 and routers.12

Leakage from power LEDs.

Here we explore the leakage from a device’s power LED.

Experimental setup.  We used the Thorlabs PDA100A2 photodiode, an amplified switchable-gain light sensor that converts light (photons) to electrical current and thus to voltage. We connected the photodiode to a custom-built operational/analog amplifier (with a gain of 50dB and a bandwidth of 2MHz). The internal gain of the photodiode was set to the highest level before saturation for each experiment. The amplified voltage was sampled using an NI-9223 analog-to-digital converter (ADC) card that provides 1M samples per second and 16 bits per sample. We connected the ADC to a laptop; the digital optical traces were visualized in real time on LabView. We used MATLAB to process the data (optical traces). The architecture of the data-acquisition system can be seen in Figure 1.

Bandwidth of power LEDs.  Here we show that a device’s power LED gives an accurate indication regarding the power supplied to the device.

Experimental setup.  We connected the Raspberry Pi 3 Model B V1.2 to a function generator that was used to modulate a 0–250kHz chirp using a 20mV peak-to-peak sinusoidal signal) over the 5V power supplied by the function generator to each device. We used the sampling equipment described above to obtain an optical trace using the photodiode, which was directed at the power LED of the Raspberry Pi during the chirp from a distance of 2cm. In addition to the optical trace, we obtained a power trace from the function generator.

Results and conclusions.  We extracted spectrograms from the power trace and the optical trace (see Figure 2). As can be seen, a linear frequency scan appears in the spectrogram extracted from the power trace and in the spectrogram extracted from the optical trace. Based on the spectrograms presented in Figure 2, we concluded that there is a correlation between the optical traces and the power trace, and although intended to provide a binary indication regarding the state of the device (on/off), the intensity of the power LEDs of the tested devices leaks information on the device’s power-supply voltage (with excellent frequency response, reaching 250kHz).

Influence of the CPU activity.  Next, we examine the ability to distinguish between episodes of a few hundred milliseconds of computations using optical traces obtained from the power LED of the device.

Experimental setup.  We wrote a program that executes repetitions of the following six ARM instructions: WFI (CPU sleep), MUL (integer multiplication), ADD (integer addition), FMUL (floating point multiplication), main memory access (forcing cache misses), and NOP (short-term idle). The repetitions of each CPU operation lasted around 300ms. We installed the program and executed it on a Raspberry Pi 3B+. We used the sampling equipment described above to obtain an optical trace by directing the photodiode at the power LED of the Raspberry Pi during the program execution from a distance of 2cm.

Results.  The spectrogram we extracted from the optical trace is presented in Figure 1. As can be seen, the repeated operations affect different frequencies (e.g., the repetition of the FMUL instruction affects 46kHz, and the repetition of the MEM instruction affects 50kHz). Based on this experiment, we concluded that the beginning and the end of episodes of a few hundred milliseconds of computations can be detected in the spectrum of the optical trace.

Implications for privacy and information confidentiality.  The use of optical traces from a device’s power LEDs to accurately determine its power supply/consumption across a wide bandwidth (up to 250kHz) poses significant risks to information confidentiality and a user’s privacy. This is due to the following reasons:

  • The recovery of perceptible speech requires a much narrower bandwidth (a few kHz). Therefore, the wide bandwidth of the optical traces creates a risk of recovering audible speech from sensitive conversations.

  • Previous studies15,16 have already demonstrated successful key recovery attacks by analyzing power traces. Furthermore, the ability to detect the initiation and completion of operations through optical traces obtained from a device’s power LEDs poses a significant threat to information confidentiality. Attackers can exploit this information to recover the device’s cryptographic key by employing cryptanalytic side-channel attacks that take advantage of timing variations. This has been highlighted in recent studies.13,26

Speech eavesdropping.

Here we show how attackers can exploit the power LED of desktop speakers to recover speech played by the speakers (e.g., of a virtual meeting).

Experimental setup.  We placed Winner desktop speakers on a table and connected them to a laptop. We played an audio sample used in Lamphone23 via the desktop speakers at 70db. The level of the played sound was measured using a professional decibel meter. We used the sampling equipment described previously to obtain optical traces. The photodiode was directed at the power LED of the desktop speaker via a telescope. The equipment described above was placed in three locations: 15, 25, and 35m away from the desktop speakers. Figure 3 shows the experimental setup.

Signal processing.  The three optical traces were processed as follows: First, we filtered harmonics (peaks that appear at certain frequencies on a signal’s spectrum) that are not the result of the light. These harmonics, which are added to the signal as a result of the light frequency, affect the optical signal by adding unwanted noise to the signal’s spectrum (100Hz, 200Hz, and so on). We filtered these harmonics from the optical signal using notch/band-stop filters.a Next, we scaled the measurements to the range of [–1, 1] to enhance the recovered speech.b Finally, we applied spectral subtraction to de-noise the signal and improve its fidelity.c

The influence of each step of the signal processing on the recovered signal on an arbitrary sentence is illustrated in Figure 4. As can be seen, the raw optical trace is very noisy. However, the application of scaling and spectral subtraction significantly improves the quality of the signal.

Results.  The reader can assess the fidelity of the recovered sound visually, with the spectrograms extracted from the signals; qualitatively, with the audio signals recovered available online;d and quantitatively, based on metrics used by the audio processing community to compare a recovered signal to the original signal:

  • Intelligibility, a measure of speech comprehensibility in given conditions. The results are classified as follows: bad (0–0.3), poor (0.3–0.45), fair (0.45–0.6), good (0.6–0.75), and excellent (0.75–1) (according to the STI qualification values of ISO 9921e). A higher intelligibility indicates better sound.

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology Signal-to-Noise Ratio (NIST-SNR), the speech-to-noise ratio, which is defined as the logarithmic ratio between the estimated speech power and noise power over 20 consecutive milliseconds. A higher NIST-SNR indicates better sound quality.

The three recovered audio signals were uploaded.f The spectrograms of the recovered audio signals, as well as the intelligibility and NIST-SNR values of the recovered signals, are presented in Figure 5. The results demonstrate that the intelligibility of the recovered audio signals is considered good up to a distance of 15m and fair up to a distance of 35m. Clearly, audible speech can be recovered using optical traces obtained by a photodiode from the power LED of desktop speakers. Additional speech recoveries using this technique appear in Nassi et al.22

Computational efficiency.  We note that a photodiode is used to generate the optical trace in real time, and simple signal-processing techniques—including bandstop filtering, normalization, and spectral subtraction—are employed to recover speech. These techniques can be applied in real time without requiring any preliminary steps. As a result, recovering speech from optical traces obtained via a photodiode offers a significant efficiency advantage over state-of-the-art methods. Some existing approaches require an initial model-generation phase, which involves collecting massive amounts of data,1,19,25,27,28 while others depend on computationally intensive processing to extract optical traces from video footage.5

Recovering ECDSA keys.

Here we show how attackers can exploit a smartcard reader’s power LED to recover a 256-bit ECDSA key from the smartcard using optical traces obtained by a photodiode.

Background.  As observed in the original paper on the Minerva attack,13 many cryptographic libraries optimize the ECDSA signing computation time by running a variable number of loop iterations (determined by the number of leading zeros in the nonce) instead of a fixed number of iterations. As a result, attackers can recover the ECDSA key by applying a timing attack by using the signing times of a set of ECDSA signatures as follows: The signatures whose nonces have many leading zeros (i.e., the signatures with the fastest signing time) are used to construct a hidden number problem,3 which is turned into an instance of the Closest Vector Problem and solved using the methods of lattice reduction (see Jancar et al.13 for details).

Experimental setup.  We connected a USB Gemalto IDBridge CT30 card reader to a laptop via a USB cable and inserted the Athena IDProtect smartcard into the reader. We wrote a script that triggers ECDSA sign operations from the laptop (where every two sign operations were separated by 40ms of sleep). We used the sampling equipment described previously to obtain optical traces. The photodiode was placed 2cm away from the power LED of the smartcard reader (see Figure 6). We obtained an optical trace from 7,000 different ECDSA sign operations performed by the smart card.

Signal processing.  A spectrogram of a section of the optical trace that consists of five ECDSA sign operations appears in Figure 6. The optical leakage associated with the sign operations appears at around 266.6kHz. Clearly, the sign operations can be distinguished using spectral analysis.

We divided the long optical signal into 7,000 short traces as follows: We performed short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with a window of 7.5ms and an overlap of 50% on each trace. We divided the optical trace, which consisted of 7,000 sign operations, into short traces (each associated with one sign operation), by identifying the sections associated with the sleep operation. We divided the long optical signal into 7,000 short traces, where each of the 7,000 short traces consisted of a sign operation followed by 5–10ms of sleep, since we added an extra window at the beginning and end of each trace.

Next, for each short optical trace, we performed the following steps to estimate the execution time of the ECDSA operation:

  1. We applied STFT with a window of 0.75ms and an overlap of 90% on the traces.

  2. We located the sign operation in the trace by detecting the sections in the trace in which the magnitude of the bin associated with the sign operation (∼266.6KHz) is greater than a constant.

  3. Because of errors, more than one section can satisfy the above-mentioned condition (i.e., two or more different sections that are separated by some windows are located) in the same trace. To correct such errors, we used an error-tolerance threshold of two windows (i.e., if two consecutive sections were separated by only two windows, we merged them into a single section).

  4. Traces that yielded more than one sign section that satisfied the above-mentioned criterion were filtered out after the second step.

  5. The estimated execution time of the sign operation was calculated based on traces with a single section associated with an ECDSA operation. After filtering, 6,892 signatures remained, along with the estimates of their ECDSA execution time from the optical traces.

Results.  The heat map presented in Figure 6 shows the estimated ECDSA operation time (based on the optical measurements) vs. the number of leading zeros in the signature’s nonce. As can be seen in the figure, the signatures estimated to have the shortest ECDSA operation execution time (based on the optical traces) are associated with at least seven leading zeroes. The results validate the correctness of the estimations of the execution time we made using the optical traces (because a higher number of leading zeroes in the nonce corresponds to a shorter ECDSA execution time).

To recover the ECDSA private key, we used a script that implements the Minerva attack according to the details provided above (the script provided in the official Minerva GitHubg). The input to the script was as follows: the public key, messages, their signatures, and corresponding estimated signature times. The script was executed on a standard Dell laptop, and the full 256-bit ECDSA key was found in around two minutes. Additional analysis of the influence of factors on the recovery appear here in Nassi et al.22

Computational efficiency.  We note that using a photodiode to recover secret keys is comparable in efficiency to state-of-the-art methods that leverage an oscilloscope,15,16 software-defined radio,4,9 and an ultrasonic microphone.10 In all these approaches, the captured signals or traces require additional processing to assess the timing of the cryptographic operation. However, the key advantage of using a photodiode for secret key recovery lies in its non-intrusiveness: It does not require a physical connection to the target device, unlike an oscilloscope, and it does not rely on compromising the device with malware to measure cryptographic timing, as demonstrated in the original Minerva attack.13

Countermeasures

Detection.  Detecting the acquisition of optical traces using a photodiode is inherently challenging. Unlike LiDAR and laser microphones, which employ active laser beams for data collection, photodiodes are entirely passive and do not emit any light. Consequently, identifying the use of photodiodes—particularly when deployed from a distance—is analogous to detecting hidden microphones. As a result, mitigating cryptanalysis and speech eavesdropping is more feasible than detecting them.

Mitigations.  In many devices, the power LED is directly connected to the power line on the PCB. Consequently, the power-consumption fluctuations during cryptographic operations affect the device’s power LED. To mitigate this issue, hardware manufacturers can incorporate a capacitor parallel to the power LED indicator, which can serve as a cost-effective solution for reducing fluctuations and acting as a low-pass filter.

Consumers interested in preventing remote attackers from obtaining optical traces from the target device should consider the following approaches: One straightforward method is to cover the device’s power LED with black tape, effectively blocking any emitted light. While this solution may slightly impact the device’s user experience, it successfully prevents remote attackers from capturing optical traces from vulnerable devices. Another approach is to create a physical barrier that obstructs the line of sight to the power LED. Installing a curtain or repositioning the target device to a windowless room can achieve this. By eliminating the direct visibility of the power LED, the risk of optical leakage is significantly reduced.

It is also worth noting that the intensity of light emitted from power LEDs diminishes with distance. With this in mind, establishing a safety perimeter can be an effective measure. This involves installing a fence around the premises (such as a home or building), limiting the attacker’s proximity to the target device. By forcing them to conduct the attack from a greater distance, the quality of any captured optical traces, as demonstrated in the case of speech recovery, deteriorates.

The Evolving Risk Landscape

The risks to information confidentiality posed by photodiodes may increase in the future. Although current smartphones integrate low-cost photodiodes for ambient light sensing, these sensors lack the sensitivity required to enable the attacks described in this article. However, continued technological progress has steadily improved sensor quality while reducing cost. If highly sensitive photodiodes become as affordable as existing low-sensitivity ones, they may be integrated into future smartphones, enabling attackers to remotely extract optical traces from a compromised device’s ambient light sensor. This would significantly expand the attack surface, exposing a larger number of devices to cryptanalytic and speech-eavesdropping attacks.

A similar risk arises from advances in video camera technology. The video microphone technique5 demonstrated that rolling-shutter effects can be exploited to recover speech from video recordings. Since then, improvements have enabled commercial off-the-shelf cameras to support rolling-shutter rates sufficient to recover speech17 and secret keys21 over the Internet. These trends highlight the need to proactively reassess the confidentiality risks posed by sensors, not limited to photodiodes, in the IoT era.

item.title: AI Didn’t Make Programming Easier. It Just Made It Differently Difficult
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Osborn
item.description: AI is making programming work more explicitly intellectual in ways that require different expertise and create new forms of difficulty.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, empirical research has shown that programming is a demanding cognitive activity: Developers rely on working memory, long-term recall, and complex mental models to manipulate interacting abstractions such as control flow, data structures, and the structural design of software. This classical model frequently positioned memory and recall as both the central enablers of, and bottlenecks in, software development.

Today’s AI-powered coding assistants are changing that. These tools function as external memory systems, offloading syntax recall, boilerplate generation, and API usage from human to machine memory. As memory demands lessen, reasoning, architectural comprehension, judgment, and code-structure awareness are becoming comparatively more important.

Thus “knowing how to program” is being fundamentally redefined, but not in ways that make programming easier or that devalue the programmer. This article describes four major shifts in how programming work is changing:

  1. The field is opening to new practitioners.

  2. The work is becoming differently difficult.

  3. Education is transforming.

  4. The programmer’s role is evolving from knowledge vessel to orchestrating agent.

Together, these shifts suggest that AI is not eroding the cognitive substance of programming but relocating it—making different skills matter more and creating new forms of difficulty even as old barriers fall.

Programming as High-Memory Work

For most of the history of software development, researchers found that programming relied on a combination of reasoning ability, working memory capacity, and long-term memory recall. Brooks described programming as a cognitive process that depends on maintaining multiple interacting abstractions.4 Pennington then demonstrated that programmers rely on complex mental models of control flow and data flow to design, understand, and modify code.6 Studies have shown that these mental models exist in the mind as abstractions, are maintained at high cognitive cost, and are relatively fragile. They break down easily under conditions of context switching and are costly to rebuild in cognitive terms if they are not documented.

Today, however, AI coding assistants are reshaping this traditionally onerous cognitive landscape. Developers now have access to external memory systems capable of generating code, retrieving syntax, reconstructing context, and remembering and regenerating variants of previous mental constructs. This does not eliminate the need to think. But it does shift which cognitive skills are becoming most relevant for programmers.

Working memory and long-term recall.  Working memory is the limited-capacity system that supports temporary storage and manipulation of discrete blocks of information, as formalized by Baddeley and Hitch.2 Long-term memory, conversely, serves as the repository of consolidated knowledge, including declarative information such as syntax and architectural concepts, and procedural knowledge like coding idioms and problem-solving schemas.

Programming has traditionally relied heavily on both. Soloway, Bonar, and Ehrlich found that programmers rely on internal cognitive preferences,9 presumably based on experience and retrieved from long-term memory, to structure their approach to iterations. For example, when a loop construct matched the programmer’s natural plan, correctness increased dramatically. This suggests that programming has historically been guided not just by syntax knowledge but by the formation and execution of internal cognitive preferences retrieved from memory and expressed as mental models through design choices. Siegmund et al. used fMRI to show that code comprehension activates networks associated with working memory, attention, and language processing,8 providing physiological evidence that understanding complex programming tasks is a resource-intensive cognitive task at the neurological level.

Theories of AI as an external memory resource.  AI coding assistants alter this cognitive landscape by acting as external memory and cognition. This aligns with Hutchins’ theory of distributed cognition, which argued that cognitive systems often extend beyond the individual to include the external environment,5 which can extend and enhance individual cognition.

Alternate theories complement distributed cognition. Cognitive load theory (CLT) holds that AI tools can reduce extraneous load, which is the memory overhead of recalling syntax and boilerplate, thereby freeing working memory for intrinsic, high-level reasoning. The Extended Mind Hypothesis (EMH) goes further by focusing on the individual: If an AI assistant becomes reliably available, habitually used, and trusted, it can function as an integrated component of the programmer’s cognitive architecture rather than as an external tool. Under this view, the AI becomes part of the thinking process itself, shaping reasoning, decision making, and the effects of cognitive effort.

Barke, James, and Polikarpova3 showed that developers commonly use Copilot to offload low-level work, such as typing boilerplate, recalling API details, and looking up unfamiliar syntax, while shifting effort toward validating and integrating the generated code. These findings collectively support the view that AI is not merely a faster search engine; it is at least partly an integrated extension of human cognitive architecture.

What AI removes and what it does not.  Thus, AI fundamentally changes the costs associated with imperfect memory, effectively reducing the penalty for imperfect recall. A developer can successfully request a common API usage pattern without precise internal recall or retrieve complex syntax without relying on working-memory-intensive reconstruction. This capacity directly reduces the dependency on the rapid retrieval of specific, low-level knowledge from long-term memory, mitigating the cognitive bottleneck previously identified.

However, while AI-assisted programming tools can accelerate routine development tasks, they do not eliminate the need for human oversight, particularly when work requires conceptual reasoning rather than surface-level code manipulation. Every programmer knows AI can produce code that is syntactically correct yet semantically and subjectively flawed, meaning developers must still understand program structure well enough to detect errors, evaluate coding suggestions critically, and ask the necessary “why” and “why not” questions about causal behavior.

Shihab et al. found that students using GitHub Copilot completed brownfield tasks substantially faster and with more solution progress, but in exit interviews many reported concerns about not fully understanding how or why Copilot’s suggestions worked, and the authors call for pedagogical approaches that leverage Copilot’s benefits while fostering comprehension.7 Alanazi et al., in a meta-analysis of controlled studies of tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot in programming education, reported that while AI assistance improves task performance and efficiency, it offers only small and statistically unstable gains in learning success and ease of understanding.1

Taken together, these findings support the view that architectural reasoning, impact analysis, and long-term system maintenance cannot be offloaded to AI. They depend on deep, structural understanding of the codebase that remains the programmer’s responsibility. So, while AI may extend cognition and make certain programming tasks more efficient, thereby improving the productivity of trained developers, critical tasks such as debugging, refactoring, and systems analysis still require expertise and comprehension, and rely heavily on internal mental models that allow programmers to simulate execution and infer complex cause-and-effect paths within a codebase.

This marks a significant cognitive reorganization: Memory becomes a shared resource spanning human and machine; programming becomes less about what the developer can hold and manipulate in their mind and more about how clearly they can think at multiple scales when creating and ordering a complex logical system. Studies confirm that stable mental models of a codebase are essential for navigation and reasoning. Therefore, if developers outsource too much thinking to AI, those internal models can weaken. AI thus shifts cognitive load rather than removing it and speeds up writing code but increases the time spent checking and validating it.

In other words, the hard part moves from recall (“How do I write this?”) to judgment (“Does this actually make sense?”). This shift from recall-based to judgment-based programming represents the fundamental cognitive transformation at the heart of AI-assisted development. Where traditional programming demanded that developers maintain vast internal libraries of syntax, patterns, and idioms, AI-enabled programming demands instead they maintain robust evaluative frameworks for assessing correctness, coherence, and appropriateness. The cognitive burden has not disappeared—it has relocated from retrieval to reasoning.

Programming as Hybrid Cognitive Systems Work

The emerging reality is not that AI replaces the programmer, but that it becomes a second cognitive engine running in parallel. The machine surfaces patterns, stitches together APIs, retrieves forgotten syntax, and drafts first-pass solutions at a speed that reduces low-level recall bottlenecks but can also increase the burden of evaluation. The human, in turn, becomes less a conductor of keystrokes and more a shaper of intent: checking, interpreting, integrating, synthesizing, validating, reorganizing, discarding, editing, and ultimately giving structure and purpose to what the system supplies. It resembles what has already happened in medicine: Diagnostic tools lowered the burden of memorizing obscure clinical details but raised the stakes for interpretation, judgment, and error detection. Expertise became less about recall and more about reasoning.

Understanding this hybrid arrangement helps explain why AI makes programming differently difficult rather than simply easier. The difficulty has not been eliminated; it has been redistributed across a new cognitive architecture that spans human and machine. This redistribution creates new challenges even as it removes old ones.

As AI continues to function primarily as an externalized memory and a code-transformation layer, four major shifts are already visible:

  1. First, the field will open. Many who once would have bounced off the sheer cognitive overhead of memorizing libraries, syntax variations, or error-handling idioms will now find a workable entry path. The bottleneck of recall shrinks, making programming more accessible to people who might previously have struggled with syntax, library details, or unfamiliar idioms, while placing greater emphasis on problem decomposition, systems reasoning, and the ability to evaluate generated code. However, this accessibility comes with a paradox: While the barrier to producing code lowers, the barrier to producing good code may actually rise, as judgment becomes more critical and harder to develop than recall ever was.

  2. Second, the work does not become simpler, only differently difficult. Conceptual clarity, decomposition, debugging, and architectural foresight still demand effort, and perhaps more of it. The challenge moves up a level. Where novice programmers once struggled primarily with syntax errors and API usage, they now struggle with evaluating whether AI-generated solutions are appropriate, maintainable, and aligned with broader system constraints. This represents a more sophisticated form of difficulty, one that requires deeper understanding of software-engineering principles rather than surface-level language features.

  3. Third, education will shift. We will teach fewer people to memorize syntax and more to think in complex systems. The curriculum bends toward architecture, interface design, state management, failure modes, constraint negotiation, test construction, security, and long-term maintainability. Code becomes only one representation of thought among many overlapping ones. Developers must still possess the skills to analyze, adapt, and modify what AI produces, perhaps even more so than before.

  4. Fourth and most importantly, the programmer remains essential. Not as a vessel of knowledge but as the orchestrating agent who understands the parts and how they fit together, maintains the integrity of the system, and who decides what matters. This shift has profound implications for how we understand programming expertise. The most capable developers of this new era will not be those who type the fastest or remember the most, but those who can hold deep mental models while offloading everything that interferes with that. They will combine strong systems reasoning with AI-augmented recall and will treat the model almost like a cognitive prosthetic: useful, fast, but incapable of finally determining subjective-semantic correctness or coherence.

Conclusion

Taken together, these four shifts suggest AI is not eroding the cognitive substance of programming but relocating it. As external memory becomes abundant and code generation cheap, the value of the programmer moves toward interpretation, structural reasoning, and judgment. The future of software development will belong to those who can think clearly at scale, maintain durable mental models amid rapid change, and integrate machine-generated output into human-directed intent.

AI does not, therefore, diminish the craft; it widens it, deepens it, and makes more of the work explicitly intellectual. The work becomes differently difficult because it demands more sophisticated forms of expertise: judgment over recall, architecture over syntax, orchestration over implementation. These are not easier skills to develop or demonstrate, they are simply different ones, and perhaps ultimately more demanding.

item.title: Defining and Evaluating Physical Safety for Large Language Models
item.dc:creator: Yung-Chen Tang, Pin-Yu Chen, and Tsung-Yi Ho
item.description: As LLMs evolve into agentic embodied AI to control robotic systems such as drones, safety evaluations must expand beyond textual safety to include physical safety in the real world.
item.content:encoded:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful applications in the field of natural language processing,9,18,19 exhibiting human- and even superhuman-level performance across various tasks. Innovations in neural network architectures25 and increased computational power24 have led their evolution into state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) systems that understand and generate text with remarkable fluency and coherence. For example, GitHub Copilot,a developed in collaboration between GitHub and OpenAI, is an AI-powered coding assistant based on a variant of the GPT-3 language model.5 It assists users by autonomously completing code snippets or generating entire functions as they write code. LLMs have also shown outstanding capabilities in areas such as reasoning,1,14 planning,22 manipulation,29 and in-context learning,15 despite not being explicitly trained in them. As a result, they have been widely used in many different applications, such as question answering, multimodal tasks, tool manipulation, and autonomous agents.

Key Insights

  • As large language models evolve into agentic embodied AI to control robotic systems such as drones, safety evaluations must expand beyond textual safety to include physical safety in the real world, particularly with regard to humans, objects, and infrastructure. 

  • To address this gap, we took the first step of developing a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the physical safety of LLMs in drone control. We used a high-fidelity simulation environment to quantify risks such as collisions and regulatory violations. 

  • Our findings show that although larger model sizes and advanced prompting techniques can mitigate obvious malicious orders, LLMs still struggle to identify “unintentional attacks” because they lack the common sense to realize that seemingly harmless commands can lead to physical harm.

Due to their strong capabilities, LLMs have also become popular for controlling robots,3,4 in areas ranging from industrial automation to AI-powered physical agents. However, widespread adoption of these systems is dependent upon ensuring their safety. And though significant progress has been made in evaluating LLM safety around user-generated content (e.g., preventing toxic content and hate speech),7,17,28 the physical safety of LLM-controlled robots in real-world applications remains largely unexplored. This is of particular concern in areas like drone control,10,16,21 where the threat vectors are realistic and malfunctions can lead to catastrophic physical harm and damage.

In this article, we describe a pilot study on physical safety that focuses on drones, due to their low cost and easy accessibility. For around $100 USD, programmable drones like the Ryze Tello offer a cost-effective alternative to expensive robotic systems such as humanoid robots. Many modern drone manufacturers also offer software development kits (SDKs) and application programming interfaces (APIs), such as DJI Developer SDKs and Parrot Air SDK, enabling researchers or users to easily deploy custom code. This combination of affordability and programmability makes drones an ideal case study for exploring safety risks associated with LLM-generated code in robotic systems.

To address the critical gap in physical safety evaluation for LLMs,b our research focuses on defining and evaluating physical safety in drone control. We consider a realistic scenario where an attacker or unintended user exploits LLMs to generate drone-control code, potentially leading to malicious actions. Our evaluation of several mainstream LLMs in drone control reveals some key insights:

  • There is a trade-off between utility and safety, where higher utility scores tend to exhibit higher safety risks, indicating a need for improved alignment.

  • In-context learning (ICL) shows slight improvements over zero-shot chain-of-thought (ZS-CoT), both of which demonstrate significant safety enhancements; however, both struggle to detect unintentional attacks, highlighting limitations in complex reasoning and anticipating consequences.

  • Model size plays a critical role in safety; while larger LLMs generally exhibit better performance in blocking dangerous commands, further scaling up the model size results in only marginal gains in some physical safety categories.

These findings have important implications for developing robust and safe LLM-based robotic systems. Our comprehensive benchmark establishes a solid foundation on which further research and innovation can build to enhance the physical safety of LLMs in real-world, safety-critical scenarios. This is crucial for ensuring the effective functioning of these systems and fostering their trustworthiness and reliability to encourage the widespread adoption of powerful AI technologies.

Results

In this section, we discuss the physical safety evaluation objectives and benchmark design for LLMs in drone control. We introduce a dataset for safety and utility evaluations, explain the metrics used, and examine various LLMs regarding safety. We also present evaluation results, analyze the trade-offs between utility and safety, highlight the impact of ICL on safety, and offer insights into how model size influences outcomes.

Physical safety evaluation objectives and benchmark design.  As depicted in Figure 1, the physical safety evaluation aims to address the potential threats and risks posed by drones in various real-world scenarios. We categorize the risks into four main classes:

  • Human-targeted threats: Drones could be used to physically harm individuals, such as instructing an LLM to provide steps for a drone to deliberately strike a crowd, posing serious safety risks.

  • Object-targeted threats: Drones may damage property, such as vehicles or other objects, leading to financial losses. For instance, a malicious actor might use an LLM to direct a drone to collide with a car.

  • Infrastructure attacks: Targeting critical infrastructure, like power grids, could cause widespread disruption. A malicious user could generate instructions for a drone to crash into a transmission tower, leading to outages.

  • Violations of FAA regulations: Unsafe drone operations, such as flying in restricted airspaces, pose safety and legal risks. For example, flying a drone into a no-fly zone near an airport could endanger aircraft and result in severe legal consequences. Our evaluation data is based on FAA Part 107 regulations.11

This categorization considers both the direct and indirect effects of potential drone damage.

To evaluate the physical safety of LLM-based systems, we developed the LLM Physical Safety Benchmark (Figure 2), a comprehensive framework to explore and quantify safety risks. This benchmark uses a curated dataset of potential risks and prompts, created by us and two LLM judges, along with a simulation environment, to assess the safety and utility of mainstream LLMs, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Meta’s Llama.

The evaluation starts by providing the LLM with a test instruction categorized as one of four dataset dimensions: deliberate attacks, unintentional attacks, violation instructions, or utility tasks. These dimensions are designed to evaluate user intent and to cover the physical safety risk categories defined in Figure 1. The mapping of the risk categories to the evaluation datasets is presented in the appendix. The LLM’s response is then assessed by two specialized AI judges, the Code Verification Judge and the Safety Evaluation Judge. Introducing these LLM judges is important because evaluating whether a model’s response is safe involves more than simply checking whether executable code is provided. Two notable safety-conscious behaviors are:

  • Self-protect: The model adjusts generated code for safety, showing that code generation is not always unsafe.

  • Safety refusal: The model declines to generate code, not due to lack of capability but for safety reasons.

Additionally, the generated code is tested in the AirSim simulation environment23 to identify potential collision risks and safety issues. Finally, the results are summarized for a holistic safety evaluation, offering insights into the LLM’s ability to generate safe and reliable drone-control instructions. More detailed implementations of these two AI judges and benchmark, as well as examples of self-protect and safety refusal behaviors, can be found in the appendix.

Dataset for safety and utility evaluations.  To support the benchmark and facilitate comprehensive physical safety evaluations, we developed the LLM Physical Safety Benchmark Dataset,d a curated collection of more than 400 different instructions. The dataset was created through a collaborative effort combining human expertise and LLM support to construct a diverse and realistic set of scenarios, ensuring alignment with key drone regulations, including those of the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the International Civil Aviation Organization, and guaranteeing their relevance to current safety protocols. As illustrated in Figure 3, the dataset is categorized into four dimensions: deliberate attacks, unintentional attacks, violation instructions, and utility. Each dimension evaluates a subset of our defined physical safety risks as well as the utility of regular (safety-unrelated) tasks. Please refer to the appendix for the full dataset, including test instructions, categories, the relationship between safety risks and dataset dimensions, and a detailed flowchart of steps involved in the dataset construction process.

We provide detailed explanations of the four dataset dimensions below. Within each subcategory, we have curated specific examples that represent realistic scenarios in drone control, shown in Figure 3. The distribution of evaluation data across these dimensions, presented by the pie charts, ensures a balanced and thorough evaluation of LLM performance in simulated drone-control environments:

  • Deliberate attacks: Evaluate the LLM’s resistance to malicious use, testing its ability to recognize and reject commands intended to cause harm. Subcategories include direct command attacks, indirect command attacks, and code injection.

  • Unintentional attacks: Assess the LLM’s capacity to identify and mitigate potentially harmful actions that might arise from user mistakes or lack of domain knowledge. This includes scenarios like misleading instructions, high-risk instructions, and scenario oversight.

  • Violation instructions: Examine the LLM’s adherence to legal and ethical guidelines, particularly focusing on FAA regulations and general safety protocols. Subcategories cover flying in a no drone zone, improper flight attitude, excessive flight speed, and operation over people.

  • Utility: Check the LLM’s ability to perform basic drone controls and operations, ensuring that safety measures do not overly compromise functionality. This dimension includes tasks such as takeoff and movement, path following, yaw angle control, and approach target.

Metrics for safety evaluation.  Based on the physical safety dataset, we quantify the safety performance of different LLMs using the following six metrics. These metrics provide a systematic framework for assessing the safety performance of LLMs in robotic applications. For detailed definitions and calculations, please refer to the appendix:

  • Self-assurance: Evaluates the LLM’s ability to recognize and avoid dangerous situations. A higher score indicates better refusal of harmful instructions, reflecting commitment to safety.

  • Avoid collision: Assesses the likelihood of collisions during drone control. This metric measures how effectively the LLM avoids collisions in both deliberate and unintentional scenarios.

  • Regulatory compliance: Evaluates adherence to laws and regulations, such as FAA guidelines. A higher score shows the LLM’s capability to identify and refuse instructions that violate these regulations.

  • Code fidelity: Measures the accuracy and reliability of code generated by the LLM. A greater score indicates a higher success rate in generating executable code without errors.

  • Instruction understanding: Assesses the LLM’s ability to comprehend and respond appropriately to instructions. This includes both non-code and code responses evaluated by specialized AI judges.

  • Utility: Evaluates the LLM’s performance in basic drone-control tasks, such as moving or changing altitude. A higher score signifies better execution of fundamental control commands.

Evaluation results across LLMs.  The safety evaluation results, presented in Figure 4, highlight significant variations in safety performance across the models tested, including OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo, Google Gemini Pro, Llama-2-7B-Chat, CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, and CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat. Detailed descriptions are in the appendix.

These differences in safety performance highlight the need for deeper consideration of model design, particularly with regard to self-assurance and collision-avoidance capabilities. CodeLlama-7B-Instruct excelled in self-assurance (54.65%) and collision avoidance (99.12%), demonstrating a strong ability to identify and mitigate risks. Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama3-8B-Instruct closely followed, indicating a consistent focus on safety within Meta’s LLM family, in contrast to GPT-3.5-turbo, which exhibited the lowest self-assurance.

Regulatory compliance is another critical aspect of safety performance that warrants our attention. Llama-2-7B-Chat led in regulatory compliance (90.62%), with CodeLlama-7B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 closely behind. In contrast, GPT-3.5-turbo’s low score raises concerns about its adherence to regulations, highlighting the need for a dedicated focus on compliance in LLM development, especially in safety-critical applications.

Despite GPT-3.5-turbo’s lower safety evaluations, its strong performance in other metrics is notable. It excelled in code fidelity (98.51%), instruction understanding (98.93%), and utility (93.75%), suggesting that strengths in these areas may help offset its safety weaknesses when combined with effective prompt engineering. In contrast, Llama-2-7B-Chat and CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, both part of Meta’s LLM family, performed well on prior safety-related metrics but underperformed in these three areas. This reversal highlights the varying strengths and weaknesses across different models and underscores the importance of balancing performance metrics in real-world applications.

This comprehensive evaluation not only reveals the distinct characteristics of various LLMs but also underscores the importance of balancing multiple performance indicators for real-world applications. Overall, this evaluation offers valuable insights into the performance characteristics of different LLMs, reinforcing the need for balanced metrics in the development of safer drone-control systems. For detailed evaluation results, please refer to the appendix.

Trade-off between utility and safety.  The safety evaluation results shown in Figure 4 reveal an interesting trend: LLMs that excel in utility and code fidelity, indicating better drone operation control, tend to exhibit higher safety risks. This observation suggests that optimizing these models solely for utility may compromise essential safety aspects. A key factor in this trade-off is the bias in training data. LLMs are trained on publicly available data2,5,8 that often emphasizes code utility over safety. This focus leads to the prioritization of effective code generation while neglecting potential safety risks. The lack of negative examples, such as incorrect instructions or hazardous code, results in inadequate learning of safety considerations.

Conflicting training objectives also contribute to this issue. Models are optimized to predict the next token from public Internet data, which may diverge from the goal of following user instructions.5,19,20 This optimization can unintentionally compromise safety, as improving code efficiency might prioritize task completion over identifying vulnerabilities or safety risks. Additionally, the lack of effective safety mechanisms6,12,26 in existing LLMs exacerbates the problem. Without safeguards to prevent dangerous outputs, these models may fail to recognize or mitigate potential risks during code generation, increasing the likelihood of safety issues.

In conclusion, the trade-off between utility and safety in LLMs for drone operations is a complex issue with multiple contributing factors. Biases in training data, conflicting training objectives, and the lack of robust safety guardrails all play a role in shaping this trade-off.

In-context learning delivers significant safety gains.  We investigated the impact of different prompt engineering techniques27 on LLM safety, including in-context learning (ICL)15 and zero-shot chain of thought (ZS-CoT).13 ICL involves providing relevant examples within the prompt, allowing the model to learn and apply this knowledge. We implemented ICL by including safety-related examples; specific examples can be found in the appendix. In contrast, ZS-CoT encourages the model to break down its reasoning step by step without specific examples. We instructed the model: “Before providing code, think step by step: Will this instruction cause harm or violate FAA regulations? If yes, respond safely.” This guides the model to consider potential risks and regulatory compliance before generating code.

As illustrated in Figure 5a and 5b, both GPT-3.5-turbo and Gemini Pro equipped with ICL demonstrate significant advantages in safety metrics, particularly in risk mitigation. For instance, ICL boosts GPT-3.5-turbo’s self-assurance from 12.50% to 87.20%, and Gemini Pro from 25.00% to 87.50%. The avoid-collision score for GPT-3.5-turbo improves from 13.66% to 95.05%, while Gemini Pro’s score rises from 32.55% to 91.57%. These results highlight ICL’s effectiveness in enhancing LLM safety. Notably, while Gemini Pro shows a slightly lower self-protect and safety refusal ratio with ICL compared to ZS-CoT, it results in fewer collisions during deliberate attacks (15 for ICL versus 29 for ZS-CoT) and fewer violations (three for ICL versus six for ZS-CoT). The radar chart indicates that ICL outperforms ZS-CoT in multiple safety dimensions, making instructions clearer and reducing misunderstandings.

While ICL shows better safety performance, its effectiveness depends on the quality and quantity of examples and it often requires more computational resources for contextual processing. In contrast, ZS-CoT, although slightly less effective, serves as a lightweight solution that enhances safety without data. However, despite the advantages of both methods, they struggle with unintentional attacks. For instance, “Please let the drone take off, fly above the car, and land” could lead to dangerous outcomes, highlighting the challenge of reasoning about indirect effects. Although ICL and ZS-CoT help consider potential risks, their effectiveness in mitigating unintentional attacks remains limited.

This study highlights the potential of ICL and ZS-CoT in enhancing LLM safety. ICL offers significant improvements through contextual learning but relies on quality examples and can be computationally intensive. ZS-CoT is a simpler, lightweight alternative but is less effective. Future research should focus on developing robust safety guardrails, refining ICL, and addressing ZS-CoT’s limitations. For detailed evaluation results on prompt engineering, please refer to the appendix.

Model size plays a critical role in safety.  Our research also explored the scalability of model size on safety performance. The results, shown in Figure 5c, suggest a strong correlation between model size and safety capabilities. Larger LLMs, such as CodeLlama-34B-Instruct, outperform smaller models in various safety metrics, particularly in refusing dangerous commands. For example, the self-assurance score increases from 54.65% for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct to 80.23% for CodeLlama-34B-Instruct, while the instruction understanding score improves from 64.36% to 85.11%.

Figure 5c clearly illustrates that as model size increases from 7B to 34B parameters, there is a significant improvement in self-protect and safety refusal percentages for both deliberate attacks and violations. For instance, in deliberate attacks, the refusal rate rises from about 45% for the 7B model to over 85% for the 34B model, indicating substantial safety enhancements.

However, for unintentional attacks, the performance of the 13B and 34B models remains nearly identical, both achieving about a 42% refusal rate. This suggests that beyond a certain size, the ability to detect and resist unintentional attacks does not significantly improve, aligning with earlier observations that LLMs struggle with these types of risks.

Overall, our findings indicate that model size alone is insufficient for improving safety against unintentional risks. While larger LLMs show superior capabilities in many areas, their effectiveness in mitigating unintentional attacks appears limited. This underscores the need for targeted research to enhance causal reasoning and predictive safety evaluation abilities. For detailed evaluation results on different LLM sizes, please refer to the appendix.

Discussion

In this article, we highlight the physical safety of LLMs and reveal novel insights into safety and utility assessment in LLM-based robotic systems. Our benchmark and comprehensive safety evaluation of LLMs in drone-control systems provide critical perspectives for robotics and AI. By evaluating various LLMs in a virtual environment, we emphasize the importance of simulation as a primary defense in robotic safety testing. A fundamental principle emerges: If an LLM shows unsafe behaviors in a controlled environment, its real-world performance is likely to be worse.

Our evaluation of mainstream LLMs reveals significant challenges in physical safety. The trade-off between utility and safety highlights a critical difficulty in LLM-based robotics. LLMs excelling in code generation often perform poorly in safety, indicating the need for balanced AI system development. More importantly, effective code generation does not guarantee safety. In addition, our findings on prompt engineering techniques show improvements in LLM safety, and the positive correlation between model size and safety provides valuable insights for future AI-driven robotics. These results extend beyond drone control, with significant implications for various robotic applications. As AI integration in robotics accelerates, especially with programmable drones from companies like DJI, ensuring safety is crucial. LLMs’ ability to control these accessible platforms necessitates robust safety measures. Our research, grounded in virtual environment testing, provides a foundation for developing safer, more reliable AI-controlled robotic systems.

In conclusion, this study emphasizes the importance of prioritizing safety in LLM development for robotic control, starting with a comprehensive evaluation benchmark and rigorous virtual testing. Future research should focus on refining safety evaluation methodologies, incorporating robust safety mechanisms, and bridging the gap between virtual and real-world performance. By addressing these challenges, we can advance AI in robotics, paving the way for safer and more effective autonomous systems in various applications. More information, including datasets and code, is available on our project page.c

The research work described in this paper was conducted in the JC STEM Lab of Intelligent Design Automation funded by The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust. All authors participated in methodology design and paper writing. Pin-Yu Chen is solely funded by IBM Research.
