item.title: The Origins of GPU Computing
item.dc:creator: William J. Dally and Pat Hanrahan
item.description: Government-funded academic research on parallel computing, stream processing, real-time shading languages, and programmable GPUs directly led to the development of GPU computing.
item.content:encoded:
Government-funded academic research on parallel computing, stream processing, real-time shading languages, and programmable graphics processing units (GPUs) directly led to the development of GPU computing. GPUs are used in modern datacenters and have enabled the current revolution in artificial intelligence (AI). Nvidia, which makes GPUs, is now the most valuable company in the world. This transformation of computing and resulting economic value created was enabled by more than 30 years of government-funded research. Government funding not only helped develop many of the key technical innovations; it also enabled the training of large numbers of students who have conveyed this technology to industry.

This article traces the origins of GPU computing. We start by describing the development of the technologies on which GPU computing is built (parallel computing, parallel graphics systems, programmable shaders, and stream processing), and then we detail how this technology was transferred to Nvidia and other companies and came to be applied to modern machine learning.

Enabling Technologies

GPU computing builds on earlier work in parallel computing, parallel graphics systems, and stream processing. These technologies were developed through more than 30 years of government-sponsored academic research.

Parallel computing.  When you learn about computing, you learn about a central processing unit (CPU) executing a sequence of instructions one after another. In reality, chips contain billions of transistors switching in parallel and connected by wires. Switches and wires are the fundamental building blocks of physical computers and they operate concurrently. Moreover, transistor switching consumes very little energy, whereas communication along wires consumes much more energy. Communication requires power to send the signal from one point to another; the power increases with distance and is very large if signaling between one chip and another. Although a sequential computer may be easier to think about than a parallel computer, a sequential computer must be implemented with transistors switching concurrently and wires transmitting information simultaneously. Sequential computers use many transistors to compute results in parallel and then carefully assemble these results in a way that is consistent with a sequential execution. The need to create this illusion—that execution is sequential—is inefficient in both power and performance. As the number of available transistors grows, the inefficiency increases. The natural way to build a computer in modern semiconductor technology is to design a parallel computer. GPUs are more efficient than CPUs because they are massively parallel computers.

GPU computing built on earlier work on parallel computing. As with all parallel computers, the parallel tasks or threads running on GPUs must synchronize and communicate with one another. Communication is needed for one thread to use data produced by another thread. Synchronization is needed to signal when data is available to ensure the correct value is consumed. Many of the fundamentals of parallel computing, synchronization, and communication were developed by government-sponsored academic research. The DARPA-funded Cosmic Cube project led by Chuck Seitz at Caltech35 developed much of the fundamentals of parallel computing. The hardware developed on this project was the model on which the Intel iPSC, Delta, and Paragon machines were based, as well as several of the early Department of Energy ASCI machines.6 The Cosmic-C programming language introduced asynchronous message passing and collectives, which later became the norm for programming large parallel machines in the form of message passing interface (MPI).29

The DARPA-funded J-Machine10 and M-Machine21 projects at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) developed low-overhead mechanisms for communication and synchronization and many key aspects of modern interconnection networks. These mechanisms enabled parallelism to be exploited at a very fine grain, with as little as 10 or 20 instructions being a schedulable unit of work. Many of the features of the J-Machine were directly adopted by the Cray T3D24 and T3E34 computers.

There is a rich history of parallel computing that goes beyond this particular branch of history. We do not have space to give a complete survey. A good review is in Culler et al.9

GPU computing, like all high-performance computing, draws heavily from this legacy. It uses MPI for communication between nodes, interconnection networks to connect these nodes, and many of the communication and synchronization mechanisms developed during the course of this research are used to coordinate the parallel computations.

Parallel graphics systems.  Although less well-known than traditional parallel computing and supercomputers, there has been a long history of parallel graphics and imaging computers. Processing and generating images requires enormous amounts of computation. For example, if a one-million-instructions-per-second-computer (1MIPS) applies one arithmetic operation to each pixel of a one megapixel image, the computer takes one second to process one image. Rendering 3D virtual worlds for movies and games takes many orders of magnitude more computation per pixel than image processing. For example, an image generated for a modern movie requires about a billion floating point operations per pixel. As a result, to be useful in practice, graphics and imaging requires high-performance parallel supercomputers. These computers parallelize computations over large collections of data.

One early DARPA-funded research effort was the Geometry Engine, led by Jim Clark at Stanford.7 The Geometry Engine led to the formation of Silicon Graphics, a company that pioneered the development of 3D graphics workstations. The SGI hardware architecture and OpenGL software library defined the modern GPU architecture. Another notable government-funded research effort was the Pixel Planes series of high-performance graphics systems led by Henry Fuchs and his collaborators at the University of North Carolina.22 The Pixel Planes 5 was in fact a quite general single-instruction, multiple-data (SIMD) computer which ran parallel computations on a 128 x 128 image. Other examples of early parallel graphics and image computers were the NASA Massively Parallel Processor (MPP),1 the Ikonas Graphics Systems,15 and the Pixar Image Computer.27

Early GPUs implemented a fixed-function graphics pipeline similar to the early SGI workstations. The term GPU was introduced by Nvidia when it became possible for the entire OpenGL graphics pipeline to be implemented on a single chip. The Nvidia Geforce 256 introduced in 1999, which consisted of 17 million transistors, was the first commercially available GPU.

Earlier, while at Pixar, Hanrahan developed RenderMan, a system to generate photorealistic images. This system revolutionized the movie industry because it enabled the generation of images that could be seamlessly combined with live action captured with cameras. A key component of RenderMan was the shading language, which enabled users to extend the system to model complex materials and lighting.

Although the first GPUs implemented a fixed-function pipeline, they were constructed from programmable components. Unfortunately, these processing elements changed from system to system and from generation to generation. What was needed was a portable programming model. Since the major application for GPUs was computer games, it seemed natural to adapt the RenderMan shading language to GPUs so game developers could create new lighting and shading effects.

At Stanford under a DARPA funded project, a real-time shading language (RTSL) was designed and implemented for the then-current GPUs. Shading language programs are now called shaders. Bill Mark, a post-doctoral scholar, led the design of the Stanford RTSL and later joined Nvidia, and along with another former Stanford graduate student Kurt Akeley enhanced that technology and created the Cg shading language. Cg led to the development of Microsoft’s HLSL and OpenGL’s GLSL.

It was quickly realized that these early shading languages were flexible enough to implement many algorithms in scientific computing. Researchers adopted algorithms such as matrix-matrix multiplication, linear solvers, fluid-flow solvers, and molecular dynamics to run on shaders. This led to the GPGPU (General-Purpose GPU) computing movement.28,36

Stream processing.  DARPA- and DOE-funded work at Stanford on the Imagine stream processor and the Merrimac streaming supercomputer developed stream processing, a form of parallel computing that leads to increased arithmetic intensity (the ratio of computation to bandwidth). As mentioned previously, the majority of the power consumed by a processor is in communication. Sending signals between chips is particularly power hungry. Off-chip communication is also much slower than on-chip communication. Stream processing involves two main ideas that reduce the need for memory bandwidth. The first is to exploit producer-consumer locality so that one stage, the producer, forwards its results to the next stage, the consumer, without the need to write and to read from memory. The second major idea was to organize the computation into functions called kernels. Each kernel takes a packet of data, executes a function on that packet, and outputs another packet of data. The number of arithmetic operations in the function is greater than the number of reads and writes to memory. These two techniques significantly decrease the number of memory accesses and improve the efficiency of stream processing architectures.

In a stream processor, a computation was organized into kernels that produced and consumed streams of data. A producing kernel would write its output stream into a stream register file (SRF). The consuming kernel would read its input from the SRF without the data ever needing to be written to or read from memory. With appropriate scheduling to match the batch size of streams to the capacity of the SRF, this organization enabled applications to sustain very high arithmetic intensity (the ratio of arithmetic to memory bandwidth).

A DARPA-funded project to design and build the Imagine Stream Processor was started at MIT in 1997 and migrated to Stanford later that year.12,23,26 Imagine was a graphics- and media-processor intended for signal- and image-processing workloads. It consisted of a number of parallel arithmetic units with local register files, a central stream register file, and a memory system. Kernels read streams from the stream register file passing intermediate results through the local register files and writing output streams back to the stream register file to be read by the next kernel.

The Stream-C programming language was developed to program Imagine. It extended the C programming language with constructs to describe kernels and streams. Numerous graphics,32 signal-processing, and image-processing33 applications were developed to tune and evaluate the architecture. The performance on texture-mapped raster graphics was comparable to a contemporary fixed-function GPU.

At a DARPA principal investigators meeting, the authors of this article realized this technology could be applied to high-performance computing and conceived of the Merrimac project. The computer science (CS) part of the Stanford DOE ASCI Center was redirected to pursue this approach to high-performance computing. The Center’s annual reports offer a great history of the development of stream processing.a

The Merrimac architecture11 was defined to adapt stream processing to scientific applications. The major changes from Imagine were the addition of data types (like FP64) needed for scientific computations, scaling the architecture to multiple nodes connected by an interconnection network to handle problems at scale, and the addition of a number of resilience features17 to support computation at scale with a reasonable failure rate.

The Stream-C programming language evolved into Brook.2 The key idea behind Brook was to merge ideas from stream programming with more traditional data-parallel computing. Kernel functions became the key processing primitive to maintain high arithmetic intensity.

Brook was adapted to target GPUs of the early 2000s.3 These GPUs ran programmable vertex and fragment shaders. The shaders implemented kernels but had a limited number of instructions and a few registers. Common data-parallel programming primitives such as map, reduce/scan, filter, gather, and scatter were implemented by building a virtual data parallel computer on top of the low-level graphics shaders. This abstraction enabled a large number of existing parallel algorithms to be run on GPUs, and gradually the limitations of the early shaders were eliminated.

A good example of an early application of a kernel to perform computations with high arithmetic intensity is dense matrix-matrix multiplication, which underlies modern neural-net algorithms. When performing matrix-matrix multiplication, two n×n matrices need to be read and one n×n matrix needs to be written. The matrix multiply requires n3 multiples and accumulates. Thus, the arithmetic intensity is of O(n). This fact is well known and leads to efficient methods for blocking matrix multiplies for CPUs with caches. Blocking works well when run on GPUs.19

The numerical scientists in the Stanford ASCI Center ported several scientific codes to Brook to run on a Merrimac simulator. These included computational fluid dynamics,20 magnetohydrodynamics, and n-body simulations.16 The n-body simulation is a good example of an efficient GPU application. The force between a pair of atoms is a given by the gravitational law in astrophysical simulations, but the interactions between non-bounded atoms are approximated by the Lennard-Jones potential (or even more complicated empirical potentials). These functions require many arithmetic operations. For these simulations, neighboring atoms are stored in a “neighbor list.” Molecular dynamics simulations immediately became a major application for GPUs.14

A key feature of GPUs and stream processors is they have multiple forms of hardware parallelism. Each GPU consists of many cores. Each core contains a SIMD processing unit (typically 32-wide). In addition, each core is multithreaded. Recall that GPUs were developed for gaming applications whose performance was dependent on efficiency of applying textures to triangles. Texture mapping involves computing-texture coordinates for each pixel fragment inside a triangle and then fetching from an image using those coordinates. These texture fetches have spatial locality but very little temporal locality. Spatial locality can be handled with small caches, but caches cannot handle temporal locality because of the lack of coherence. Efficient texture mapping required that the GPU hide the latency of these texture fetches. Early GPUs did this by having a fragment request a texture, suspend execution of that fragment, and immediately switch to processing another fragment. This is a simplified version of multi-threading, which means the GPU needs to have many parallel threads running simultaneously. The total number of tasks is the number of cores times the number of SIMD arithmetic units (termed a warp) times the number of threads. A Blackwell B200 GPU has 384 streaming multiprocessors (SMs). Each SM has 64 resident warps of 32 threads each. Thus, there are 786,432 tasks executing simultaneously on this GPU.

Technology transfer.  The stream-processing architecture and programming system were transferred from Stanford to Nvidia by moving people. John Nickolls, an architect at Nvidia, heard about stream processing and recruited Bill Dally to consult at Nvidia on the architecture of the NV50 in 2003.31 (The NV50 was launched as G80 in 2006). Many of the features of stream processors were incorporated in the architecture. The “shared-memory” of the NV50 served the function of the SRF in Imagine and Merrimac.

Ian Buck (a graduate student on the Merrimac project and the principal developer of Brook) joined Nvidia in 2004. Ian worked with John Nickolls to evolve Brook into CUDA.30 CUDA incorporated the best features of Brook and Cg (a graphics shading language) as well as incorporating feedback from Brook programmers. The story of how the technology was transferred from Stanford to Nvidia is described in a presentation.4 Mike Houston (another graduate student on the project) joined AMD and used Brook directly as the programming language for their GPUs. The G80 (NV50) and CUDA were launched at Supercomputing in 2006.

When CUDA was launched in 2006 few people understood parallel programming, let alone GPU stream programming. To overcome this workforce deficit, Wen-Mei Hwu and David Kirk evangelized GPU computing by teaching CUDA programming courses for professors.25 The faculty who attended these courses went on to teach thousands of students parallel programming in CUDA. Parallel computing technologies borrowed from the Cosmic Cube, J-Machine, and M-Machine were applied both within a GPU—to coordinate multiple SMs—and across GPUs as multi-node GPU systems were built to tackle large problems.

Enabling AI.  Modern machine learning relies on three key ingredients—massive data sets, large models with many layers and weights, and the computing power to optimize the weights. The core algorithms (deep neural networks, convolutional networks, training using back propagation, and stochastic gradient descent) have all been around since the 1980s or earlier. Large, labeled datasets, such as PASCAL18 and Imagenet13 appeared in the early 2000s. Recent advances, such as embedding text into vector spaces, enabled deep learning for natural language. Transformers (attention is all you need)37 replaced hard-to-train recurrent neural networks with hidden states with easy-to-train neural networks with history. GPU computing enabled the training of large networks with massive data sets economically. Once this capability was demonstrated (Alexnet, GPT), the capabilities of AI improved rapidly. The rapid adoption of AI provided even more impetus for improving GPU computing systems.

Machine learning at Nvidia was also enabled by academic-industry synergy. A 2010 breakfast conversation between one of the authors (Dally) and Andrew Ng led to the initiation of a joint project between Nvidia and Stanford to build deep neural networks on GPUs.8 Bryan Catanzaro led the Nvidia portion of the project. The software developed during this project became CuDNN5 which provides a readily available library for deep learning on Nvidia GPUs—democratizing deep learning.

Conclusion

The technologies behind GPU computing, which has enabled modern machine learning, were largely developed thanks to 30 years of government-funded academic research. Research in parallel computing, parallel graphics systems, and stream processing laid the groundwork for GPU computing. Many of the students trained during these research projects took positions in industry transferring the technology and using it to develop innovative products. The transfer from the Stanford Stream Processing project to GPU computing was very direct with the academic Brook language evolving into CUDA and stream processor features being incorporated in the G80 GPU. The efficient, easily programmed, and very-high performance computing platform provided by GPUs with compute shaders enabled the current revolution in machine learning—providing the missing ingredient to complement the algorithms and data that had been available for some time.

Acknowledgments

The late John Nickolls played a critical role in transferring the Stanford stream processing technology to Nvidia. Scott Rixner, Brucek Khailany, Ujval Kapasi, John Owens, Jung Ho Ahn, Peter Mattson, Abishek Das, Jinyung Namkoong, Brian Towles, Andrew Chang, and Ben Mowery contributed to the Imagine project. Several of these students along with Mattan Erez, Ian Buck, Mike Houston, Timothy Knight, Nuwan Jayasena, Francois Labonte, Jayanth Gummaraju, Ben Serebrin, and Binu Mathew contributed to the Merrimac project. Several of these students along with Tim Foley, Daniel Horn, Jeremy Sugarman, and Kayvon Fatahalian contributed to the development of Brook. Kekoa Proudfoot, Bill Mark, Kurt Akeley, Ravi Glanville, Randy Fernando, and Mark Kilgard contributed to the development of RTSL and Cg. David Kirk and Wen-Mei Hwu evangelized CUDA programming. Massimilano Fatica, Vijay Pande, Eric Darve, Juan Alanso, Alan Wray, and Tim Barth developed early scientific Brook applications on Merrimac. Grants from DARPA, DoE, NSF, Intel, Sun, SGI, NVIDIA, and AMD supported this work.

item.title: Federal Funding of Public Key Cryptography
item.dc:creator: Martin E. Hellman
item.description: Federally funded research has paid handsome dividends in both economic benefits and national security.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Federal support is currently being cut to academic institutions in ways that will adversely affect both the U.S. economy and national security. While changes are probably needed, they should be made carefully, taking into account the positive economic impact that Federal support has already had in developing the Internet and other major technological developments. This article covers the key role Federal support played in my work on public key cryptography, which earned the 2015 ACM A.M. Turing Award. It also explains that technology.

My Experience with Federal Support of Basic Research

In November 1976, Whitfield Diffie and I published New Directions in Cryptography,2 which disclosed the idea of public key cryptography (PKC) and provided an algorithm now known as Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange—but which I have argued12 should be called Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange because it is based on independent work of Ralph Merkle at the University of California at Berkeley.8

Today, PKC forms the foundation for e-commerce, allowing more than US$1 trillion per day in foreign exchange transactions in North America alone.10 This technology also allows electronic banking, credit-card transactions on the Internet, and secure software updates.

Our 1976 paper notes that, “This work was partially supported by the National Science Foundation under NSF Grant ENG 10173.”

My research in those days was supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation and a contract from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR). As can be seen from what was said above, that relatively small funding has paid handsome dividends.

Given the U.S. National Security Agency’s (NSA’s) concerns at that time about academic research in cryptography, I had been initially hesitant to use any of my Federal support for this work and had used unsupported time to work on the subject. But my NSF grant monitor told me NSF would allow me to use their support for this work. Later, my Air Force contract monitor said the same thing, and I was able to also use funds from AFOSR to work in cryptography.

In an interesting twist, Adm. Bobby Inman (U.S. Navy, Retired), who was director of NSA during that period of resistance to open publication of papers in cryptography, has a very different perspective today. MIT (and soon to be University of California, Berkeley) Professor Henry Corrigan-Gibbs wrote a 2014 article1 which says:

“Inman was not excited about the prospect of high-grade encryption systems being available for purchase, especially abroad. ‘We were worried that foreign countries would pick up and use cryptography that would make it exceedingly hard to decrypt and read their traffic.’ …

“[But], today Inman is as worried about protecting nongovernmental computer systems as Hellman was in the 1970s. When asked if he would make the same decisions about nongovernmental cryptography now as he did then, Inman replied, ‘Rather than being careful to make sure they were[n’t] going to damage [our collection capabilities] … I would have been interested in how quickly they were going to be able to make [cryptosystems] available in a form that would protect proprietary information as well as government information.’

“The theft of portions of the designs for the F-35 jet, Inman said, demonstrates that weak nongovernmental encryption and computer security practices can grievously harm national security.”

Flexibility in how grant money was spent was also key. Whitfield Diffie had worked at Stanford’s Artificial Intelligence Lab but had left when his desire to do more research on cryptography conflicted with its contract requirements. He then traveled around the country learning about cryptography and, when he visited IBM’s Watson Research Center at Yorktown Heights, NY, the head of their cryptographic research effort told him that I had been there a few months earlier, saying similar things (which IBM’s management discouraged them from following) and that he should contact me when he returned to Stanford.

Thus, Whit showed up at Stanford in the fall of 1974, and we had an immediate rapport. I wanted to keep him here and the flexibility in my NSF grant allowed me to hire him even though that was not contemplated at the time of the grant. My partnership with Whit was crucial to the work that led to New Directions in Cryptography and the applications which followed.

The importance of this work was immediately clear to many, but some had a very different perspective. For example, Irwin Feerst, a perennial write-in candidate for IEEE president, stated, “The [IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] are indeed full of crap. . . . In fact, I can’t even tell if I’ve got it right side up or upside down.”3

In addition to New Directions, those IEEE Transactions published work which led to several important start-ups, including Qualcomm, which has a current market cap of more than US$150 billion.

How Our System Works

Imagine that Alice and Bob want to exchange messages written on pieces of paper, but Eve (an eavesdropper) gets to relay messages from Alice to Bob.

Alice writes out her private message and locks it in a strongbox. She would like to tell the lock’s combination to Bob, but doing so would allow Eve to open the box when Alice passed it to Eve to give to Bob. Alice therefore keeps the combination secret, so Eve is unable to read the message. Unfortunately, neither can Bob.

But the hasp on the strongbox is big enough that Bob can add his own lock, to which only he knows the combination. Bob then passes the doubly locked strongbox to Eve who cannot take off either lock. Eve then passes the strongbox to Alice who removes her lock, leaving only Bob’s.

Alice then passes the strongbox back to Eve, who cannot remove Bob’s lock to read the message, but when Bob gets it, he removes his lock and reads the message. We have accomplished the seemingly impossible!

In this physical analogy, it was crucial that the hasp on the strongbox was big enough to hold two locks. If it had only been big enough for one lock, when Bob got the locked-up strongbox, he could have put it in a bigger strongbox that he then locked with his lock. But when Alice received the doubly locked message, she would be unable to remove her lock from the inner strongbox.

It was important that the locks could be added and removed in any order—that the process was commutative. If the hasp were big enough for only one lock, adding and removing the locks would not have been commutative.

While this explanation came after I developed what is now usually called Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, what I needed (but did not know at the time) was a commutative one-way function. A one-way function is easy to compute but extremely difficult (effectively impossible) to invert.

I had been looking for one-way functions with strong mathematical structure prior to Whit and I working on public key cryptography. As part of that effort, I met with Professor John Gill, at the time a new faculty member who had his doctorate in mathematics from UC Berkeley. (John was also one of the first Black graduates of Georgia Tech, an interesting story in itself.)

John first suggested factoring as a one-way function. But we had looked at and discarded it—although we wish we hadn’t since the RSA system is based on factoring.11 John then suggested indices, which is what mathematicians call discrete logarithms.

Thus, late one night in May 1976, I was “playing” with equations, trying to find a usable public key cryptosystem. In such a system, each user has a public key and a secret key. While a user’s secret key is, in theory, computable from his public key, that computation must be effectively impossible, taking eons to accomplish.

I wrote the equation for discrete exponentiation:

Y = a x   m o d   p (1)

where p is a prime number. Discrete exponentiation is easy, much as a to the 2101 power can be computed with 100 multiplications (squaring operations) followed by a single multiplication:

a ∧ 2 101 = a ∧ 2 100 * a ∧ 1   m o d   p (2)

And, because arithmetic is done modulo p, the numbers never get larger than p.

Implicitly, Eq. 1 also defines the discrete logarithm function:

X = log a   ( Y )  mod p (3)

While it has never been proved that discrete logarithms are hard, 50 years of experience indicate it is not an easy problem.

I had four parameters with which to play: X,Y,a, and p. At one point, I assumed that a and p were publicly known, in which case X had to be a user’s secret key and Y his public key. User i could randomly choose his secret key Xi, and easily compute his public key Yi as:

Y i = a ∧ X i   m o d   p (4)

But computing his secret key Xi from his public key Yi would be effectively impossible because that required computing a discrete logarithm.

I then tried to combine user i’s and user j’s keys and came up with the following method of computing a common key for them to use:

K i j = Y i ∧ X j = Y j ∧ X i = a ∧ X i ∗ X j   m o d   p (5)

Not trusting my equations, I programmed these operations on an HP scientific calculator with a small prime such as 97 and confirmed that the same key was obtained by user j (by raising user i’s public key Yi to his secret key Xj) and by user i (by raising user j’s public key Yj to his secret key Xi).

Note that commutativity is crucial. It doesn’t matter if one first raises a to the Xi power (to obtain Yi) and then raises that number to the Xj power, or vice versa. You get the same result.

But instead of a public key cryptosystem, which Whit and I had been trying to find, this turned out to be a Merkle public key distribution system. In the latter system, users i and j compute a common key that neither of them could have predicted beforehand. That is why, if names are to be assigned to this system, I have argued it should be called Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange.

Ralph Merkle independently came up with the privacy half of public key cryptography as a master’s student at UC Berkeley. His 1978 article in Communications8 gives the impression that his work followed ours (published in 1976) and RSA’s (published in 1977). But the delay in the publication of Merkle’s article was due primarily to people not appreciating his work, which fits with the next section of this article on “The Wisdom of Foolishness.”

When Ralph had to do a term project in CS 244 in the fall of 1974, he proposed “secure communication over insecure channels” (the privacy part of public key cryptography), but the professor wrote: “Project 2 [a much more mundane proposal] looks more reasonable, maybe because your description of Project 1 [the privacy part of PKC] is muddled terribly.”

Merkle dropped the course and pursued public key distribution on his own.

When Ralph submitted an early version of the paper to Communications, it was rejected with the editor telling him in an Oct. 22, 1975 letter, “I … was particularly bothered by the fact that there are no references to the literature. Has anyone else ever investigated this approach?”4 Partially in the editor’s defense, Ralph should have included references, as he did in the final version of the article that appeared three years later.

The editor was also hindered by the reviewer on whom she relied. The reviewer recommended rejecting the paper because it “is not in the mainstream of present cryptography thinking.” He was right. It was totally new and groundbreaking.

Today, Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange (usually called Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange) is often done with respect to elliptic curves. Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), suggested independently by Neal Koblitz7 and Victor Miller,9 makes use of the fact that any commutative one-way function can be used in the algorithm, not just exponentiation in modular arithmetic. ECC uses addition on elliptic curves and allows smaller keys for a given security level than either exponentiation in modular arithmetic or the RSA algorithm.

The Wisdom of Foolishness

As seen by the treatment Ralph Merkle’s work received, it is important not to let conventional wisdom dictate the work that is undertaken. My own research in cryptography was also met with universal resistance at first, leading to what I now call “the wisdom of foolishness.” The following anecdote, taken from a book my wife Dorothie and I wrote on “creating true love at home and peace on the planet,”6 provides a good example:

Dorothie: Recently, we were at a birthday celebration for a good friend and one of the other guests asked Marty what he did. When he told her that we were writing this book, her reply was polite, but she made it clear she thought we were on a fool’s errand. To which Marty replied, “Thank you! That’s the best compliment you could pay me.” I’ll let him explain.

Marty: It’s ironic that one of the last things most people want to be seen as is foolish, yet many great advances were initially derided as fools’ errands before they paid off.

I had a personal experience of this. My work in cryptography (which today is called cybersecurity) has earned me some of the highest honors in my profession, but when I was starting out, all of my colleagues told me I was wasting my time. Luckily, one of them—former UCLA Professor Jim Omura—was standing near me when that birthday party guest basically told me that we were wasting our time writing this book. I asked Jim to come over and tell her what he had thought of my cryptographic research in the early days, and he obliged.

Jim had told me that I could quote him, so I knew that he would tell her how foolish my effort had seemed at first—which he did. In an interesting twist of fate, after my work panned out, Jim left UCLA and co-founded a Silicon Valley startup that capitalized on it and later sold the company for $35 million.

In 2013, when I was inducted as a “Stanford Engineering Hero,” my lecture on “The Wisdom of Foolishness”5 included several examples of breakthrough technological work that was initially derided.

Vint Cerf, who with Robert Kahn developed the now widely used TCP/IP protocol, emailed me, saying that “Packet switching was regarded as crazy, even after the great example of the ARPANET. Most conventional communications engineers thought it would not handle speech let alone video. Of course, it got better and better over time. The naysayers believed that store and forward would have too high a latency to be useful. They were wrong.”

Today, all major streaming video services use packet switching to deliver video. Cerf and Kahn were awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation by President Clinton for their work. It also won them the ACM Turing Award.

Brad Parkinson, who pioneered GPS, told me, “The Air Force thought GPS was foolish. They saw no value in precision weapons delivery and certainly did not identify with the civilian applications (which I told congress from the start was a part of the system).

“They also thought that the user equipment would be prohibitive, but we could foresee the digital revolution underway. The first GPS units weighed about 150 pounds, used about 2 Kw, and cost about US$250,000. Today, a GPS receiver fits on a chip weighing a fraction of an ounce, uses milliwatts of power, and costs (chip only) under US$5 [updated in 2025].

“None are so blind as they who refuse to see. The Air Force generally persisted in their view, until the first Gulf War showed what the system could do.”

In 2018, Brad won the IEEE’s highest award, its Medal of Honor, for that work.

John Cioffi, sometimes called “the father of DSL,” emailed me saying, “In 1979, as a young kid fresh out of Stanford, I got laughed out of the room in my first DSL meeting at Bell Labs when I pushed for more speed than the 160kbps then coming into discussion. I said 1.5 Mbps should be possible on the existing twisted pairs.

“Today [2013], DSL speeds are more than 100X greater than even that projection, and DSL has 70% of the worldwide broadband market.”

John was awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation by President Biden for that work.

Federico Faggin, who designed the first microprocessor at Intel wrote, “In 1970, when I was designing the world’s first microprocessor, the CEO of American Micro Systems, then the largest producer of random-logic custom ICs [a technology which lost market share to microprocessors] was quoted in Electronics News as saying something like, ‘Whoever thinks that a CPU (the word microprocessor had not yet been coined) will replace random logic is out of his mind.’ I remember cutting out that article and posting it in my office as an added incentive to prove such myopic observation wrong!”

Federico was awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation by President Obama for his work.

Since I received the 2015 ACM A.M. Turing Award for my work on public key cryptography, I have had the opportunity to ask six Nobel Laureates if the work that won them their prizes was initially encouraged or discouraged as “foolish, crazy, never go anywhere.” Five of the six were clearly in the latter camp.

Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on quasi-crystals, told me that no less an authority than Linus Pauling—who had won Nobel Prizes in both Chemistry (1954) and Peace (1962)—derisively referred to it as “quasi-science.”

Lou Ignarro, who won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, told me that his dean came to him and said something like, “Lou, we hired you because you did good work. Why are you doing this crazy stuff?” Crazy stuff that won the Nobel Prize.

Chapter 4 of the book that Dorothie and I wrote is on “The Power of Belief Systems” and starts out with a Mark Twain quip: “They did not know it was impossible so they did it.”

Conclusion

Federally funded research has paid handsome dividends, with my personal experience being just one example. Such research has had economic benefits, but it also has enhanced national security as evidenced by Adm. Inman’s earlier comment.

And, as shown in this article, seemingly foolish research can pay great dividends.

Study is needed to determine if some areas of research that are currently funded should not be, but such determinations need to be based on careful analysis and reasoned debate.

item.title: Working Together and Working at a Distance
item.dc:creator: Judith S. Olson and Gary M. Olson
item.description: What we know today about success with distance work is the result of 30 years of federally funded research.
item.content:encoded:
We are cognitive psychologists by training now in a subfield of computer science (CS) called human-computer interaction (HCI). We have spent more than 30 years studying how technology supports teamwork both when teams work face-to-face or at a distance. We are delighted to tell our story of how federal dollars supporting our research not only advanced science in important ways but also helped new areas of “big science” work more successfully. Our work also generated important practical advice to everyday people, both during Covid and now that we are working remotely. We had studied group work for a number of years, but in the early 1990s, we pivoted our research to focus on whether people could work at a distance, whether the quality of the work suffered, or productivity fell, as well as how people felt about working that way. What could employees do to make it work well? What could managers do? What equipment was needed and how should it be arranged? What mattered? In the early 1990s, video conferencing was very expensive, and laptops were not practical yet. But the things we learned about people working together with advanced technology are still applicable today.

Thirty years later, Covid hit, and almost everyone was working from home. Video conferencing was free or at least inexpensive. Drawing on our decades of federally funded research, we knew what could help and seized a multitude of opportunities to get the word out. We were interviewed on television and reported in mainstream print publications, not just academic journals. Word got out that it is possible to work from home, but you had to set things up right and practice good habits. You can make distance work really work. Here is that story.

A Place for Teamwork

We were professors at the University of Michigan: Gary in the Psychology Department and Judy in the Business School’s Department of Computer and Information Systems. Our first joint research involved studying teamwork, both in real life, called “field work,” and in laboratory experiments. To run experiments, we needed space, a place where groups could come together to be recorded on audio and video while working. This was the late 1980s. As it happened, the business school had just built a new building for research, and it had a big open space with offices surrounding it. The dean knew we needed dedicated space to carry out our federally funded research, which he deemed highly relevant to current business practices: how to manage teams of workers so productivity is high, how they should be arranged, and what technology they needed.

The dean gave us the space and introduced us to two Michigan corporate sponsors. Impressed with our track record publishing sound work and our continuing support from the National Science Foundation (NSF), one sponsor offered us money and access to their teams for observation; another offered us money and design help in furnishing the open space in the new research lab. They could help us design the room that would serve as a sophisticated meeting room as well as a place to run groups in our experiments. That meant the room was not only beautiful and functional but was also equipped with hidden cameras and microphones. These were controlled from an observation room with one-way mirrors so we could see them, but they could not see us. The room (Figure 1) was named the Collaboration Technology Suite (CTS).11

The room’s striking feature was its eight workstations, individual desks on wheels embedded with the then-large computer monitors. These were the late 1980s, before there were functional laptops. Today, you put your laptop on any meeting table and set it at any angle for viewing and making eye contact. In the late 1980s, all we had were desktop computers, the bigger the better. But the large monitors blocked sight lines, making them unsuitable for working with others. Our newly designed desks allowed us to set the computer screens at any angle between flat and fully upright to suit the work at hand. In addition, the desks could be set in any configuration in the room: a circle, a long table (as in Figure 1), or clusters of two for breaking up into subgroups. The large rear-projection screen in front could project a video, PowerPoint slides, or any team member’s computer screen, depending on the meeting’s purpose.

The CTS served us for our lab studies that we’ll soon discuss. While it was built with corporate funds, it was federal funding that made the scientific research possible by supporting experimental technology development, supporting students and assistants, and paying research expenses. The CTS also served as a showcase in tours of the business school. On a number of occasions once the word got out, people from across campus would use the room because of the technology and arrangement it offered: Everyone had a computer at hand and any of them could be projected to the front screen. And, of course, our lab meetings took place here with us together taking notes on our designed shared editor.

Showing That the Lab Work Applied to the Real World

As mentioned earlier, throughout our research career, we collected data from field work and from experiments run in the CTS. We wanted the work in the lab to be as close to real work as possible. In many of the experiments, we had people who already knew each other and had worked together to design an automatic post office. (This was 10 years before automated post offices became popular.) To make sure our results from experiments applied to the real world, we needed to show that the setting and task are comparable to real teamwork.

We had recordings from ten real-life design meetings from four projects in two organizations. We transcribed these video recordings with time stamps on each utterance. We coded each of their utterances about design, for example, stating an Issue, offering an Alternative, and then giving reasons, Criterion, to evaluate the Alternative. There were then other labels having to do with managing the session and clarification. Overall, only 40% of the meeting times were spent on design; the rest had to do with summarizing, planning the time, and digressions.

In Figure 2, we show the transition diagrams of real meetings side-by-side with that of the lab meetings. The size of the circles represents total time spent, and the width of the arrows indicates the relative frequency with which that transition is made. The white areas inside the circles indicate the original statement in that category; the black indicates questions and their responses.

There are some understandable differences in that those in the lab did not do longer-term project management. But the overall pictures were remarkably similar. Indeed, the activity from laboratory tasks in general matched that of the meetings in the real world, meaning findings in the lab would apply to the real world.15

Building the Shared Editor and Testing Its Effects

One of the first tools we developed in the early 1990s was a shared editor, which we unwisely called ShrEdit. The application was very similar to Google Docs released 15 years later; any number of people can have a document open and edit it at the same time. Figure 3 shows ShrEdit, with two shared windows at the top and one private one at the bottom. The boxes in the middle illustrate a feature that today’s collaborative editors should have but do not: a way to move to where someone else is working and when done, pop back to where you were last working. We wanted to see if ShrEdit affected work.

One of our first experiments showed that the groups using ShrEdit created significantly better designs than those using a whiteboard and Microsoft Word.16 But they did it in an unexpected way. They considered fewer Issues but more Alternatives, apparently expanding on the major issues with good ideas. Not surprisingly, the groups using ShrEdit wrote significantly longer final reports, mainly because more people could write at the same time.

In 2005, Google Docs was introduced, and we found it was very similar to our ShrEdit. So, in 2014-16, Judy asked her students in a project management class to use Google Docs for their assignments.17 We asked the students permission to use their data for research and all of them complied.

Ninety-five percent of the documents exhibited some amount of simultaneous work. The documents in which authors wrote about equivalent amounts were judged to be higher quality. We also used their data to look at the different styles of working. We created visualizations similar to the work of Viegas, Wattenberg, and Dave visualizing Wikipedia collaborations.21 Ours were called Docuviz. Figure 4 shows two exemplary styles of work. The one on the left shows an outline style, where the person depicted in blue wrote an outline and then the others filled in their assigned portions of the document with very little editing of each other’s contributions. The one on the right shows a case where they found a document similar to what was asked for, pasted it in, and pared it down to fit the details of the assignment. Then they embarked on many sessions of simultaneous work to include their material in the style of the found document. The occurrence of simultaneous work is shown by the number of colors (participants) at the top in each time slice. The document on the right had many sessions of simultaneous work, whereas the one on the left had one simultaneous session in the second-to-last time slice.

The new generation of information workers embraces simultaneous work. Fifteen years after our original ShrEdit experiments, our findings about collaborative work are even more relevant now that online shared editors like Google Docs are widely adopted. Today, Google Docs has more than a billion active users.

Lab Work on Working at a Distance

All our experimental work on face-to-face teamwork was done in the CTS, which, because of its functionality and beauty, was also a stop on many tours of the business school. At one such session, a visiting executive said to us, “I think this is very exciting work, but if you want to really make an impact on the world, study distributed teams and watch them over time. We need help in making that work.”

This comment caused us to pivot our whole research program from co-located teams to distributed teams. We focused on investigating not only what technology helped them but also the most effective styles of work. We simulated distributed conditions by commandeering three offices and outfitting them with ShrEdit and video equipment (See Figure 5). This was 10 years before the first affordable video conferencing system (Skype) and 20 years before Zoom. We ran groups of three people in our experiments, so each room had two monitors, one on each side of the computer, arranged so that when the two remote people looked at each other, it looked to this person as if they were looking at each other.

Our work15 again used ShrEdit and the automatic post-office design task among people who knew each other, communicating face-to-face, remote with video, and remote with only audio. It turned out the designs where people had video were statistically equal in quality to those created when they are face-to-face. In contrast, those using only audio created significantly poorer designs. Adding video to audio makes the participants not only better at what they are doing but also significantly more satisfied than those using only audio. Video was especially helpful for non-native English speakers because they could see when the other person did not understand (e.g., eyebrows down), so they explained more fully without being asked.20

How the monitor is positioned has an effect:9 If you view the remote person from the monitor placed high, they look tall and dominant. If the monitor is low, the person looks short and weak. Indeed, people seen on higher monitors had more influence than those on lower ones. Since laptops are small and the view of the person is low, many people using video on laptops today appropriately put them on stacks of books so they see the other person at eye level, and the remote person does the same.

We also ran a series of studies where some people were colocated and others were remote and alone, one of the hardest configurations to work in but adopted by many employees today calling it “hybrid work.” The ease of communication among those colocated creates a strong bond. Those colocated preferred to work with other co-located workers, even though remote workers could perform the work better.4 Remote workers, being ignored by co-located staff, worked with each other. Even when remote people are from one’s own subgroup, the ease of communication with those who are colocated makes one select co-located people to work with.2 And, when remote workers become colocated, they will also work closely with co-located workers even though they had previously preferred working with other remotes.3

We also studied trust development in the lab, knowing that trust is very essential for work to be smooth and satisfying.8 We measured trust using the Prisoner’s Dilemma, a game-theory thought experiment involving rational agents who can either cooperate for mutual benefit or betray their partners for individual gain. The dilemma arises from the fact that while defecting is rational for all agents, cooperation yields a higher payoff for each. In playing this game, we had three-person groups: Conversing face-to-face, by video and audio, by audio only, or by text chat. Participants played 30 rounds, with discussion encouraged in breaks after every five rounds. Those meeting face-to-face trusted and acted trustworthy throughout.6 Those with audio only and video plus audio had less trust than face-to-face, but their trust grew throughout and eventually reached a level equal to face-to-face. Those communicating only by text had significantly lower trust and did not increase over time.

Our follow-on experiment showed it was possible to effectively pre-build trust in distributed collaborations. We knew from the literature that if people met face-to-face before working remotely, they will exhibit trust. We ran an experiment showing that if people engaged in a get-to-know-each-other activity via video, they developed nearly the same level of trust as if they had met face-to-face.22 Having a team get to know each other by video is fortunately a much cheaper way to foster success than paying for their travel and lodging; it saves time and effort as well.

In summary from findings in the laboratory, we first established that the design task we used in the lab was close enough to real-world design sessions to have faith that our findings in the lab would apply to the real world. We created a shared editor, similar to today’s Google Docs, and found that groups that used it created better designs than those using whiteboard and single-user Word. In examining people using Google Docs for academic group homework, we found that 95% of the documents exhibited simultaneous work, though they did it in a variety of styles. The best designs came from groups whose members contributed equally.

When working at a distance, using video created designs not significantly different from those working face-to-face, whereas those working only with audio had designs that were significantly lesser quality. Video was particularly important for those who were not native speakers of English. Placement of the camera and monitor could affect one person’s influence over the others, where being artificially tall gave one greater influence. Remote workers with audio only or audio plus video trusted others at lower levels than those face-to-face, although the trust grew over time. Remote workers who conversed only with chat were significantly lower in trust and did not improve over time. But trust could be jump-started if remote workers have conversations beforehand getting to know each other when they conversed by video.

If some people are distant and others colocated, those colocated preferred to work with those in their same location; those remote worked with other remotes because they were rarely contacted by co-located people, even when some of the people who are remote have a long relationship with some of those who are colocated. The ease of communication is very strong in deciding with whom to work.

Findings from Observations in the Field

In the early and mid-1990s, the scale of the problems facing the world—fighting cancer, addressing climate change, and so forth—required the collaboration of larger teams of researchers from different institutions and different but related areas of science. This new style of scientific work became known as “Collaboratories,” or laboratories without walls. NSF was spending huge amounts of money supporting their development; some of them succeeded, some failed. We convinced them that it would be money well spent if NSF could have us focus on these big science projects: finding out what makes them succeed and what makes them fail, possibly developing some assessment techniques to tell which are which, and hopefully coming up with remedies to help all of them succeed. We joined with Tom Finholt, Stephanie Teasley, and Dan Atkins, all at Michigan, to secure funding from NSF for a five-year project.

The Science of Collaboratories group gathered data on collaboratories in two ways:

  • First, we were collecting some basic data on all the collaboratories we could find. In 2008, the year our book Scientific Collaboration on the Internet18 came out, we had identified 212 collaboratories: 150 could be classified, and for 70 of them, we created summaries with more detail.

  • Second, the team joined a set of collaboratories to both assist in their building or adoption of technologies and to observe them with the goal of finding out what made good collaboration and where the failures were. The team joined collaboratories in several fields, including upper atmospheric physics (UARC and SPARC), earthquake engineering (NEESgrid), HIV/AIDS research in Africa (IARC), astronomy (The National Virtual Observatory), particle physics (the Large Hadron Collider collaborations), and biomedical research (Biomedical Informatics Research Network, BIRN) among others. Results appear in Olson et al.18

For example, the first large-scale project we were involved in was the Upper Atmospheric Research Collaboratory (UARC, pronounced “You-Ark”).12 UARC joined domain specialists, computer scientists, and us, behavioral scientists, to build state-of-the art technologies to collect and analyze data from the upper atmosphere and allow scientists from around the world to collaborate. The domain scientists studied interactions of the solar wind, the Earth’s magnetic field, and the characteristics of the upper atmosphere. The northern lights are beautiful manifestations of some of these interactions, when a burst from the sun hits the upper atmosphere and creates not only the lovely hues in the sky visible to the human eye, but also disruptions in the upper atmosphere that tell scientists more about the Earth’s atmosphere. The five-year project began in 1993 using a “user-centered iterative rapid prototyping design strategy” throughout the project, meaning we would continuously be asking the scientists how the interface could be better and what new functionality they wanted. They collect data from observatories, with particularly rich data coming from the Arctic. Our goal was to connect the observatories to the Internet, allowing scientists to collect and analyze data from around the world without having to travel to cold remote locations. Scientists would see data simultaneously from around the world, and they would be able to communicate various analyses and not only determine together model components but also plan the next steps.

The initial application mimicked the interfaces of the physical devices to help the scientists learn quickly. But over the ten major redesigns in seven years, the space physicists wanted more aggregated data, data from around the world and eventually side-by-side views of data analysis and model representations. There were more scientists from all over the globe wanting access. And because there were so many choices of what to view and who to interact with, they developed “rooms” with coordinated sets of data and “clubs” as groups of collaborators. And, like ShrEdit, collaborators could see the same view and all share the pointer to aid discussion. Figure 6 shows the interface as it was in 1997. The “chat” is on the lower left of this screen. This was particularly helpful because the collaborators came from all over the world, with drastically different time zones. The “chat” allowed them to read back in time to catch up to the topic at hand and to contribute appropriately.

Near the end of UARC, the Internet became popular, so the whole desktop application became a website. By converting everything to the Web, this gave them modularity, so that the suite of tools could be used by other communities of collaborating scientists, interoperability over platforms, and the possibility of integrating with other Web tools and data sites. Because of these achievements, the project was funded by NSF for another five years under the Space Physics and Aeronomy Research Collaboratory (SPARC).

Two major advances were made in the understanding of these collaboratories. First, from the broad-scale data we collected, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboratories,5 and second, from all observations of the collaborations witnessed in depth, we developed a first-level theory of what makes them successful.14

The seven types in the taxonomy, a short description of each, and an example of each are:

  1. Shared Instrument: Remote access to expensive instruments, such as telescopes, frequently supplemented with video conferencing, chat, electronic lab notebooks, or other communication tools, for example, the Keck Observatorya

  2. Community Data Systems: An information resource created, maintained, or improved by a geographically distributed community, for example, the Protein Data Bankb

  3. Community Infrastructure Project: Infrastructure to support work in a particular domain. Software tools, standardized protocols, new scientific instruments, and educational methods, for example, The Grid Physics Network (GriPhyN)c

  4. Open Community Contribution System: An open project that aggregates the efforts of many geographically separate individuals toward a common research problem. Contributions come in the form of work rather than data. Results are made available to AI systems, for example, The Open Mindd

  5. Virtual Community of Practice: People share a research area broadly and communicate it online. They share advice, techniques, and pointers to other resources, but do not undertake joint projects, for example, the National Ocean Servicee

  6. Virtual Learning Community: The goal is to increase the knowledge of the participants, not to conduct research, for example, The Ecological Circuitry Collaboratoryf

  7. Distributed Research Center: These function as research centers at universities but are distributed, for example, Inflammation and the Host Response to Injuryg

The second advance was the Theory of Remote Scientific Collaboration (ToRSC), the synthesis of findings from the field, both science and corporate, and the laboratory, building on our earlier heavily cited work.10 They list the five aspects of collaboration that lead to success.

  1. The nature of the work. Structure the tasks so that interdependence across distance is reduced.

  2. Common ground. Construct common vocabulary and ask questions if you don’t understand something.

  3. Collaboration readiness. Create incentive structures that support a mix of competition and cooperation.

  4. Management, planning, and decision-making. Provide good leadership. Team members should feel that decisions are being made fairly and clearly.

  5. Technology readiness. Provide technology to support creative activities, coordination support, storage of information, and bandwidth to support both the work and people’s communication without delay. Create a “communication covenant,” a template for which is shown in Figure 7.

The same chapter outlines what we considered “success.” It encompassed a wide variety of outcomes beyond advances to the science itself, including impacts on scientists’ careers, learning and science education, inspiration to others, funding and public perception, and new tools built and used.

Federal funds supported many years of our work so that team science could be more successful bringing results.

Broader Impacts

The group of scientists and behavioral scientists interested in team science, like us, grew into a conference, what today is called the International Network for the Science of Team Science (INSciTS, pronounced “insights”). Its webpage says the group includes those “leading, engaging in, managing, facilitating, supporting, evaluating, and producing scholarship on team science.” There are Special Interest Groups (SIGs) that focus on education, beginning a collaboratory, data analytics, and fostering team science in academics. The creation of INSciTS is a testament to federal funding producing self-perpetuating research communities.

Clearly, having people succeed in their collaboratories speeds up the discovery of important things for everyone, like medical breakthroughs, actions to reduce global warming so weather calms down, planning and constructing buildings that survive a large earthquake, and so on. The fact that the association INSciTS exists, where people do research on how to do research better, says that people are continuing to want to do their own collective work better.

Several resources have been established to help people collaborate. The Mendeley Science of Team Science Libraryh is one. It houses 2,500 team science references, and is a good example of one of the seven collaboratory types, an Open Community Contribution System. One can sign up free to be a user but is also encouraged to submit other papers in a crowdsourcing fashion.

There are two committee reports on team science put together by the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, the combined National Academies: One committee of experts in the field developed a report called Enhancing the Effectiveness of Team Science,7,i published in 2015, and the more recent committee published a report in 2025 called The Science and Practice of Team Science.19,j

Both sites offer the substantial reports to download for free.

For people wanting tools to help their own collaborations go better, we offered the Collaboration Success Wizard1 for five years. This software asked a number of questions about the collaboration and automatically returned a written report on the strengths and weaknesses of the collaboration as well as what actions to take to make success more likely.

We also gathered the Team Science Acceleration Lab Toolkit. The toolkit is a website offering 40 different exercises or tasks that have been used to help collaboratory members be successful. It organizes the tools in terms of what stage the team is in: whether they are planning it, launching it, or helping it with ongoing work. For example, it includes instructions on how to create a Communication Covenant, lists things that foster trust among team members, offers a tool to help when conflict arises, and even gives advice about recognizing a “bad apple” and dealing with them. A special section highlighted on the homepage is “How to work at a distance.” It lists advice such as selecting players who have worked well at a distance, and assigning distant workers semi-independent work so they don’t have to contact each other often, and so on. The advice there is closely aligned with advice in our 2014 book for non-scientists called Working Together Apart: Collaboration over the Internet.13

When Covid Hit and Most People Were Distant

When Covid hit the world, it forced most workers to work from home. Because we created practical advice for working remotely, our research was picked up in the general press. Although our work did not say anything about working while parenting small children or having cats walk in front of the camera, much of the advice fit. Our findings, such as advice about trust, communication covenants, and so on, did hold. And because impressions matter, we had advice about making the camera the height of your eyes, so it looks to the remote people that you are looking directly at them. The idea of putting your laptop on a pile of books even made it onto a New Yorker cover.

During Covid, we were interviewed by a number of outlets including The Atlantic, titled “When Working from Home Doesn’t Work.” In June 2020, soon after the pandemic hit, Judy was interviewed on NPR for an article titled, “Get a Comfortable Chair: Permanent Work from Home is Coming.”k The article does talk about other aspects of distance work, but we were amused that the advice about getting an ergonomic chair made it to the title.

Many companies these days are adopting a “hybrid” model, where people are allowed to work from home some days but are required to come to the office on others. Our research4 shows that this is probably the worst model if people choose themselves which days they work from home. On some days, they might be the only person on their team who is remote. Unfortunately, as the saying goes: out of sight, out of mind. In partially distributed teams, the remote person is likely forgotten when information is exchanged. If managers want to allow people to work from home some days, the people on a team should all choose the same days. When everyone is remote, when communication needs to happen, it happens, either when everyone reads Slack or when everyone is on video.

Conclusion

Today, we know a lot about distance work and how to make it work. Thirty years of federally funded research brought significant knowledge about how to do a now-common work style well. It brought a huge benefit from smaller teams, to companies, to large-scale scientific research.

From our laboratory work, we know that having a shared editor like Google Docs improves the work. And today’s young professionals adopt it and work together simultaneously in many of their documents but do their work in a variety of ways. We know that distant work with video is more effective than with audio only, nearly as good as face-to-face work as well as more satisfying than audio only. Having the camera at eye level makes the participants equally dominant. When teams are split so that some are colocated and some remote, those colocated prefer the easy communication with other co-located colleagues. This effect is very strong, overriding empathy acquired from having been remote, and even overriding cases where the remote colleague has a long history with the co-located colleague. Trust was highest when people have been colocated and got to know each other. With video connections, trust can be built, whereas with text chat, trust stays at a low level. Trust can be jump-started by a purposeful get-to-know-you session over video before teamwork starts.

From our field work, we know that collaboratories tackling big questions in science can take many shapes, such as shared instrument, community data systems, community infrastructure systems, open community contribution systems, virtual community of practice, virtual learning community, and distributed research center. To succeed, you must assign the work to distributed colleagues so the need for communication is low. You must create common vocabularies and adopt similar working styles. There should be a culture of cooperation with some competition. Leadership must be clear and fair. And, the right suite of technologies should be available and taught so colleagues can communicate easily; coordinate, store and retrieve material; and have sufficient bandwidth and storage capacity to support easy communication and unlimited storage. Success in collaboratories can be defined as advancing science, enhancing individuals’ careers, increased learning and science education, inspiring others, funding and public perception, and the building of new tools.

The work has had broad impacts, including the coming together of like-minded scientists to share information and to continue the Science of Team Science’s productivity. There are several collections of information available to those studying team science and a toolkit on the Internet to offer myriad exercises to do at any stage of building or running a collaboratory. All this was made possible by federal funding over 30 years.
